title: UK charity shop profits plummet amid shift in secondhand clothes market
author: Harry Cockburn
text:
Oxfam describes ‘exceptionally challenging’ trading after retail profit reportedly fell 23% year on year

Profits at some of the UK’s best-known charity shops have plummeted as they face a number of pressures, including from online secondhand clothes platforms, prompting claims that a key part of the sector’s fundraising model could be under threat.

According to unpublished accounts seen by the Financial Times , Oxfam’s retail profit fell 23% to £4.9m in the last financial year, compared with £6.4m in the previous year.

The British Heart Foundation (BHF), which has the biggest high street presence of any charity in the country, has announced plans to close 150 stores after they made a loss in the last financial year. Cancer Research UK and Scope have also closed, or are closing, some of their shops.

But these losses come despite UK spending on secondhand clothing having quadrupled over the past decade, rising to £8.8bn a year, according to GlobalData.

The shift has come alongside the rise of websites such as Vinted and Depop, suggesting that people who might previously have donated clothes to charity shops are instead selling them directly to other consumers and profiting themselves.

Alongside this change, Chinese companies are selling more clothes in developing countries, particularly in Africa, which has long been a major market for unwanted secondhand clothing.

“It has been challenging … and it is going to be painful for the sector,” Lorna Fallon, the head of Oxfam’s retail operation, told the Financial Times.

Oxfam’s latest filings reveal that for every £100 people spend in its shops, just £6 now goes towards the charity’s work on alleviating global poverty. As recently as 2022, the figure was £22, the FT reports. However, the organisation’s focus on books and music means it has no plans to reduce its number of shops.

In June, BHF carried out a major review of its retail arm, which employs almost 3,700 staff, after profits from its shops plunged from £18.8m in 2024 to £3.6m in the year to 31 March 2025.

The charity cited “an exceptionally challenging trading environment”, and said it was aiming to close 90 stores by the end of March 2027 and another 60 by the following March.

The rapid change in fortunes for charity shops also highlights their limitations in the face of greater competition. Whereas Vinted and Depop directly connect sellers with buyers, charity shops remain at the mercy of high street and warehouse rents and other associated costs and inefficiencies, including collecting, sorting, pricing and storing clothes.

Another issue hampering high street charity shops is that the clothes being donated are increasingly substandard. Speaking to the Guardian earlier this month, Tansy Hoskins, the author of Charity Shop World, described the sector as dealing with “avalanches” of poor-quality clothes across the country, as people use charity shops as convenient dumping grounds for unwanted purchases.

“Quality is the big change marker – it’s gone through the floor. You’re just fighting against the waste,” Hoskins said.

Robin Osterley, the chief executive of the Charity Retail Association, said: “Fast fashion has had an impact on donations quality, there’s no question about that.”

But he added: “We don’t see Vinted or any of the other online platforms as an issue at all. It might be having a little bit of an effect – where people have one bag for charity shop donations and one for Vinted – but we believe these effects are significantly mitigated by two things.

“The first is that Vinted and other platforms are having a very positive effect on people’s attitudes towards secondhand shopping, and creating an environment where it’s much more normalised. A rising tide floats all ships.

“The second factor is that there are a lot of people who buy things from charity shops to sell on the online platforms. Our members get a significant income from them.”

Osterley instead suggested the November 2024 budget had had a much larger impact on bricks and mortar charity shops, in which national insurance increases and the lowering of the national insurance threshold – affecting more part-time staff – has had a “really significant” effect on the costs charity shops face, as well as inflationary pressures across the economy.

Richard Hawkes, Oxfam GB’s chief executive, said: “Whilst there is no getting away from the fact that the charity retail sector has been impacted by the cost-of-living crisis, like the rest of the high street, there is still much to be hopeful and positive about for the future.

“The growth of secondhand presents real opportunities for the whole sector, but it also means we need to think differently about the traditional charity retail model.

He added: “Our shops also offer much more than just an income. They give us a presence in communities where we might not otherwise be, while providing opportunities to engage with more than 20,000 volunteers. This wider role remains a vital part of what makes charity retail so valuable.”

title: Hirakawa replaces Ocon for Mexico City Grand Prix
text:
Esteban Ocon has been replaced at Haas by the team's Japanese reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa for the remainder of the Mexico City Grand Prix weekend.

Ocon, who is leaving the team at the end of the year, drove in Friday practice but the team released a statement on Saturday saying Hirakawa would drive instead of the Frenchman on Saturday and Sunday.

The team gave no further details about the reasons behind the decision, although a spokesperson at Haas said it was not because the Frenchman was ill.

The move comes after Ocon had a dispute with his race engineer Laura Mueller during second practice on Friday about tyre strategy.

Mueller told him over the radio that they were switching him to use the medium tyres on his race-simulation run because team-mate Oliver Bearman's run on the soft was "not great".

After Ocon asked for clarity, Mueller told him: "We have to do medium."

Ocon replied: "No, no. I wanted the soft. Don't do that to me. Come on."

Haas declined to comment on whether the decision to replace Ocon was related to the exchange and whatever aftermath it might have had.

Ocon is currently looking for a race seat for next year and it appears his chances are slim.

title: All the reasons the Ocon-Haas relationship fell apart
author: Ben Anderson
text:
Haas is staying tight-lipped, but its sudden decision to replace Esteban Ocon with Ryo Hirakawa at Formula 1's Mexican Grand Prix suggests its regular (and soon-to-be-former) driver has been benched.

In this piece, first published at the end of September when Ocon's end-of-2026 exit was announced, Ben Anderson and Scott Mitchell-Malm look at how the move turned sour.

Such comments inevitably lead to speculation over what is really behind the decision if not purely a choice based on driver performance.

As Ferrari-backed Rafa Camara is the favourite to replace Ocon, some sympathetic to Ocon's cause have inferred that Ferrari's support of its junior driver is shoving Ocon out the door.

There have also been some suggestions of Haas prioritising a commercial element. And Ocon has his own detractors too, those who believe he has simply not been good enough after being outscored by team-mate Ollie Bearman over the two years.

Haas had a contractual option to retain Ocon for next year and decided not to activate it quite a long time ago, subsequently notifying Ocon just after the summer break that he was unlikely to be kept on.

It has been a significant shift since Ocon being so highly coveted by Haas. When Ocon was signed, team boss Ayao Komatsu was faced with a lot of questions about whether it would work, though there could be no doubt about Ocon's pedigree coming in.

Not since 10-time podium finisher Romain Grosjean joined for the team's inaugural F1 season in 2016 as Haas employed such a successful driver.

He also arrived carrying the label of sometimes being a difficult driver to work with, who had clashed with team-mates multiple times, and joined after being dropped by Alpine before the final race of 2024 and replaced with Jack Doohan. And was known to disagree with his past teams over the extent of perceived car issues he said were holding him back.

It's also worth remembering that Mercedes ultimately decided Ocon wasn't quite good enough to warrant replacing Valtteri Bottas in the way George Russell ultimately did.

Komatsu was still willing to gamble. It just did not pay off as hoped.

Komatsu, who pushed hard to bring Ocon to the team, felt their previous relationship dating back to Komatsu's time as a senior engineer at what's now Alpine during its Lotus era, when Ocon was a member of the Lotus F1 junior team (pictured together in 2014 below) before Mercedes snapped him up, would help smooth things along and prevent any tensions that arose spilling over.

In one specific aspect this has been a success: Ocon and team-mate Bearman have maintained a good working relationship throughout Ocon's spell with the team, and even when there have been flashpoints, such as a collision at the 2025 British Grand Prix and another at Spa this year, those moments have been addressed internally and fostered no ill-will between the two drivers.

What Komatsu misjudged is how well it would work more broadly. He was fully aware that Ocon had some difficult moments, but put that down to Alpine handling him poorly as that team was going through frequent turmoil and upheaval during its transition from the Cyril Abiteboul regime Ocon began with, to the Flavio Briatore-led one that ousted him.

Haas had to work hard in the early part of 2025 to push past the mental baggage Ocon carried from how he felt he was mistreated during the final races of his Alpine stint, as that team coalesced around Pierre Gasly and edged Ocon toward the exit.

But the team began to notice a worrying pattern: when results didn't go Ocon's way he would become defensive and tensions in the garage would rise and Haas gradually felt there was ultimately a lack of accountability for his own issues.

This is not a problem unique to Ocon. Many drivers get trapped in a paranoid mindset and it's worth remembering the specific background to Ocon's racing career. He got to F1 against all financial odds, with absolutely no silver spoon in his mouth, overcoming adversity right from his earliest days in karting.

So he was probably always more likely than most to have a 'me against the world' mentality. When you have to fight your way into F1 in the first place, that combative streak can be a very powerful weapon - but it can also become all too easily ingrained.

As the defeats to Bearman piled up through the course of 2025, Ocon began repeating complaints publicly about his car, in particular the brakes. At the start of 2026 Haas made a concerted effort to get proper alignment between Ocon and all the staff working on his side of the garage.

But as the year has gone on and Haas has slowly realised it has deeper technical issues itself to deal with, tensions have risen again.

The team ultimately feels Ocon has been too combative internally when backs have been against the wall, as well as questioning car specifications or performance discrepancies, or wasting time on blind-alley set-up work.

This is likely to be a matter of perspective. Ocon almost certainly believes he is just being straightforward, doing the job of trying to push the team forward by being demanding, as was mapped out right from the start - and therefore Haas is simply now using the thing they said they wanted from him originally against him.

Why mini-revival hasn't saved him

Ocon has only occasionally shown the best of himself at Haas. Some excellent race results in his first year were overshadowed by a general qualifying struggle over the season and a particular, inconsistent problem pushing the car on the brakes in the final part of the year.

This year, he missed the small window to score big results when Haas was more competitive before its form declined in the midfield - a mix of his own misjudgement like in China and some genuine misfortune with safety car timings.

That has warped the points situation versus Bearman, who scored 17 of his 20 points in the first two races. Since then it's 7-3 in Ocon's favour. And he has been better than what some seem willing to credit him for.

Haas's decline and the onset of more car inconsistencies - this time on both sides of the garage - have prevented Ocon from doing anything standout to plead his case. This has to be considered a degree of mitigation for Ocon. Bearman said it makes it “really challenging” for the drivers because the behaviour can change completely from track to track.

Still, even a mini-revival hasn't changed Ocon's fate.

His general performances and attitude did improvesince Haas told him his F1 career with the team was hanging by a thread. And had Ocon performed at the level he's shown since the end of the summer break consistently over the majority of the past 18 months, Haas would view the situation very differently. Ocon would have a strong case for being retained.

Komatsu rates Ocon very highly when he's at his best, and also likes him as a person - feeling he is a genuinely nice guy when all is well and amicable. It's simply the case that Ocon's working relationship became strained and his time at Haas has been a cycle of short bursts of sustained improvement, followed by a regression to old bad habits.

Taking Baku as an example, where Ocon qualified 13th but beat Bearman to eighth in the race, Haas was left unimpressed by the way Ocon reacted to his Q2 exit in qualifying, failing to take responsibility for an error on his first run then reacting badly to a yellow flag interruption on his second run that Bearman - who also went out in Q2 in the same circumstances - handled much better, despite being the younger and less experienced driver.

Ocon also switched the running order of the cars without informing the team, seen as further evidence Ocon can sometimes act in his own interests rather than those of the team. Although by this time you could argue he knows he's on his way out - so why bother going the extra mile to keep Haas happy?

Ocon's Baku race performance reminds everyone of the calibre of driver Ocon is and what he can bring at his best. But it was not simply a case of too littletoo late, just generally too late.

Money factor is secondary

Other speculation has surrounded Haas's perceived financial uncertainty and claims that owner Gene Haas wants Camara because it will bring in necessary commercial backing.

The eponymous team owner's position is said to be far less involved than that, though. He will just rubber-stamp whatever Komatsu decides or have the final say if there's a close call. There is not an indication that Haas himself is ordering this move or has even guided its direction.

So, where might money have crept into it?

The Race understands that Komatsu told Ocon he was unlikely to be retained in 2027 after the summer break, although it was not a definitive ‘you're out'.

Haas felt that, on the balance of the results and performance levels Ocon had delivered so far, it couldn't justify paying him what is understood to be a multi-million dollar salary.

It's fair to wonder how much of this is purely driven by Ocon failing to justify the money Haas is paying him, and how much is down to the commercial reality of Haas operating below the cost cap and generally being underfunded.

And it's possible that Ocon took this as the team not being willing to pay for a driver of his track record, hence his remarks about there being elements at play behind the scenes that are “out of my control”.

Money was at least a secondary factor in who should replace him. Komatsu has admitted that if two drivers were of equal perceived performance then “affiliations or the packages they've got matters”.

There is an understanding that Camara's arrival will come with commercial benefits from South America that Ocon himself cannot match. That's undeniably to Haas's benefit that Camara comes with a big commercial benefit - from his personal Brazilian backers, rather than Ferrari - but the package he offers is not thought to be at the scale Haas title sponsor Toyota could bring to get current test driver Ryo Hirakawa that seat, for example.

If Haas was purely prioritising money/marketing reasons over competitive considerations, Hirakawa would be the obvious choice here.

But it was agreed he would only get the nod if he was also fastest in the shootout. He wasn't. Toyota knows this and has accepted it.

The prospect of Camara lining up alongside Bearman - long considered a future Ferrari driver and a long-time protege - has caused some to draw unfair comparisons to Red Bull controlling two teams' driver line-ups in F1.

Haas is not a Ferrari-controlled vehicle for it to just test junior drivers. The affiliation affords access and makes it a lot more convenient, so it greases the wheels certainly. But there is no prerequisite and nothing Ferrari can do to force Haas to take a driver it does not want.

In that sense, Haas likely having an all-Ferrari pairing has been described to The Race as more of a ‘coincidence' than anything else.

Ocon was never going to be retained over Bearman, considering Bearman's Ferrari support, age, and higher potential, as well as his Max Verstappen-esque tolerance for rear instability in the car.

So, with Bearman set to stay, Ocon had to ward off these external threats to earn his own seat. As these alternatives pressed their case during various Testing Of Previous Cars evaluations, so Haas realised: why pay Ocon for a job they felt, over a season, someone else could do - and potentially do better - without the baggage and hassle following the incumbent driver around?

The emergence of Camara sealed the deal. Haas tested him at Portimao and was blown away by Camara's immense one-lap pace - so strong that, on the day, even Bearman couldn't match him with the reference work he did.…

title: A world-first focus on long-term outcomes could transform UK government – or create new spending fights
author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
text:
Tucked away in John Healey’s budget is decision to ringfence preventative projects where future savings outweigh initial cost

It merited the briefest of mentions in John Healey’s speech and just one paragraph in the 166-page budget document , but some believe it could revolutionise not just public spending but the very process of government itself: a new focus on long-term outcomes.

The idea in the broad sense is very simple. Any spending deemed to be “preventative” – that is, the initial outlay will be more than made up for by future savings – will from now on be ringfenced, meaning it cannot be raided for more immediate needs.

This might sound uncontroversial, but it follows many years of long-term spending being pillaged to plug day-to-day gaps, particularly so during and after the austerity measures of the 2010 coalition government, which slashed numerous prevention-based services, not least the Sure Start programme for families with young children.

But now, starting from the upcoming spending review, which kicks off next year, projects that can be shown to bring down costs in the future will be protected via a new piece of jargon – a preventative departmental expenditure limit, or PDEL.

“It could end up being quite a major change in how the government runs spending reviews, and the entire spending framework,” said Stuart Hoddinott, at the Institute for Government thinktank, which had called for such a system to be implemented. Officials in the Treasury agree, with one calling it an “important reform”.

That is, however, about as straightforward as it gets. The budget document uses Andy Burnham’s new spending to prevent rough sleeping as an example of the sort of thing that would qualify. A few other areas would seem likely: for example, public health programmes to prevent future illness, and Sure Start-type early years schemes.

But beyond that, no one really knows what might or might not qualify for PDEL status. Departments say they are waiting for Treasury guidance, which has not yet been drawn up. “A lot depends on the definition,” Hoddinott said. “While it sounds simple, it becomes quite difficult when you think about how it will work in practice, as you could make any argument that almost all types of spending are preventative.”

Government officials agree, with one making the point that, in theory, the Ministry of Defence could argue all its spending is preventive, given the very obvious costs to the country of fighting a war, let alone losing one.

There is therefore the potential for a new variant of the endless spending-review tussles between departments and the Treasury, as ministers try to protect their pet projects from future plunder.

But what is perhaps just as important is the symbolism. Some other governments around the world protect specific preventative budgets – public health, for example – but this is believed to be the first time one has introduced this as a blanket policy.

Government officials are billing the decision as part of a wider focus under Burnham to try to deal with knotty and neglected issues that have longer-term costs and repercussions, including rough sleeping and adult social care.

One said: “Too often government departments have ended up raiding these types of budgets to fund short-term measures. This is an attempt to combat that as part of a wider push to transform the way the state operates.”

Those whose work revolves around trying to generate long-term benefits to the public are cautiously delighted.

“This does feel like a really good thing,” said Greg Fell, Sheffield city council’s director of public health and the president of the Association of Directors of Public Health.

“There are a lot of questions about how it will work. Is it about preventing future acute demand, or creating the conditions for communities to thrive? Those are different things and they require a different mindset and way of operating. And with some spending, it might take decades to realise the benefits.

“But as a country we have never been very good at this sort of thing, so it’s up to all of us to make sure it works.”

title: Maurene Comey ruling offers hope of check on Trump’s assault on rule of law
author: Victoria Bekiempis in New York
text:
Legal experts welcome judge’s rejection of firing of James Comey’s daughter prosecutor but warn an appeal is likely

A recent legal ruling against an effort to fire the star-prosecutor daughter of a former FBI chief targeted by Donald Trump could send a strong message about politicized firings – and influence other judges weighing similar cases, legal veterans said.

Judge Jesse Furman ruled this week that the Department of Justice’s firing of assistant US attorney Maurene Comey without cause was unlawful. Comey, the daughter of former FBI director James Comey, successfully litigated numerous high-profile cases during her tenure at the southern district of New York, including guilty verdicts against Ghislaine Maxwell and Sean “Diddy” Combs.

“It looks as if Judge Furman has completely vindicated her and rejected just about all of the arguments made by the government,” said Carl Tobias, Williams chair at the University of Richmond School of Law. “And so it’s really important to have this because of the way she was essentially summarily fired, and so it sets a valuable precedent.”

The Department of Justice, which fired her without cause, had argued thatarticle II of the US constitution, which defines presidential power, imbued Trump and his attorney general with a right to fire line prosecutors – who are not political appointees.

But Furman this week rejected the department’s position, ruling Comey’s firing was not greenlighted under any law and in fact, violated the Civil Service Reform Act.

The justice department’s claim “flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent”, Furman said. “It is also without merit. Indeed, to accept Defendants’ argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation’s constitutional system.”

For legal observers, Furman’s decision is cause for optimism – even if optimism of the cautious sort – amid the Trump administration’s alleged repeated attacks on the rule of law. While one judicial opinion does not a panacea make, they said, such a ruling can send a strong message and be considered by other judges weighing similar cases.

“One thing I would caution is that it’s very clear the government will appeal this,” Tobias said. The justice department would do this via the second circuit court of appeals.

“I expect that Furman would be affirmed by that court, and then I assume the administration would then appeal to the US supreme court,” he added.

Then, it would up to the US supreme court to decide whether they even want to hear the case – and if they decline, the lower appeals court decision would stand.

“You are seeing the courts step up and stop and prevent the administration when they are violating the rule of law,” said Neama Rahmani, founder of West Coast Trial Lawyers and a former federal prosecutor. Just this Monday, Los Angeles federal court judge David Carter rejected Trump’s attempt to set aside 20,000 ballots in California, Rahmani noted.

“Whether it’s the supreme court and birthright citizenship, or even individual cases like this, there have been limited, I would say, rulings by the court that have limited what President Trump can do.”

Like Tobias, Rahmani said the justice department can fight federal district and appeals court decisions. And, this kind of case does contain legal issues that might pique the supreme court’s interest – especially if different federal appeals courts were to reach different conclusions.

If the supreme court did decide to hear arguments on Comey’s case, it would by no means guarantee a check on Trump’s power.

“There are a lot of the justices on the supreme court that really don’t believe there should be much of any restrictions on what the president can do,” Rahmani said. “So this is far from the silver bullet.”

For now, though, Furman’s decision can prove influential.

“The decision can be used by other folks who do believe that they were terminated lawfully,” Rahmani said, adding, “It is not binding at all, but it’s certainly something that judges look to with similar or exact same facts.”

Elizabeth Wolstein, a partner at Schlam Stone & Dolan LLP and former Manhattan federal prosecutor in the civil division, said that a judge’s decision in one case could potentially affect how other judges’ weigh similar issues.

“It doesn’t have any binding effect on another judge, even in the same district, as opposed to how a second circuit or US supreme court case would be binding,” Wolstein said. But, “if it’s well reasoned and persuasive, it is definitely going to be persuasive to another judge faced with a similar issue.”

Comey filed suit over her ouster in September 2025. Comey said she neither received notice nor explanation of her firing. Instead, Comey on 16 July 2025 got a letter that stated “your employment with the Department of Justice is hereby terminated, and you are removed from federal service effective immediately.”

When Comey asked the then Manhattan US attorney, Jay Clayton, about this notice, he allegedly said “all I can say is it came from Washington. I can’t tell you anything else,” per court papers.

The Department of Justice has said Comey’s firing was directed by the former US attorney general Pam Bondi and subsequently “ratified” by her successor, Todd Blanche.

Comey’s lawyers and critics of the US president have claimed that she was fired because her father is longtime Trump foe James Comey. Trump’s justice department has repeatedly tried prosecuting James Comey, this week making public its third case against him; one prior proceeding was dismissed, another is pending.

The department had defended the idea that someone’s familial relations could be considered in termination proceedings.

Maurene Comey’s legal team viewed Furman’s ruling as a positive development in protecting the rule of law. Comey’s attorneys are Ellen Blain, Nicole Gueron and Deepa Vanamali at Clarick Gueron Reisbaum, as well as Margaret Donovan at Koskoff Koskoff & Bieder.…

title: Ads accusing Republican candidates of protecting Epstein fill airwaves in final midterm push
author: Ariana Baio
text:
But select Democrats, too, are being accused of having ties to the late sex offender as country prepares to vote

In races across the country, Democratic candidates or groups that support them have released ads accusing Republicans of protecting pedophiles by voting against legislation to release files related to Jeffrey Epstein .

The ads appear intended to evoke an emotional response by accusing candidates of “protecting” Epstein, a notorious pedophile accused of running a sex-trafficking ring involving minors.

An analysis from CNN found that candidates and outside groups have spent more than $35m on Epstein-related ads. Another from the Washington Post found that Democrats spent more than $40m on Epstein-related ads across six key Senate races.

In Colorado, ads targeting Republican Jeff Crank note that the lawmaker voted against releasing the Epstein files. In one , the family members of Virginia Giuffre, a woman who survived abuse at the hands of Epstein and died by suicide last year, claim Crank “covered up Epstein’s crimes to protect Donald Trump”.

Ashley Hinson, a Senate candidate in Iowa, was accused of voting to “protect her donors” by refusing to vote to release the Epstein files.

“This week I had to explain to my boys, ‘No, Mom does not protect pedophiles,’” Hinson said in a campaign ad responding to attacks over the Epstein files.

An ad targeting Mike Collins , the Republican running for a Georgia Senate seat, says “Mike Collins voted against releasing the Epstein files even after he knew Epstein’s sex-trafficking operation exploited 14-year-old girls for sex”.

Florida Republican Jimmy Patronis faced an attack from his Democratic opponent, claiming he called investigating Epstein “a waste of his time”.

A spokesperson for Crank’s campaign accused the Epstein-related ad of being “intentionally vague”, in a statement to the Washington Post, because his position was that he would vote against the file’s release until he could be confident that victim information was properly redacted. The campaign also said it was “unfortunate” that his opponent, Jessica Killin, was “preying on a grieving family with the help of the Washington Democrats”.

Crank’s staff invited and met with Giuffre’s family, though Crank himself did not meet with them in person, the New York Times reported. Crank’s campaign also said it offered to meet with Epstein victims before the vote on the legislation.

Last year, Democrats and a select few House Republicans tried to force a vote on the Epstein files through a discharge petition – a procedure used in Congress to bypass the traditional steps of legislation and force a vote on the House floor.

Donald Trump, who knew Epstein in the 1990s and early 2000s, opposed the discharge petition for the files, reversing his campaign promise to increase government transparency. House Republicans largely aligned themselves with him, prompting anger from high-profile Trump voters.

Eventually, under pressure from allies, Trump supported the legislation, giving Republican lawmakers the go-ahead to vote for it. All but one House Republican voted for the Epstein Files Transparency Act.

Many of the ads omit the fact that nearly every House Republican voted to release the Epstein files when the Epstein Files Transparency Act came to the floor, although at that point Trump had agreed to sign the legislation and release the files. Instead, the ads refer to Republicans opposing early attempts to force the legislation to the floor.

Republicans have pointed to this fact when disputing the attack ads.

“Of course I voted to release the Epstein files,” Hinson said in a direct-to-camera ad, accusing her opponent, Josh Turek, of lying. While Hinson voted for the final Epstein Files Transparency Act, she did not sign on to the discharge petition.

Patronis, meanwhile, never called the investigation a “waste of time”, but told a local radio station that while he had “no problem getting everything all released”, the issue was a “massive energy and time suck at the end of the day”.

Melissa Stone, a spokesperson for Patronis’s campaign, highlighted his work with Trump to obtain disaster funding after Hurricane Isaias and said his opponent, Gay Valimont, was “still talking about a dead pedophile in a sad web video than helping the people of [the first congressional district] recover.”

Some Republicans and groups supporting the GOP have sought to flip the script, accusing Democrats of taking money from donors who had ties to Epstein.

During a Georgia Senate debate, Collins accused his opponent, Jon Ossoff, of accepting campaign donations from Reid Hoffman, a tech billionaire who had ties to Epstein. Hoffman has said he only knew Epstein through fundraising relationships and regrets it.

“You can claim to fight against the Epstein class, but I’m going to tell you, this call is coming from inside the house and the Epstein class is on stage right now and it’s you,” Collins said .

In New Mexico’s gubernatorial race, an outside group released an ad accusing Democratic candidate Deb Haaland of accepting a ride on Epstein’s private jet and taking “tens of thousands of dollars from Epstein businesses” and then “asking for more”.

Haaland did not fly on Epstein’s jet, but did take a flight booked by one of Epstein’s companies in 2014. Haaland has said she was unaware the chartered flight was owned by an Epstein-owned company.

title: Vic Mensa can’t live without the Voice Memos app
author: Terrence O’Brien
text:
Between his music, acting, podcast, activism, and businesses, Vic Mensa wears a lot of hats.

Between his music, acting, podcast, activism, and businesses, Vic Mensa wears a lot of hats.

Vic Mensa is one of those people who has done so many things that it’s hard to remember where you were first introduced to him. Was it his debut mixtape Innanetape , which finally hit the major streaming services for the first time in September? Or maybe his house-influenced single “ Down On My Luck ”? Maybe you didn’t even realize that Mensa was a rapper. Maybe you know him from his roles on The Chi or Bel-Air . Or perhaps you’re mostly aware of him through his activism, social media presence ( peeling oranges and waxing poetic ), or his podcast The Vic Mensa Show .

Point is, the man wears many hats. Part of the secret to being so prolific, it turns out, is Voice Memos. Just capture those ideas before they disappear.

Voice Memos. Everything starts there for me. Songs, essay ideas, orange tree thoughts, voice notes to myself at some wild hour, little things my son says that I do not want to lose. My phone is a million distractions in one rectangle, but Voice Memos is one of the few parts of it that still feels honest. Just press record before the thought disappears.

Which social media platform do you use the most?

Instagram, for better or worse. That’s definitely where my voice has really found its legs. I started out peeling an orange and talking through whatever was on my mind, and it turned into this whole conversation with people about politics, history, music, grief, jokes, fatherhood, all of it. That response helped show me there was room for The Vic Mensa Show too. Instagram can be a circus, obviously, but it’s also a very valuable tool for connection.

Which tech trend do you wish would go away?

Maybe Meta glasses . Them motherfuckers seem like they’re being used for evil.

Probably my upcoming album right now. It’s the first album that I’ve really taken myself completely seriously as a producer. The surrounding art, videos, design, clothing, and world I’m building around it is something that really excites me as well.

I either do my Shambhavi Mahamudra meditation that I learned from Sadhguru or the Wim Hof breathing method. Ideally, I’ll do the Wim Hof breathing method in the steam room and then the meditation.

What do you think is worth splurging on?

Anything that touches your life every day. A good mattress. Good headphones. Quality food. Clothes you will actually keep for years. Experiences with your child. I have wasted money on plenty of dumb shit, so I am trying to be better about buying things that either last or make a real memory.

title: Ocon suddenly replaced at Haas for rest of Mexico F1 weekend
author: Josh Suttill
text:
Esteban Ocon will sit out the rest of Formula 1's Mexican Grand Prix with Haas reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa replacing him.

Haas unexpectedly released a short statement on Saturday morning announcing the switch.

"TGR Haas F1 team reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa will replace Esteban Ocon for the remainder of the weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix," the statement read.

"Hirakawa, a two-time winner of the FIA World Endurance Championship and 24 Hours of Le Mans Winner with Toyota Gazoo Racing, participated in FP1 at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on Friday 30 October - his third free practice outing of the season driving the VF-26, finishing 15th overall.

"The Japanese driver will partner team-mate Ollie Bearman through final practice and qualifying on Saturday and Sunday's 71-lap grand prix - Hirakawa's Formula 1 race debut.

"No further statements will be made at this time."

No reason has been given for the change but Haas has confirmed it is not due to illness for Ocon.

It is logical therefore to reason that he appears to have been benched.

Ocon had a frustrating Friday in Mexico, publicly expressing his dissatisfaction with his runplan in FP2 - his only session in the car, after 32-year-old Hirakawa drove in FP1 to satisfy the rookie practice rule.

His time was not bad - after getting the car back off Hirakawa for FP2, Ocon beat team-mate Ollie Bearman to end up a respectable 13th - but there was friction on the radio with his engineer Laura Mueller.

: We've swapped the high fuel run to medium because Ollie's [tyre] appearance is not great.: Still doing soft, right?: No, we have to do medium.: No, no, I wanted the soft, like, don't do that to me. Come on.

Ocon was visibly dissatisfied in the paddock after the session, keeping his helmet on as he returned to Haas's hospitality unit.

Camara beat the likes of Toyota-backed driver Hirakawa to secure the seat.

Two-time WEC champion Hirakawa has completed multiple F1 practice outings for McLaren, Alpine and Haas since the end of 2024, with a long-stated aim of racing in F1.

The team is making no comment on its driver line-up for the next race in Brazil, in keeping with its statement.

title: Manchester United crisis deepens with Chelsea defeat and Martínez red card
author: Jacob Steinberg at Stamford Bridge
text:
Get ready for another week of agonising over the sorry state of Manchester United . The legends of old will rage, clips of a fuming Gary Neville will fly around social media, the airwaves will reverberate with complaints from angry supporters and by the time United play again there is every chance a new manager will be in the dugout.

There were echoes of Erik ten Hag’s final game in charge as the walls closed in on Michael Carrick at Stamford Bridge. United missed a series of golden chances when the scores were level, just as they did when Ten Hag lost to West Ham a day before his sacking two years ago, and Chelsea made the most of the reprieve after initially delivering a performance so bad it had you worrying for the nascent Xabi Alonso project.

Chelsea could not have been worse during the first half. It helped that their opponents were in a giving mood. United had opportunities to make their decision to give Carrick a stay of execution look like a wise move rather than the consequence of executive level confusion, but their finishing was awful and their defending even worse. They watched as Morgan Rogers breezed through to make it 1-0 early in the second half and their seventh defeat in 13 games was sealed when Lisandro Martínez earned a red card for giving away the penalty that allowed Cole Palmer to push Chelsea into fourth place.

It symbolised United’s decline under the Glazer family and Sir Jim Ratcliffe. Martínez has had a lot to say recently , but the Argentinian should have been sold long ago. That he is yet to go sums up United’s shoddy recruitment. They are carrying so much deadwood and it is hard to see their problems being fixed by a change of manager. Carrick is merely one of many issues. He will probably have gone by the time United face Roma on Tuesday and whoever takes over will inherit a team sleepwalking into a relegation battle.

This is not a happy ship. The ending was similar to last week’s defeat to Bournemouth . Carrick was applauded when he walked over at full-time. They sang his name and booed when the United players made a sheepish trudge to the away end at full time.

The spotlight was also on Alonso, defeats to Tottenham in the league and Liverpool in the Carabao Cup sparking criticism over team selections, and he lifted his side by handing Estêvão Willian his first start in the league this season.

Overlooked at Anfield, Estêvão was dangerous on the right flank after Alonso adjusted without the injured João Pedro up front. Pedro Neto rather than Danny Welbeck led the line in a 4-2-3-1 system but it was United who threatened first. Diogo Dalot combined with Mateus Cunha on the left and Andrey Santos, who left Chelsea for United last summer, swept a shot just wide from 20 yards.

Both sides brought vulnerabilities to the table. Chelsea had a long list of absentees – illness ruled Jordan Henderson out in midfield – and their defence wobbled without Maxence Lacroix. United, though not exactly secure whenever Chelsea punched through on the counterattack, felt optimistic at first.

The visitors had an escape when Senne Lammens spilled a Neto shot and an offside Estêvão tapped home but Carrick was the happier manager during the first half. Fernandes, back after clear the air talks with Carrick, shimmered in a floating role from the left. Bryan Mbeumo and Cunha were lively, although the worry for United was making their dominance count.

Fernandes was wasteful at the end of a flowing counterattack, firing over from Mbeumo’s pass. Amad Diallo, dangerous against Marco Palestra, cut inside to fire two efforts on target and Chelsea, enjoying neither possession nor control against Santos and Carlos Baleba, were forced into emergency mode.

Levi Colwill intervened when Cunha broke through and Wesley Fofana took flak from the home fans after a couple of trademark brain farts. Mbeumo and Diallo missed after mistakes by the Frenchman, though it is worth stressing that a dismal half from Chelsea was a team effort. They were lucky when Cunha had what would have been the opening goal disallowed by the video assistant referee (VAR) for offside.

The away end ran through the anti-board chants – urging the Glazers to sell up and questioning Jason Wilcox’s credentials as technical director – and United feared being punished for their profligacy. There were a couple of flashes from Chelsea; Moisés Caicedo diverted a Fofana header against the woodwork and Neto shot wide after a stumble from Harry Maguire.

Chelsea were more assertive at the start of the second half and it was easy to predict United’s unravelling. They were punished when Mbeumo turned into trouble in midfield. Caicedo blocked his path, Roméo Lavia nicked the ball past Baleba and Rogers took over. Facing no resistance, the £117m man’s saunter through the middle placed United’s failure to strengthen in defence into sharp focus.

It was a bit like a goal you see at the end of a casual five-a-side between a group of dads playing for the first time since 2019. Maguire barely lifted a leg, Martínez gawped and Rogers dinked over Lammens for 1-0.

The challenge for United was to dig deep, to stand tall. Good luck with that. Lavia was running the midfield for Chelsea now.

There was a sense of the players in red giving up when Martínez elbowed Fofana at a corner. The Argentinian was already on a booking and he was off when Peter Bankes reviewed the incident, leaving Palmer to put United’s 10 men to bed by making it 2-0 from the spot.

title: Rogers shines, 3/10 for sent-off Martinez - player ratings for Chelsea v Man Utd
text:
Morgan Rogers and Cole Palmer scored second-half goals as Chelsea secured a 2-0 home win over 10-man Manchester United , who endured another desperate day.

Chelsea 's record £117m signing Rogers opened the scoring in the 50th minute before United defender Lisandro Martinez was sent off after conceding a penalty, which Palmer converted.

Here's how BBC Sport's reporters at Stamford Bridge rated the players and your verdicts on the performances.

Chelsea beat 10-man Man Utd to heap further pressure on Carrick

What do BBC Sport's player ratings mean?

Mike Penders: The Belgian goalkeeper remains under pressure after his mistake against Tottenham last week, but he was steady here and made several comfortable saves. 7

Josh Acheampong : The young defender looked shaky early on but recovered well, making a fantastic block from a Bruno Fernandes volley and improving as the game went on. 6

Wesley Fofana : The Frenchman made a brilliant block from one of Amad Diallo's shots but was twice at fault as the winger broke clear on the counter-attack. His header also struck the post after taking a deflection off Moises Caicedo in a chaotic display. Fofana also won the second-half penalty. 5

Levi Colwill : The England defender was part of an overall poor defensive display but did not make any obvious errors himself. 6

Marco Palestra : The Italian made some good recovery runs on his first start for Chelsea but was also part of a below-par defensive display from an organisational perspective. 7

Moises Caicedo : Influential presence in a scrappy midfield battle, helping Chelsea compete physically in the centre of the pitch. 6

Romeo Lavia : Often the player who helped Chelsea play through United's pressure, sparking several counter-attacks with intelligent passing. Won the ball for Chelsea 's opener. 7

Pedro Neto : Arguably Chelsea 's most dangerous attacker but finishing let him down, with one effort saved and another fired well wide in the first half. 6

Cole Palmer : A quiet game by his standards and unconvincingly scored a second-half penalty. Aside from that, he attempted an ambitious effort from inside his own half and gifted United one of their major chances. 6

Estevao Willian : Lost possession with his first touch but recovered impressively. Looked lively throughout, having a couple of dangerous-looking shots on goal and two that he scored but were ruled out for offside. His set-pieces were also of consistent high quality. 8

Morgan Rogers : A surprisingly anonymous start and struggled in the number nine position until he was given the chance to run at United's defence, scoring with a sublime dink in the 50th minute. 8

Pep Chavarria (on 71, Palestra): Game was already won when he entered. 6

Senne Lammens: Alive to Palmer's attempt to catch him out with a quickly taken free-kick. Was lucky to get away with a poor save early on, thanks to offside flag. Solid after that. No chance with Rogers goal. 7

Leny Yoro: Speed essential to deal with Chelsea counter-attacks but sometimes ran out of position. 7

Harry Maguire: Authoritative presence at heart of defence for most part but yet again unable to stop gap opening up for Rogers to score. 7

Lisandro Martinez: Did OK and looked good - until Chelsea scored. Then gave penalty away and red-carded for ridiculous moment of recklessness. 3

Diogo Dalot: Played out of position again at left-back and Estevao threatened down his side, but Dalot stuck to his task gamely. 6

Andrey Santos: So close to a memorable goal against his old club. Crucial intervention to deny Moises Caicedo a clear sight at goal at the other end. Difficult second half. 5

Carlos Baleba: Was having his best game in a United shirt so far and tried to prod the visitors forward. But impetuous tackle in midfield proved extremely costly as Rogers ran through to score. 5

Amad Diallo: Looked sharp. Tested Mike Penders from long range and also at his near post. Fofana blocked another goal-bound effort. Should have scored before half-time. 7

Bruno Fernandes: Returned as captain and should have put the visitors ahead when Mbeumo picked him out. Nearly set up Mbeumo. Better but not brilliant. 6

Matheus Cunha: Most impact of any recent game. Linked well with the visitors' attack but didn't threaten a goal. 6

Bryan Mbeumo: Set up a chance for Fernandes, then nearly reached a far-post cross from his captain. Gave Chelsea a problem but couldn't get last bit right. 6

Kobbie Mainoo (on 58, Baleba): Not on long enough to make an impact before Martinez red. After that it was damage limitation. 6

Ayden Heaven (on 66, Andrey Santos): Time for a regular start? 5

title: What has haunted the Yankees in the 2020s?
author: John Griffin
text:
Ah, Halloween. On this glorious intersection of Allhallowtide and capitalist consumerism run rampant, we herald in the year’s final days by celebrating all things spooky, as we let ghouls, goblins, and children dressed up in overpriced costumes run wild in one last day and night of outdoor tomfoolery before the cold darkness of a lockout-lengthened winter sets in.

In the spirit of this haunting-filled day, let’s look back at the last few years. While, perhaps understandably, we tend to focus on the Yankees’ recent history, many of the decisions made over the last couple of years have been influenced by actions — or the lack of action — taken by the team as long ago as a decade. Which moves have haunted the Bronx the most in recent years? Let’s take a trip down memory lane.

To some extent, everything comes back to the 2018-19 offseason, when Manny Machado and Bryce Harper were free agents. Following a year in which the Yankees won 100 games but were absolutely shellacked by the eventual champion Red Sox team. That Bombers team had an aging Brett Gardner in left, Didi Gregorius out for months due to a torn UCL, and a ton of uncertainty in the infield — Luke Voit’s breakout was fun, but there’s always reason to be wary of an age-27 breakout at first base; meanwhile, a young Gleyber Torres and Miguel Andujar had finished second and third in the AL Rookie of the Year voting, but there was reason to skeptical of Andujar’s performance at the plate and his ability to stick at third long-term. In short: the Yankees were good, but not so good that they couldn’t benefit from adding a superstar in his age-26 season, and lo and behold, not only were there two of them out there on the market, both were interested in donning the pinstripes — and Harper was supposedly even willing to learn first base to do it.

So naturally, the Yankees prioritized getting under the luxury tax, and well, since then, they’ve had problem after problem that could’ve been solved by literally having paid one of these two guys — especially Machado. Concerns about Andujar turned out to be warranted, and then he tore his labrum. It’s only now as a part-time player over the past two years that he’s finally been able to carve out a role for himself. Gio Urshela was really good replacing him during the #NextManUp campaign, and followed that up with a solid 2020, but soon regressed into the journeyman utility player he had been. The Josh Donaldson experience? A disaster. DJ LeMahieu? The first contract worked, but he soon became always injured. Oswaldo Cabrera? Although a fun player, never more than a fill-in. Jazz Chisholm Jr.? A second baseman out of position. Ryan McMahon? Somehow a brief improvement before an ugly 2026. Sure, Machado’s contract is now a bit of an albatross, as he’s owed $39 million through 2033, but that’s the result of the extension the Padres signed him to, not the original deal.

The biggest excuse given for not seriously pursuing Harper in 2018 was that he was an outfielder, and the Yankees had plenty of depth there. Well, Father Time came for Gardner, injuries caught up to Giancarlo Stanton and Clint Frazier, and Aaron Hicks experienced a severe and sudden decline. Since 2019, the Yankees have traded for Joey Gallo, Harrison Bader, Alex Verdugo, Juan Soto, Trent Grisham, Cody Bellinger, and Heliot Ramos in order to fix their outfield — and that doesn’t include the small army of players acquired simply to get injuries, such as Mike Tauchman and Jake Bauers, or the multiple prospects who have failed to stick. The team sure could’ve used Harper in any of those stretches … oh, and as it turns out, he’s a decent enough first baseman, too — yet another position that has been a bit of a revolving door.

Sure, the Yankees may currently be fine at the first base/DH spot and have their corner outfield set, but let’s be real, each of the last few seasons has ended with Hal Steinbrenner on the podium saying the team needs to be more consistent at the plate, and either one of these two would have gone a long way towards remedying that problem.

In the days following the 2014 season, the main question surrounding the Yankees was, “How are they going to replace the legendary Derek Jeter?” The solution, as it turned out, was rather easy: Didi Gregorius, a young shortstop acquired from the Arizona Diamondback as part of a three-way deal in exchange for Shane Greene. While it wasn’t quite as seamless as the DiMaggio-to-Mantle transition in the 1950s, Sir Didi went on to become a fan favorite — and, at least during the juiced ball era, a veritable middle-of-the-order bat.

Unfortunately, once Gregorius’s years of team control ran out after the 2019 season, the Yankees embarked on a years-long merry-go-round trying to replace him. First, the team turned to former top prospect Gleyber Torres, who had performed admirably filling in at shortstop when Gregorius was injured but was clearly most comfortable at the keystone — something that was clear to anybody with eyes after the 2020 season; the team then had to keep him at short after re-signing LeMahieu instead of making a harder push for Francisco Lindor. When that, rather predictably, failed, the team had to use Urshela and the anonymous Andrew Velazquez there down the stretch in 2021.

Rather than trying to sign Carlos Correa to the pillow contract he ended up getting from the Twins or making a play for future Rangers World Series MVP Corey Seager, the Yankees then swung a deal for Isiah Kiner-Falefa (not a bad player, miscast as a starting shortstop on a contender). When that went bust, they then handed the keys over to another top prospect who profiled more as a second baseman while in the minors, Anthony Volpe. The 22-year-old beat out fellow acclaimed up-and-comer Oswald Peraza, but neither were truly up for the job. Despite some stretches of time in which he looked to be taking the next step offensively — and a Gold Glove in what was admittedly a down year for AL shortstops — that ended as well as the Torres experiment. In the meantime, they opted not to pursue a shortstop in free agency, leaving them with no other options.

Will George Lombard Jr. help get the Yankees out of their post-Gregorius cycle, and finally allow this ghost to reset? I’m hopeful, but it remains to be seen.

The Devin Williams Conundrum

Once the Yankees signed Max Fried during the 2024-25 offseason, the rotation seemed to be a bit overflowing with arms, especially lefties. As such, the team decided to package Nestor Cortes with Caleb Durbin, a relatively minor infield prospect whose stock had risen during the 2024 season, and sent them both to the Brewers in exchange for arguably the best closer in baseball, Devin Williams. It was a move that, at the time, made sense: Clay Holmes was departing in free agency, the team needed another bullpen arm, and at the time, Nasty Nestor was behind Fried, Gerrit Cole, Carlos Rodón, Luis Gil, and Clarke Schmidt in the rotation pecking order.

This move, though, has already had major consequences — and will continue to do so, for the foreseeable future. First, the injury bug hit the Yankees rotation hard in 2025: Cole missed the full season with a torn UCL, Schmidt was gone for the latter half, and Gil made just 11 starts. The team was forced to rely on Marcus Stroman, who they had tried to dump that winter, and Ryan Yarbrough, who was signed as a bullpen arm, for 17 starts (oh, and both of them also hit the shelf). If it wasn’t for Cam Schlittler’s breakout and the trio of Fried, Rodón, and a rookie Will Warren making 33 starts apiece, the season would’ve been a disaster; and while Cortes himself spent much of the year injured, the psychological part of trading away what would have been sorely-needed depth stung.

To make matters worse, Durbin has developed into a solid third baseman with a league average bat, who finished top-three in the NL Rookie of the Year vote in 2025 before getting shipped to the Red Sox over the winter. Although he’s no superstar, his 4.4 rWAR/2.8 fWAR would have been miles better than the replacement-level play the Yankees got at the hot corner this season.

Had Williams been a dominant closer, this would have been an OK pill to swallow. Except … he was easily the second-worst closer the Yankees have had in recent years, and probably the worst when you factor in only the performance on the field.

The list of baseball-related things my Boston friends and I agree on is very short. Johnny Damon was fun to watch. The Mookie Betts trade was a disgrace. Aroldis Chapman sucks.

Yea, that’s pretty much it. From a purely baseball perspective, the decision to trade for Chapman was great — the prospects the Yankees sent over didn’t really amount to anything. The decision to trade him to the Cubs was even better, as it introduced Gleyber to the Bronx and brought Adam Warren back where he belonged. The decision to sign him again that winter was…defensible, even if I didn’t exactly love the idea of spending big money on a reliever during what I expected to be a down year (remember, expectations heading into 2017 were ). So why does this move haunt the Yankees? Well, because I absolutely despise the fact that he ever donned the pinstripes, and hate the fact that, if I ever need to look up his stats on Baseball Reference after he retires, there’s a solid chance the site will use a picture of him in a Yankee uniform as his profile picture since his seven seasons in the Bronx represents—and will likely forever represent—his longest tenure with any one team.

You’ll hear boos from more than just ghosts if you ever play that clip in the Bronx.

title: What F1 teams have done to tackle Mexico's altitude challenge
author: Gary Anderson
text:
The Mexico City track is one of the outliers of the Formula 1 season, mainly because of the altitude: it is 2240 meters above sea level, which equates to roughly 25% less dense air, so it makes everything just that bit more difficult.

For the drivers it's basically harder work, but for the cars it's a very different story, because at that altitude the cars will produce less downforce and with that less drag. In the past, teams would use more or less Monaco-specification wings but this season with the change in wing regulations and active aero they don't have that possibility.

So, basically the ars will slide around more but the reduced drag means that top speeds are even faster than normal. This means that you will arrive at the end of those long straights faster and require a longer braking duration, which generates more heat in the brakes.

These cars are turbocharged so in reality even though the turbo has to work harder and will be running at or as near to its maximum rpm as possible for most of the lap, it will still produce similar levels of power output. This means the engine's heat rejection isn't reduced, so you need to cool the cars roughly 25% more than you normally have to.

Also, as it's an electrical energy-rich circuit layout you will also generate more heat into the battery pack and its control systems simply from harvesting and deployment.

Basically, everything needs higher levels of cooling and below I have had a look at the top-four teams' changes from what they normally run. It's not easy to alter the inlet area on these cars as it is part of the side impact structure, so changing it would basically require redoing the side impact tests, so instead everyone will focus on the cooling exits, size, location and quantity.

First of all we can have a look at the rear exits.

The red ellipse highlights the rearwards-facing outlet. McLaren has raised the section above the exhaust outlet to increase the exit area.

It already ran a spec-two outlet at Austin and as can be seen by the red ellipse Mercedes has retained that for Mexico. Now it is more of a triangular opening, which it has achieved by lifting the upper engine cover surface, especially in the central section, above the exhaust outlet.

Ferrari has gone for simply a bigger exit at the sides, as highlighted by the two green ellipses. The central section is similar in height to the previous version.

From what I can see, Red Bull hasn't really bothered to alter the outlet in this area.

The rear exits are in more or less the same position and, in reality, are more or less the same size for all the teams - so the effect they have on the overall cars efficiency will be well understood.

When you are getting the maximum from that area then it's onto the sidepod and engine-cover louvre outlets. This is the most critical area as far as maximising the cooling is concerned, and major changes in this area can affect the airflow structure of the rest of the car coming along behind. It's not just about bigger louvres, it's more about placement relative to the body-surface pressure and how and where those louvres are placed can have a major influence.

The top two cars in this comparison, Mercedes and Ferrari, are fairly similar in placement and both have two fairly well-defined locations. These positions are normally placed where the internal radiator flow is at its weakest.

The McLaren on the other hand has a more aesthetically pleasing placing and the fact that it all connects together also adds to the aesthetics. My sentiments are that as long as it achieves the objective, why go for ugly when it can be visually appealing to the eye?

Red Bull on the other hand externally looks like it has made the fewest changes to compensate for the altitude in Mexico. Perhaps it was overcooled at other races but I would doubt this - as most teams will push the limits for each individual track.

That's all the engine and its ancillary cooling requirement changes compared. The other big cooling requirement is for the brakes and it's difficult to see who has done the best job there.

For the teams, it's difficult to simulate those early race laps when the car is at its heaviest and you are running in traffic; when the brakes overheat, the only way to cool them down is to use them less - which means more lifting and coasting.

So, who has done the best job on all of this while minimising the aerodynamic losses? I think it's going to be Sunday night before we know that.

title: 'They’ve destroyed cycling' - Bardiani-CSF-7 Saber boss gives scathing assessment of the UCI after Italian team unable to race Giro d’Italia in 2027
author: Dan Challis
text:
Veteran team boss Bruno Reverberi has called the UCI “incompetent” after his Bardiani-CSF-7 Saber team finished outside of the UCI’s top-30 rankings in 2026, making them ineligible to race a Grand Tour next season.

Reverberi said that it is likely that Bardiani-CSF-7 Saber will shutter due to the current regulations, which he says are making teams at the ProTeam level increasingly fragile, with no guarantees of invitation to the world’s biggest races.

The long-standing team has raced every edition of the Giro d’Italia since 1982 and is well known for its attacking style. Bardiani-CSF-7 Saber has been a fruitful breeding ground for Italian talent over the years, including the team’s last Giro stage-winner, Giulio Ciccone , who won in Sestola in 2016. Sonny Colbrelli and Giulio Pellizzari are two other names to have emerged through this system.

The team has also been involved in several doping scandals over the years, with the likes of Emanuele Sella and Stefano Pirazzi banned during their time on the team.

“Our project is to stop,” Reverberi told the “How can you spend €5 million and not have the right to race? There is no future, and cycling has no future. We have already thought about closing in two years. In fact, we have taken four or five new riders and made them sign for only one year.”

“You don’t even have the courage to go to the sponsor and ask for money,” he said, despite signing a “multi-year agreement” with Uzbek clothing company 7 Saber at the start of this season.

Reverberi’s main charge towards the UCI is its points system, which he believes is encouraging teams to race for top-10s rather than chase glory in the breakaway.

It is perhaps the team’s reticence to play the game as other teams have done which left them languishing down the UCI points rankings, 121 below Euskaltel-Euskadi, who travelled to Algeria and Panama in the last weeks of the 2026 season in their search for points.

“Our way of racing was to break away,” he said. “Now you don’t even break away, because you try to keep the rider there to sprint for tenth place for those damned UCI points,” he said.

“The UCI is incompetent. They’ve destroyed cycling,” he concluded, suggesting that while the top of the sport explodes in its popularity and financial investment, the lower-level is breaking apart.

“We’ve reached a bit of a peak with Pogačar in some ways, but everything is falling apart underneath,” he said. “Cycling is disappearing, and nobody’s looking at it.”

title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘Josh said he feels the fatigue?’
author: Antonio Losada
text:
The Sixers beat the Knicks on Friday…

…meaning they are 2-0 in the head-to-head matchup. That’s it, that’s all it means. No parade down Broad Street.

Here’s what we heard coming out of Cheesesteak Arena.

On losing to the 76ers in the NBA Cup:

“I don’t look it as a statement game. It’s the next game in front of us. Obviously, it’s a [NBA] Cup game and you always want to push yourself to have an opportunity to try and win something. This means taking a step toward that goal.

“But I just want to get a little better every time we play. These guys really hurt us in transition last game. Our transition defense right now stinks. But it’s gotten a little better. Tonight, it will be tested. Obviously Jaylen is not playing and he’s one of the best in transition. You look at little things and you hope to get better at the little things while getting a win.”

On the Knicks allowing Philadelphia to attack the paint too easily:

“They were getting in our paint left and right, right and left, and it was really, really easy doing it.”

On the Knicks forcing difficult plays instead of executing simple offense:

“It’s been going on all year. Like, we’re trying to hit a home run every time we get the ball. And we have to hit singles. We can’t hit a home run. We gotta hit singles offensively and then if our play breaks down, we have to move. There’s too many times where we have too many guys trying to iso and the other four guys sitting there and staring at the ball a whole possession.”

On the Knicks improving their turnover management in the second half:

“We did a better job with our turnovers (in the second half). But more importantly, we reacted better when we turned the ball over and we had five turnovers for six points (against).”

On the Knicks failing to maintain their focus throughout an entire game:

“Against a good team on the road, if you let go of those things in a half, you’re in trouble. And so somehow some way we have to be cognizant of doing this stuff for 48 minutes, which we’re not doing right now.

“Tonight it was the first half and it was almost like [we thought] we’re just gonna show up and go hoop and not do the little things that we need to do to go get a win.”

On the importance of executing the fundamentals consistently:

“It’s a little thing here, a little thing there, a little thing there. … We’re competitive when we need to be and that’s why all of our games that we’re in we have a chance down the stretch, but trying to make sure we continue to do the little things throughout the course of the game is gonna be huge for us because we’re not doing it right now.”

On LeBron James making decisive plays against the Knicks:

“[LeBron’s] a great player, and when you have a great player out there, with his ability, he’s gonna make plays, and he made big plays down the stretch. It’s the NBA, and it’s not surprising when a guy like Maxey or LeBron or Jalen makes a big play. You just hope that it doesn’t come down to that all the time.”

On Ernie Johnson’s retirement announcement and his impact on NBA coverage:

“I’d like to give a quick shoutout to Ernie Johnson. I don’t know him well. Obviously I know him from the TV. I try not to watch a lot of basketball shows because it gets me too high or gets me too low. But their show is one that I always get good laughs at.

“Just from afar, Ernie seems like he’s a big time human being. And the little bit I know about his story, it’s fascinating. He will be sorely missed, not only from the fans out there and other media members, but I know from a coaching standpoint too in keeping everything light and enjoyable and all that other stuff.

“So I hope you have a heck of a year, Ernie. We’re gonna all miss you, but thanks for doing what you do to make people smile everyday.”

On the Knicks’ careless turnovers and hesitant decision-making:

“Just a little careless. And sometimes it can be us being hesitant as well, wanting to make the right play, but they’re also not trying to turn over, and then it’s just a little late to our decision-making. It could be a lot of things, but obviously, we got to clean it up.”

On Josh Hart’s fatigue excuse six games into the season:

“Josh said he feels the fatigue? Well, Josh is old as s–t, so.”

On the Knicks needing to learn from their losses and stop relying on comebacks:

“I’ve said in the past that it’s always important to learn from wins. Obviously, you learn from losses, as well. There have been plenty of times that we’ve learned from being down. In those same games, we’ve made adjustments to where we weren’t down anymore and came back and won the game. Obviously, we have to understand what we need to do. It’s starting the game that way. I think that has to be our biggest point of emphasis going forward.

“I thought we played decent in the second half, took care of the ball better, played better defense, but we have to put a full 48 minutes together.”

On the Knicks lacking energy against Philadelphia:

“Today we played like a team that was on the end of a road trip. We gotta find that gear. We gotta find that energy.

“We picked up the pace in the second half, but what makes this team special is doing it for 48 minutes. We didn’t do that tonight. We put ourselves in a bad spot, and give credit to the team over there. They hit the shots when they needed to. We just got to execute at a higher level.”

On escaping the Knicks’ offensive struggles too late against the 76ers:

“I thought we did a great job in that fourth quarter of finding that gear, like you said, just kind of getting out of the quicksand. To do that puts us in a position where you gotta make some magic happen, and we just didn’t have enough magic tonight.”

On the challenge of facing LeBron James and the 76ers:

“They’re a great team. Obviously, you have arguably the greatest player of all time. We’ve got to bring our best. We’ve got to execute at a high level. And we’ve got to continue to use these games as a learning experience.”

On the Knicks’ stagnant offense and lack of movement:

“It’s a new year. I think we’re trying to work our way into the season. But I think the flow’s tougher. Sometimes the ball is stagnant, I think that’s a little bit from fatigue and not a mental thing. You know what the other team is doing, and physically you’re trying to get your body to get to that point. So I think that that’s part of it. We got to be more deliberate with cuts and movements. And taking care of the ball.”

On the Knicks feeling fatigued after playing three games in four nights:

“We all feel the fatigue. So we got to fight through it. Six games in. So we got to find a way to make sure we get our bodies ready to play every day. I think mentally we’re there. We just gotta find it physically.”

On the Knicks needing to execute more consistently:

“We gotta find a way to execute better. And do that continuously.”

On why the Knicks keep falling behind by double digits before attempting comebacks:

“I wish I could tell you that one. If I could tell you that one, and the reason why, then maybe it would stop happening. I think we all have a great will to win. I think sometimes it takes us a little longer to find a game, whether that’s the flow, fatigue, whatever it is.

“We have to do a better job of finding the game early, making it easy and then not relying on double-digit comebacks because it’s taxing.”

On LeBron James’ performance against the Knicks:

“He’s been good, but tonight, I thought that was his best game for sure. I thought he was good all the way through tonight. I thought he got some downhill stuff. He used his size and knocked them around a little bit for some layups. I thought he obviously pushed the ball and got us organized. I thought he was a little quicker to make some decisions to shoot the 3-ball as well. And then, he obviously made those couple of big plays down the stretch.”

On how New York’s off-court opportunities can distract players after winning a championship:

“When you win a championship, especially in New York, you have all these different opportunities off the court that take place. You’re filming commercials, you’re having these different shows, you’re doing these different things. All these events are happening.

“You’ve got to try to narrow it back down and lock in on basketball because playing in New York, you can get a little bit taken away from the sport with all the activities that go along with being in New York City. But you have to now try to narrow it down back to basketball. Key in, lock in on basketball. Make it the main priority and build out from there.”

On why the Knicks deserved to celebrate their championship throughout the offseason:

“That’s normal. That’s a part of human nature, man. You win a championship for the New York Knicks. You kidding me? After 53 years, you gotta enjoy that. You will never be the first one to win it after 53 years ever again.

“So that energy, you have to capitalize on it. It’s just a matter of now being able to kind of channel that and now focus on basketball and lock in a little bit more.”

On whether the Knicks’ slow start is concerning:

“I’m not concerned. When you are the champions, man, every target is at your back. Every team’s gunning for you, so it’s tough to kind of get off to a great start the following year. I’m not concerned. I think it’s a matter of just kind of locking in and focusing a little bit more, and they’ll be okay.”
