title: Starmer says UK must get closer to Europe as US relationship changes
author: Kevin Rawlinson
text:
Shift in dealings with Washington not likely to reset once Trump leaves Oval Office, former PM says

The UK and other European nations must draw closer together as the US becomes a less-reliable partner, Keir Starmer has said in his first significant political intervention since leaving No 10.

The former prime minister warned European leaders of the threat posed by Russia, among others, and said the shift in relations with Washington during Donald Trump’s presidency was not likely to reset once he leaves the Oval Office. He accused them of being caught out by these new realities twice already.

“A stronger Europe is vital and the UK must be at the heart of it,” Starmer told an audience at the British Irish Chamber of Commerce on Friday. “Europe has twice been caught asleep, failing to anticipate and prepare for predictable events.

“First, when Russia’s attack on Ukraine exposed longstanding European weaknesses on defence and security, and second, when President Trump made clear, once and for all, that the US will no longer bankroll our European security. We have to catch up.”

Starmer had called for closer European ties before stepping down as prime minister in July. Three months earlier, amid Trump’s war with Iran and his threats to withdraw from Nato, Starmer said Europe represented a “partnership for a dangerous world we must navigate together”.

He said those ties should go further than just defence, adding that Brexit had done “deep damage” to the UK economy, and that he wanted to be “more ambitious”, including pursuing “closer economic cooperation [and] closer security cooperation”.

Starmer spoke after spending time in Dublin meeting senior business leaders and politicians, including the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, with whom he established the annual UK-Ireland summit.

“I will say here what I have said to European leaders. This is about responding to a permanent change of affairs, not an aberration of the Trump presidency. Things will not go back to the way they were before.

“That doesn’t mean the US relationship is no longer important. On the contrary, the military, security and intelligence alliance is far too strong for that. But it does mean enabling Europe to take on far more responsibility for its own defence and security.”

His comments reflect a growing consensus on the left of UK politics that closer ties with Europe are essential to ensure economic and military security. Soon after taking office as Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham said that he intended to be “bolder” about closer ties with the EU.

Next month, Burnham will attend a crucial EU-UK summit where new agreements on food standards, energy and youth mobility will be the main focus.

Burnham has also said he wants a public debate on how the UK could move to a closer relationship with the EU after the next election. At a meeting of European defence ministers in Paris this week, the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said that they were “united and unwavering” in support for Ukraine in the face of Russian hostility.

Starmer said: “We need to build up pan-European cooperation and coordination on defence and security – a common security framework as much as a common market. The EU is changing to respond to that, but it cannot be the EU alone when Europe’s periphery is core to its defence.

“Britain must be central to that project. We are one of two nuclear powers. We are a leading Nato member. We have a viable next-generation fighter jet programme. And we are pledged to work alongside European allies to guarantee security in Ukraine.

“Ireland and the UK stand side by side in the coalition of the willing and with Ukraine, working together to guarantee and shape the security of our continent. I hope and believe that Britain’s relationship with its friends and allies can and should be strengthened by this urgent and common security project.”

title: UK police should not have let US force take over airbase trial, MoD documents show
author: Rob Evans, Harry Davies,Louisa Loveluck and Emine Sinmaz
text:
According to documents obtained by the Guardian, officials accused Cambridgeshire force of breaching US-UK deal by handing over case of woman strangled by US pilot

Ministry of Defence officials have privately accused a UK police force of wrongly handing over the investigation of an American fighter pilot who strangled a British woman to the US military, according to documents obtained by the Guardian.

Cambridgeshire police allowed the US military police to quickly take control of the investigation into Capt Jacob Wulfson after he had been accused of sexually assaulting Sarah Steele in his Cambridge flat.

The decision meant Wulfson was not tried in an English criminal court. Instead he was prosecuted in a military tribunal on a US airbase in neighbouring Suffolk.

Ministry of Defence officials said the Cambridgeshire force should “absolutely” not have let the US military police take over the investigation in a clear breach of a long-established agreement with the US.

The disclosure of the case by the Guardian in June provoked immediate criticism from Downing Street , which said it was “deeply distressing” and “very concerning” that the UK authorities were not involved in prosecuting Wulfson.

The government to set up a high-level inquiry to examine how and why police forces have been transferring investigations into serious crimes to the US military police.

The Ministry of Defence, which is responsible for handling the military relationship with the US, is one of the key departments taking part in the inquiry.

A batch of documents, disclosed via the Freedom of Information Act, revealed the private views of MoD officials about the Steele case, which centres on an obscure agreement signed by the US and the UK decades ago.

Under the terms of the agreement, police in the UK have the primary right to investigate alleged crimes by Americans stationed in the country .

The MoD officials made it clear the agreement was “pretty unambiguous” and only permitted the US military to acquire jurisdiction over investigations in a “narrow set of circumstances”. These circumstances are: if the offences were committed while the Americans were on duty, or if they were committed against another member of their armed forces or property.

In a memo written on 8 July, MoD officials based in Washington wrote: “The Steele case does not, on the surface, appear to meet the bar for a visiting force to be awarded jurisdiction.” In the agreement, the US military is formally known as a visiting force.

Four days earlier, the MoD officials had referred to the Steele case in an email to colleagues, saying: “The decision-making on this specific case seemed at odds with what is very clear” in the agreement.

Another MoD official agreed that “as best as we understand the facts, this should absolutely have been for the UK courts”.

An unidentified Greater Manchester police officer wrote in an email to MoD officials on 6 July that Cambridgeshire police had “wrongly, in my view” handed over the Wulfson investigation to the US military.

Cambridgeshire police said they were conducting a review of the case with what they called “the assistance of material provided” by US Air Force lawyers. The force said it “remained engaged with the victim”.

“We are working with government, wider policing and criminal justice partners to ensure greater clarity of jurisdictional decision making,” they added.

The US military aims to prosecute as many of its personnel as possible within the boundaries of its agreement with the UK.

The Americans often ask police in the UK if they can take over the prosecution of their military personnel – requests the police agree to, even when they have primary responsibility for investigating them.

A series of cases uncovered this year by the Guardian have highlighted concerns that British victims are required to give evidence in US courts martial, an unfamiliar legal system that often does not afford the same protections as that of a court in the UK.

Wulfson was off-duty when he assaulted Steele in his Cambridge flat in December 2023 after the pair talked on the Tinder dating app.

Steele testified at Wulfson’s court martial, which was held on his airbase at Lakenheath, Suffolk in April, that her experience was “degrading and distressing” .

The verdict and sentence were decided by an all-male jury of Wulfson’s fellow air force officers. All the lawyers were American. Steele was subjected to invasive and aggressive questioning by Wulfson’s lawyer.

Wulfson was convicted of strangling an intimate partner but acquitted of sexual assault. He was dismissed from the US Air Force and confined to a military jail on Lakenheath for six months.

The cross-government inquiry, which includes officials from the Home Office, Ministry of Justice and Foreign Office, is looking at how US military personnel are not being brought to justice in British courts.

The inquiry, which also involves police chiefs, is scrutinising a series of cases uncovered by the Guardian this year.

In each case, police handed over the investigations to US military police even though the American perpetrators were off-duty and the British victims had no connection to the armed forces.

They were tried in US courts martial on American bases. Tyrion Davis allegedly raped two women in Suffolk. He was convicted of one charge of sexual assault, but cleared of 10 further counts of sexual assault and abusive sexual contact.

Hannes Marschalek allegedly exposed himself to a 16-year-old girl and four young women in Littleport, Cambridgeshire. He negotiated a plea bargain at a court martial and admitted a charge of indecent conduct. He won an appeal in a US military court that quashed his conviction on technical grounds. This ruling is now being challenged.…

title: 'It really feels like a victory' - Belgian cyclo-cross champion returns to training following surgery for cardiac arrhythmias
author: Dan Challis
text:
Two-time Belgian national champion Marion Norbert Riberolle has restarted training after the opening to her 2026/2027 cyclo-cross campaign was halted due to a cardiac arrhythmia .

The Crelan-Corendon rider opened her season in Dendermonde and also raced the Kermiscross on the 15th of October before undergoing surgery to address the issue that was causing her heart to beat with an irregular rhythm.

After several sessions on the indoor trainer, Norbert Riberolle has now resumed training outdoors. She is being closely monitored by her team’s medical staff, and a decision is yet to be made regarding her return to racing.

“After several successful sessions on the rollers, she has now also taken to the road for the first time again. Our staff is monitoring everything closely so that it can be determined later when our Belgian champion can make a restart.”

In Norbert Riberolle’s absence, Lucinda Brand (Baloise Verzekeringen-Het Poetsbureau Lions) has been dominating on the 'cross field, already taking three victories this season.

Born in France and originally racing under a French license, Norbert Riberolle switched allegiances in 2021. She won the under-23 cyclo-cross world championships in 2020 and claimed three victories last season, including her second Belgian national title. The rider born in Troyes also races on the road for Fenix-Premier Tech’s development team.

“I am doing very well and I feel that I have recovered well. The rest has done me good,” she said.

“The first training sessions on the rollers went without problems, and in the meantime, I have also completed my first ride outdoors. It really feels like a victory. I was incredibly happy to be back on the bike and to be able to train outside.”

title: Trump boosted half of US coal plants with taxpayer dollars and ‘free passes to pollute’, report says
author: Hilary Beaumont
text:
Environmental Defense Fund analysis shows administration handed out $950m and Clean Air Act exemptions

It’s a good time to be a coal plant in the US. The Trump administration has given support to almost half of the nation’s coal plants, helping them to continue operating despite economic and regulatory headwinds, according to a new analysis by the Environmental Defense Fund.

The analysis, which looked at the 184 operating coal plants that are connected to the grid, found that 90 received support from the Trump administration through “cash handouts, free passes to pollute, and requirements to stay online past their retirement dates”.

The administration provided $950m in taxpayer dollars to 24 coal plants and handed Clean Air Act exemptions from toxic pollution limits to 70 coal plants, according to the EDF analysis.

“It’s extending the life of these coal plants,” said Surbhi Sarang, director and senior attorney at the Environmental Defense Fund. “The administration has leveraged a multitude of tools to prop up coal plants, and ultimately all of that is harming Americans even more by increasing electricity costs, by increasing pollution – it’s like Americans are getting hit twice.”

In 2015, the EPA’s Mercury and Air Toxics Standards first took effect, driving down dangerous pollution from power plants by more than 90%. In 2024, the EPA updated the standards to further reduce harmful pollution from coal-fired power plants. In the early days of the second Trump term, companies were invited to email the administration to request an exemption from the 2024 standards. According to emails obtained by the EDF through Freedom of Information Act requests, companies expressed concern that the standards would cost them too much money.

The Colstrip plant in Montana has operated for more than 40 years, affecting nearby communities like the Northern Cheyenne reservation by releasing toxic chemicals like mercury, arsenic, lead and nickel. “That’s one of the dirtiest coal plants that’s still operating in the nation,” Sarang said.

In 2024, the Mercury and Air Toxics Standards for coal-fired power plants was strengthened in several ways. For example, the standard for fine particulate matter, or fPM, reduced allowable emissions of nickel, arsenic, lead and other toxic metals from coal plants by two-thirds. According to the EDF, NorthWestern Energy and Talen Energy, which own and operate the Colstrip plant, requested an exemption from the fPM requirement.

Brian Bird, president and CEO of NorthWestern, wrote an email to the Department of Energy in March 2025 asking for a 15-minute chat about the standards with administrator Lee Zeldin. In the email , obtained by EDF, he argued that it would cost $500m to comply with the new rule: “It is ludicrous that our customers would have to cover the costs of a $500m investment for such a slight improvement to particulate matter capture,” he wrote.

The Trump administration gave NorthWestern an exemption from complying with the 2024 updated standards, which the administration went on to repeal in February.

Sarang said the Colstrip plant had not installed modern pollution controls that could reduce emissions. If it had been required to comply with the 2024 updated standards, it would have had to upgrade its equipment, she said: “It would have had pretty significant impacts on air pollution.”

NorthWestern, which became Colstrip’s majority owner earlier this year, describes the coal plant as a “dependable bridge to a cleaner energy future” that supplies reliable energy “until viable, equivalent, carbon-free energy resources are commercially available”.

Asked to comment on EDF’s report, NorthWestern said its technology at the Colstrip plant is “state of the art” for removing sulphur dioxide, and is 99.6% efficient in removing filterable particulate emissions. The company said if the updated 2024 federal standards had taken effect, it would have required it to become 99.8% efficient by 2028, costing hundreds of millions of dollars. The company said its mercury emission control at the Colstrip plant meets current state and federal requirements.

Another coal plant that received a pass from the Trump administration is the WA parish coal plant outside of Houston, Texas. Community members living nearby have called for it to be shut down due to its planet-heating CO2 emissions and what they say are ‘hazardous’ levels of particulate matter.

The plant’s owner, NRG, asked the Department of Energy for an exemption for all of its coal-fired facilities including the WA parish plant, arguing that its facilities wouldn’t be able to comply with the new standards and would need to “derate in order to comply”, taking megawatts off the grid in “critical areas”, according to an email obtained by EDF. NRG wrote that complying with the regulations “with razor thin margins” would risk the affordability and reliability of the grid.

A 2018 Rice University study found that the plant is responsible for as many as 177 premature deaths each year from PM 2.5, which are particles small enough to enter the bloodstream through the lungs, causing increased rates of respiratory diseases, heart attacks and strokes. “Our research has shown that WA parish is the deadliest power plant in Texas,” explained Rice professor Daniel Cohan.

NRG did not respond to a request to comment.

Cohan said plants across the country were supposed to meet the 2024 updated standards. “Trump is letting them off the hook from the more stringent version of the standard,” he said.

“It lets them stay open longer,” Cohan explained. “Many coal plants in this country are barely on the edge of breaking even, and so any regulations that force them to spend more money to clean up their pollution is likely to cause some of them to choose to retire and be replaced by cheaper and cleaner sources.”…

title: Fallon Sherrock pulls off shock defeat of world darts No 1 Luke Littler in live TV battle
author: Tara Conlan
text:
The 15th amateur to challenge Littler in Netflix stream on Friday evening, Sherrock was ‘lost for words’ after winning £501,000 prize

The name of the programme was Beat Luke Littler and Fallon Sherrock did just that.

On one of the biggest nights of the year for British TV and Netflix , there was much at stake: not just £501,000 to any of the 20 amateur challengers who managed to beat Littler in a single leg of darts, but also the jeopardy of whether audiences would choose to watch the streamer’s first UK live entertainment event – or the final of BBC juggernaut The Celebrity Traitors.

Netflix also had no idea when or whether the world champion would be beaten at the packed event at Manchester Central arena, hosted by Gary Lineker and Richard Osman, so had put in place contingency plans to have a second place competition should Littler lose within the first few rounds.

However, watched by hundreds of his fans, “the Nuke” comfortably beat a range of contestants of differing abilities who had queued up to take part in heats during the summer, including 14-year-olds Mackinley Cooper-Johnson and Jayden Walker.

Cheered on by enthusiastic crowds in fancy dress, one contender, the former Irish youth darts player Pearse Mackle, came close to claiming the lucrative prize. But in the end it took about two and a half hours for Littler to lose, to the 15th contender, Sherrock.

There was some controversy when it was revealed this month that she was competing: after all, she has an MBE for services to darts, and some people claimed she was not a true amateur, having played at the PDC World Darts Championship and won the inaugural Women’s World Matchplay in 2022. But Netflix classed anyone who has not ever had a PDC tour card as being eligible to take part.

“I mean, it’s been tough,” Sherrock said after her victory in Manchester. “Obviously I do see the backlash and I do see all the negative comments. But at the end of the day, I fit the criteria for this. I’ve never had a tour card, and I wouldn’t class myself as a pro really, because all I do is just play darts for the enjoyment of it.”

The PDC president, Barry Hearn, who was involved in the audition process, defended the contest. Asked whether Sherrock’s inclusion was unfair, Hearn said: “No, not at all. She’s not a PDC tour card holder. She’s entitled to enter. Why should she be denied?”

Despite her experience it was still a shock to the crowd that Sherrock defeated Littler. “I can’t put into words how much this means,” she told Lineker after her win, which was greeted by huge cheers from the delighted audience and a hug from her young son. “I’m really lost for words right now. It was a great moment. Give me an opportunity and I’ll take it every time … I’m really proud of myself.”

Littler, a magnanimous loser, said Sherrock had been “world class. I’ve enjoyed every bit of it … everything leading up to this. Maybe, Netflix, we can do it again next year.”

Beat Luke Littler was undoubtedly a risk for the streamer but it looks to have paid off as sources said audience numbers stayed steady (they could vote for the order the players appeared in) despite competition from The Celebrity Traitors, and appeared to rise after the end of the BBC show.

The show, dreamed up by the Manchester-based production company Workerbee, brings more working-class audiences to the streamer and helps its drive to air more live mainstream events. It echoes similar events in other sports pitting ordinary people against the elite, such as the Million Dollar 1 Point Slam at the Australian Open tennis tournament.

Workerbee’s managing director, Michelle Chappell, told the Guardian: “Rick Murray, our CEO, came up with the idea, which was just: ‘Wouldn’t it be amazing if someone could take on Luke Littler.’ It’s a sport event but a big show at the same time and it’s got a sense of humour and real jeopardy.”

There was one winner guaranteed, though, in the battle between Beat Luke Littler and The Celebrity Traitors, and that was the global production company Banijay which owns the companies that make the two shows.

title: ‘Bunch of baloney’: calls grow for Cop summit reforms as countries on track to fail nature targets
author: Patrick Greenfield
text:
Cop17, focused on protecting nature and restoring ecosystems, concludes on Saturday with critics saying system allows ‘one idiot’ to stall progress

Calls are growing for major reforms to UN biodiversity summits as countries fail to deliver on their promises to halt the destruction of the natural world, with governments likely on track to continue their record of never having met a target in the 34-year history of the convention.

Two weeks of negotiations at biodiversity Cop17 in Yerevan, Armenia, concluded on Saturday morning with countries vowing to redouble their efforts to meet this decade’s targets, which include commitments to protect 30% of the planet for nature, restore nearly a third of Earth’s degraded ecosystems and reform $500bn (£410bn) of environmentally damaging subsidies .

Agreed just four years ago by nearly every government on the planet, they aim to transform humanity’s relationship with nature . Despite progress in some areas, governments are way off track on meeting almost all of the targets. The UK is set to meet just three of the 23.

After talks that ran overnight from Friday into Saturday morning, countries signed off several measures, including a commitment to ramp up action on meeting existing targets and reaffirming a goal to increase biodiversity finance to $30bn a year by the end of the decade.

During the conference, environment ministers, activists and officials appealed for significant changes to the way the summits function to ensure governments follow through with meaningful action on the drivers of biodiversity loss.

Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, a veteran conservationist, said the Cop process had been “designed to fail”, arguing that decisions should be taken by a majority as the consensus-based process allows “one idiot” to prevent agreement.

“A lot of what’s going on out here at the Cop is just a bunch of baloney and beautiful speeches and BS,” he told AFP earlier this week. “We cannot have – we cannot expect – a consensus between every nation on Earth on every topic. That’s ridiculous. Cops have been designed to fail, and they are not disappointing.”

He also argued that the UN should host a single environmental Cop each year to tackle the climate, biodiversity, plastics and other issues in one go.

“This just makes my blood boil, because while we fiddle, Rome burns,” he said.

The negotiations in the Armenian capital have seen Argentina, Saudi Arabia and Russia water down language on environmental ambition in the final agreement, while wealthier governments were divided on who would contribute more financial resources.

European nations would like to see additions to the list of donor states, as China and several of the Gulf states are still classified as developing countries in the UN process despite decades of rapid economic development. The final agreement in Yerevan left this issue open.

Key decisions on a fund to mobilise resources from firms that make money from digital forms of biodiversity, such as pharmaceutical companies, were postponed to the next summit in Ecuador in two years’ time. It had been hoped that the fund would generate £1bn a year for nature conservation, with a significant share going to Indigenous communities, but it has so far raised just over $10,000.

The calls for changes to the biodiversity Cop process echo an intervention by leading policy experts during climate Cop29 in Azerbaijan in 2024 who said the summit was “no longer fit for purpose” and needed to shift to focus on implementation.

Ruth Davis, the UK’s nature envoy, said she recognised that the meetings could be “extremely frustratiing”, but a huge amount of implementation was happening around the world.

“We’ve got to make the system actually deliver outcomes for people, otherwise they’ll lose confidence in it,” she said. “In the end, this is a process that is owned by governments who are parties to it. But I know we are going to find friends and allies in making the process work for the citizens of countries for whom this is really important, not least because they are the ones facing the impacts.”

Efforts to reform the UN’s sprawling environmental agenda are already under way. Inger Andersen, the executive director of the UN environment programme, said that the current systems were driving change, but they were moving too slowly.

“Right now, the environmental agenda is very cluttered. There are lots of meetings, important as each one is. Let’s begin with the easy stuff, like programmatic overlap between conventions, which has an energy-sapping effect,” said Andersen. “We identified the illegal wildlife trade back in the 70s as a problem, then we identified migratory species, then broader biodiversity, then wetlands.

“Each of these conventions came along at the right time, but we now have a plethora of them. Maybe we should think about that.”

title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: Matt Nokes
author: Jonathan Farrar
text:
Nokes brought a powerful lefty bat to the Yankees and caught one of the most memorable moments in franchise history.

Growing up in the Southern California sunshine, Matt Nokes had the kind of baseball profile most travel-ball dads dream their sons will have: a lefty-hitting catcher. That combination eventually helped him reach the majors. Nokes’ path to the pros started when the Giants drafted him in the 20th round of the 1981 MLB Draft out of Patrick Henry High School in San Diego. A decade later, it took him to New York.

Matthew Dodge Nokes Born: October 31, 1963 (San Diego, CA) Yankees Tenure: 1990-94

After being drafted, Nokes started working his way toward the show, beginning in Rookie ball while still just 17 years old. He spent the next two seasons playing in Single-A, though his first year at the level was a bit of a struggle. In his second season, Nokes broke out with Fresno, slashing .322/.410/.508 with 14 home runs. The performance was good enough to earn him a promotion.

Nokes spent the 1984 season in Double-A and returned to the level to start the 1985 season. After another solid year, the Giants gave him a September call-up. In 19 games for San Francisco, he hit .208 and launched his first two major-league home runs. The Giants used Nokes as part of a package that offseason, sending him and pitchers Eric King and Dave LaPoint to Detroit in exchange for Bob Melvin, Juan Berenguer, and a player to be named later (Scott Medvin).

Now in the Tigers organization, Nokes returned to Double-A to start the 1986 season. Detroit gave him another cup of coffee at the end of the year before moving on from longtime starting catcher Lance Parrish that offseason, opening the door for Nokes to take over behind the plate.

Nokes’ rookie year was by far the best season of his career. In 1987, he slashed .289/.345/.536 with 32 home runs and 87 RBIs. He was selected to the All-Star team and won the Silver Slugger Award, but finished third in Rookie of the Year voting behind Mark McGwire and Kevin Seitzer. It was quite a debut for the young catcher, who helped Detroit win the AL East — the Tigers’ last playoff appearance for nearly two decades .

After that amazing season, Nokes came back down to earth and saw his playing time and production slip over the next two and a half seasons in Detroit. The Tigers decided it was time to move on in 1990 and traded him to the Yankees that summer for the elder Lance McCullers and Clay Parker.

The Yankees hoped Nokes’ bat could help the struggling club, particularly against right-handed pitching. With Bob Geren and Rick Cerone also on the roster, Nokes split time behind the plate and at designated hitter. He batted .238 with eight home runs in 92 games for New York. After the season, Cerone departed, and Nokes entered 1991 as the Yankees’ primary backstop.

In his first full season in pinstripes, Nokes played 135 games. In 493 at-bats, he hit .268 with 24 home runs. Those 24 round-trippers led the team, while his 77 RBIs were good for second. Those Yankees were lousy, but it was hardly his fault.

The 1992 season saw Nokes top 20 home runs for the second straight year, finishing with 22. His average dropped to .224, and his on-base percentage fell to .293. Mike Stanley also began pushing for more playing time behind the plate.

Shifted into more of a reserve role, Nokes appeared in 56 games as a catcher and another 11 at designated hitter in 1993. He slashed .249/.303/.424 with 10 home runs. The highlight of his Yankees tenure came on September 4th, when he was behind the plate for Jim Abbott’s no-hitter against the Cleveland.

Heading into the 1994 season, Nokes was still slotted behind Stanley on the depth chart. However, a broken bone in his hand in April sidelined him for much of the season. With the players’ strike ending the season in August, Nokes was limited to just 28 games. He batted .291 with seven home runs in his final season in pinstripes. The Yankees’ last game of the season came on August 11th, bringing Nokes’ time in the Bronx to an abrupt end.

Nokes spent the 1995 season with the Orioles and Rockies, appearing in 36 games between the two clubs. That ended up being his final major league season, though he continued playing in independent leagues later in his career. He also spent time coaching and eventually returned to the San Diego area, where he has worked as a hitting instructor and consultant, doing what he can to give back to the game.

Happy Halloween to all, and happy birthday, Matt!

title: Here’s why you can’t shake those unhinged political texts
author: Lauren Feiner
text:
You might be receiving political texts even if you’ve never made a political donation.

You might be receiving political texts even if you’ve never made a political donation.

“Its James Talarico. Can you please please please please pretty pretty please rush in even just $1?”

“Who’s working to elect James Talarico? Marxists.”

“Wow! Wow! Wow! Mark Kelly just made a HUGE announcement!”

“We asked Ben Verlander, MLB analyst and former Tigers prospect, to record a quick video about the election this Tuesday, November 3rd.”

“See which of your friends or family members have voted in the past and remind them to vote this year.”

If any of these messages sound familiar, it’s likely because they’re part of the massive stream of text messages flooding your phone leading up to the US midterm elections on Tuesday. The scale of the issue is not entirely clear, but call-blocking company Robokiller found that 15 billion political texts were sent in 2022, thanks in part to a Supreme Court decision the year prior that made it easier to send some mass calls and texts without consent. Alex Quilici, CEO of spam protection service YouMail, has an even higher estimate of 25 billion to 30 billion political texts this year, but caveats it’s an informal approximation. The volume is about the same to 10 percent higher than in 2024, he says.

There’s some good news and some bad news about these messages, says PIRG consumer watchdog director Teresa Murray. “The bad news is that political calls and political texts are exempt from the do-not-call-list rules,” Murray says. “The good news is that the election is next Tuesday, and hopefully within a few days after that, we’ll know what the results are and there won’t be any need to have any texts, or calls, or emails anymore after that.”

There are still some things consumers can try to stem the flow of these messages blowing up their phones — but it likely won’t significantly reduce it before Tuesday.

“In between all of the ‘legitimate’ political texts … there are going to be some scams in there”

The simplest thing you can do is send “stop” or block and report the messages as spam, which will notify your service provider of a likely spam number. That probably won’t result in any immediate change, Murray says, but if enough people report the same number in a certain period of time, the provider might begin to block it or label it as spam. You can also file a complaint with the Federal Communications Commission or your state attorney general if you believe a number is using an autodialer without your consent — something that even the people behind political texts are not supposed to do. Whatever you do, Murray says, do not click any links you receive from numbers you don’t know.

“In between all of the ‘legitimate’ political texts that are going out to support this candidate, or vote against that candidate, or vote for this issue, or whatever, there are going to be some scams in there,” Murray says. “If you want to donate money at this point, I would recommend going directly to the website for that political candidate, or for that PAC, and donating it that way.”

How did all of these campaigns get your number in the first place? If you’ve donated to a political candidate or issue group, that might seem obvious. But campaigns are also likely getting your information — including details about whether you might be likely to contribute to or vote for their candidate or issue — through data brokers that have nothing to do with politics. Data brokers collect and sell information from both public and private sources, such as public voter rolls, your online behavior observed by advertising web trackers, and loyalty programs. By collating all of this information, campaigns can try to infer your behavior, though they also might end up with outdated info, like old addresses that lead you to getting texts about a state you no longer live in (or even erroneous info that invites them for states you never lived in).

“As a consumer protection advocate, it’s so frustrating to have to say, ‘What can each individual person do?’”

“Errors in the processing of this information and the identification of individuals are very prevalent,” says Sara Geoghegan, consumer privacy program director of the Electronic Privacy Information Center. “Sometimes multiple people use the same device. Sometimes people have similar names. Sometimes people move. And this is such an unregulated ecosystem that there aren’t really rules in place to make sure that this is being effective and accurate, let alone free from bias, discrimination, and verified for privacy impact before processing this information.

“As a consumer protection advocate, it’s so frustrating to have to say, ‘What can each individual person do, and how many numbers do they need to block, and what are the toggle and privacy settings that they should toggle on?’” Geoghegan says. Meanwhile, “the companies that are trading in our most sensitive information are the ones who should stop harmful surveillance and the use of harmful technologies to have us better engage civically with our society, and not the other way around,” she says.

“I’ve spoken to people, someone last week who said, ‘Why would I even donate again when I get put on all these lists?’”

Geoghegan worries that the harm of being bombarded with unwanted political texts isn’t just that people get annoyed, but that they stop engaging civically as a result. “Having this surveillance apparatus that invades people’s privacy and really annoys them actually pushes people away from this,” she says. “I’ve spoken to people, someone last week who said, ‘Why would I even donate again when I get put on all these lists?’”…

title: 'I still need some time to analyse what I really want' - Tadej Pogačar to return to the UAE Tour, but 2027 race calendar still undecided with Tour de France the main target
author: Dan Challis
text:
Tadej Pogačar has already confirmed his main ambitions for the 2027 race season; a sixth Tour de France title, a fourth world title and a shot at redemption at the Vuelta a España. In the coming weeks, alongside the management team at UAE Team Emirates-XRG , his race calendar leading up to those objectives will be finalised.

According to the Slovenian, on the cards is a return to the UAE Tour, a race he won in 2021, 2024 and 2025. He skipped the race of his team’s homeland in 2026 and began his season at Strade Bianche.

Speaking on a virtual community ride on MyWhoosh, the UAE-owned training platform which sponsors his team, Pogačar said that there was a “big chance” that he will then return to the Spring Classics, with that elusive victory at Paris-Roubaix surely a focus.

His comments will come as a blow to the organisers of the Tour Down Under, who have said that they are “doing everything we can” to bring Pogačar to Adelaide in January. This option appeared more likely due to Pogačar’s early season ending after his crash at the Vuelta a España. It is also one of just a handful of WorldTour stage races that Pogačar is yet to win.

The 28-year-old raced five one-day races and the Tours de Romandie and Suisse ahead of claiming his record-equalling fifth Tour de France title in 2026. Pogačar then competed in the Vuelta a España for the second time in his career, crashing out on stage 8 while in the leader’s jersey and concluding his season.

A final judgement on Pogačar’s race schedule will be made during a team training camp in December.

"There's like three options that I can do. The team gave me three options of my calendar, but it's a big decision," he said during the community ride.

"I think I still need some time to really analyse what I really want for next year. And I think the final decision will be done in December, where we have another training camp.

"There's a big chance I come back to Classics for sure, and also UAE Tour, and obviously Tour de France. There's no hiding in this, I think, so we will see."

Speaking to at a charity golf event two weeks ago, Pogačar stated his central ambitions for the season. "The goal for next year would obviously be the World Championships, combined with the Tour and the Vuelta. Even though I'd rather ride the Giro, I'll have to tick off the Vuelta at some point too. I think that will be the goal for next year," he said.

While his season will once again orbit around success at the Tour de France, Pogačar admitted that he had not yet looked at the route for the 2027 race, which was presented on the 22nd of October.

"I didn't check a lot the route yet of the Tour. I was not there for the announcement,” he said. "Obviously the Tour is always three weeks long, and there's always big mountains, flat stages, tricky stages, some crosswinds, time-trials. So you always have everything.”

"No matter which cities host the start or finish, it's always more or less the same and the toughest race in the world. You need to be ready for everything."

title: Why F1's 2026 cars are unusually quick in Mexico
author: Josh Suttill
text:
A combination of factors means Formula 1's 2026 cars have been unusually close to the performance of their ground-effect predecessors in Mexico.

Charles Leclerc's FP1-topping time, a 1m18.128s, was 0.252s quicker than the lap he set to lead first practice in Mexico last year. That's the first time the 2026 cars have outpaced the 2025 cars in an FP1 session, having usually been two or three seconds slower.

Leclerc lowered the bar by three tenths to a 1m17.827s in FP2, though that was 0.435s slower than Max Verstappen's FP2 benchmark from last year.

Pirelli's pre-weekend simulations had predicted a 1m17.0s would be pole position, but after Friday's running it's now predicted to be well below that.

Pole position last year - a 1m15.586s - ended up being 1.8s faster than the pace in FP2, so you'd expect the 2026 pole position to be in the low-1m16s.

That should mean the smallest 2025 versus 2026 dry-weather qualifying difference of the season, with the previous closest being 1.409s in Baku.

So why are the 2026 cars so competitive at the Mexican Grand Prix relative to their ground-effect-era predecessors?

A resurfaced, busier track

The track underwent a partial resurfacing ahead of the 2026 race, with resurfacing work taking place from Turn 10 to Turn 1.

"This could also be an effect," Pirelli's chief engineer Simone Berra said.

"Obviously it was partially resurfaced, so sector one and half of sector two didn't have this kind of new Tarmac, so that could be a contribution also, but it's not the only explanation about why we were so fast, or faster than we expected."

Another explanation Pirelli offered is the track being in better condition because there's more support series laying down rubber this year.

However, there has only been a 10-minute increase in the on-track action prior to FP1 versus last year, with the one-make GTM Super Copa series, Masters Historic and Formula 4 NACAM championship on the support bill this year.

"I think part of these results are due to the track in better conditions compared to last year, we have several supporting series that are helping," Berra said.

"All the supporting series run before FP1 and between FP1 and FP2, so the track was evolving quite a lot during the day."

Less of a penalty at altitude

The most important factor is Mexico's high altitude is also less detrimental to the performance of the 2026 cars and power units than the 2025 packages. There's less total downforce to lose in the first place and the ground-effect cars were more downforce-dependent.

"The conditions, the altitude here, it's in favour of these cars compared to the old one," Berra said.

"The old cars were losing more downforce, compared to what this car generation are losing.

"Also, the other point is that the engine can push more compared to a normal situation or sea level conditions.

"So that's the main point, the drivers can push and so the difference with laptimes from last year are reduced."

Altitude, of course, does not effect the electrical power, which is far more influential on performance with the 2026 power units.

The 2026 cars (Leclerc's lap in red) are quicker on the straights than the 2025 cars (Verstappen's lap in blue), with the 2026 machines over four tenths up on the run to the Turn 4 left-hander. And it should be noted that Leclerc's Ferrari is one of the weakest in this section among the top-four teams because of its power unit deficit. So the gap is even larger if you compare to Verstappen's 2026 car.

The 2026 cars quickly lose that built-up advantage in the low-speed corners that follow and never recover it, but the drop-off is far less stark than at other circuits such as Spa (3.799s between 2025 and 2026 poles) and Monza (2.994s between them).

The cars actually end up relatively energy-rich in Mexico, so it's one of the better tracks for showcasing the performance of these cars.

title: Seabirds racing home over the ocean can get jet-lagged
author: John Timmer
text:
Flying across several time zones often causes jet lag, a feeling when the body insists it's the middle of the night while the clock says it's lunchtime. Now it turns out this nuisance is not exclusive to humans.

A new Science study on Manx shearwaters, seabirds that can fly hundreds of kilometers a day over the North Atlantic, shows they jet-lag themselves during their excursions. And because these birds navigate by the Sun, that jet lag leaves a measurable mark—it skews their compass.

Patrick Lewin is a behavioral and sensory ecologist at the University of Oxford and lead author of the study. “Manx shearwaters are medium-sized birds, about the same size as a pigeon,” Lewin said. “They are white underneath and black on top, but they have very long wings, and they are closely related to albatross.” Manx shearwaters nest in burrows on coastal islands around the North Atlantic. Most breed around the UK and Ireland, with about half of their population living in Wales.

title: 'I think things could have been done better' - Visma-Lease a Bike departee regrets slow development on Dutch team as he drops to continental level for 2027
author: Dan Challis
text:
24-year-old Loe van Belle is leaving the Dutch squad after three seasons, plus two in its development team. Once viewed as a promising Classics rider and time-triallist, Van Belle was informed in the summer that his services were no longer required.

Speaking in an interview with Van Belle has lamented his development while on the team, suggesting that things could have been done better, both by himself and the backroom staff. Crashes, injuries and an iliac artery flow limitation also played roles in his inability to prove his potential, ultimately leading to his departure.

“I look back on my years at Visma-Lease a Bike with a good feeling,” he told “When you look at the guidance and what you learn there as a rider in terms of tactics, racing style, and preparation for races and training camps, I don’t think you could have a better training ground. I benefited enormously from that, and I appreciate that immensely.

“But when I look at my physical development, I think things could have been done better, both from the team and from myself.”

Van Belle’s ability was clear as an under-23 rider, when he won a stage at the Flanders Tomorrow Tour and finished 9th at the 2022 Tour de l’Avenir. He was promoted to the WorldTour team in 2024 and was utilised as a domestique for the most part, picking up a handful of top-10 results during his three seasons on the team.

While Van Belle is appreciative of the investment that Visma-Lease a Bike gave to him, he now believes that he should have spoken up for himself when it was clear that he wasn’t progressing as planned.

“I want to look at myself first and foremost. I should have been more professional in taking responsibility for my own career.

“I have actually always very politely complied with what others said. That is how I was raised, too. If someone tells you what to do, especially when it is your boss, you do it. You assume that it is best for you. But over the past two years, I have regularly asked myself what I missed out on.

“Shouldn't I have taken more responsibility to get the most out of my career? Shouldn't I have chosen myself a little more now and then, or banged my fist on the table more? Perhaps my situation would look different now. Do I blame myself for that? I think so, actually,” he said.

Van Belle never raced a Grand Tour with the team and has signed for Dutch continental outfit BEAT CC p/b Saxo for the 2027 season. His hope now is to return to the professional ranks in the future, having overcome health issues that have limited him.

Along with a concussion after a crash at GP de Denain this year, which kept him away from racing for six weeks, the native of Zoetermeer had an iliac artery operation in 2025 - a procedure to ease a lack of blood flow, which is common for cyclists.

“I had probably been riding around with that for three and a half years. After that surgery, it felt like a mental brake was released. Finally, I could race freely again, without constantly being afraid that I wouldn't be able to continue after just one effort,” he said of his iliac artery issue.

“That blockage was huge, not only physically but also mentally. Together with the team, we tried to figure out what was going on. But precisely during that period, in hindsight, I perhaps should have taken more responsibility myself. I will take that lesson with me.”

After the surgery, Van Belle made progress on the bike and hoped for a renewed contract for 2027. However, Visma-Lease a Bike decided to let the rider go, bringing in British rider Mark Donovan from Pinarello-Q36.5 and Belgian Matisse van Kerckhove from the development team.

title: The FDA wants to pull its approval of a drug. It’s not so easy.
author: Sara Talpos, Undark Magazine
text:
In May 2021, the US Food and Drug Administration released a lengthy briefing document on an experimental medication for a rare autoimmune form of vasculitis that often damages the kidneys and lungs. The agency was on the fence about whether to approve the treatment, and it wanted an independent advisory committee to weigh in. Among the questions at hand: Was the drug meaningfully better than existing therapies?

Participants in the study, which had been conducted by the California biotechnology company ChemoCentryx, did appear to have slightly higher rates of symptom remission after one year. But according to the FDA, it was hard to interpret the results because the study’s design had been less than optimal. Some advisory committee members expressed a similar view. The effect of the drug, said one, “is just not well verified by this study.”

At the same time, many patients, and some physicians, saw in the data a potentially helpful medication, one that might lessen patients’ reliance on steroids, which are highly effective but often cause severe side effects.

title: Winners and losers from MotoGP's Sepang sprint
author: Eden Hannigan
text:
Sepang produced another chaotic MotoGP sprint, as Pedro Acosta walked away with the race victory and Marc Marquez established an ever-increasing grip on the riders’ title.

After the 10-lap sprint in near-mixed conditions, here are our winners and losers.

Winner: Pedro Acosta (1st)

Out of Acosta's three various-distance race wins in MotoGP so far, this one may well be the nicest - though he admitted it owed a lot to him having no championship implications to worry about unlike Marquez and Marco Bezzecchi.

Considering he isn't really convinced about his strengths in this kind of mixed weather, this was an important win, too, and certainly not something that would dissuade you if you have him pegged as a 2027 title favourite.

Winner: Marc Marquez (2nd)

Marquez marches on, muffling the heartbeats of the already on-life-support title battle.

This was a slightly precarious race, though not quite as precarious as it could've been. It was just controllable enough for Marquez to control it exactly to his liking - as his gameplan was to stay ahead of Bezzecchi but also to not lead, to not be the pathfinder having to figure out the wet patches.

It worked out well, and while he should have been beaten by his brother today, he wasn't, meaning that it's now been 12 races (across GPs and sprints) since Marquez last wasn't the top Ducati in the classification.

Loser: Alex Marquez (DNF)

It’s not too far-fetched to say the younger Marquez was a pre-weekend contender for a potential 37-point haul, and he looked well on-course when he took pole position and built up a healthy lead three laps into the sprint.

His error that might’ve come from “too much confidence” after his first pole since the 2025 Catalan GP or being “too optimistic” going into Turn 14 threw away a very likely 12 points - and, already injured, it's fortunate he's come away unscathed from what was a fairly high-speed off.

“It’s something tomorrow that we need to control a bit more,” was Marquez’s assessment of that specific corner. At least he’s lucky to have a second go at it, and he normally learns his lessons from Saturday to Sunday.

Loser: Jack Miller (DNF) and Pramac Yamaha

Everybody involved is more than a little lucky here that the rain didn't unfold like Miller thought it might in pitting at the end of the second lap.

Running 18th, with no hope of points, and aware that a deluge was coming at some point, Miller hoped to pre-empt it by pitting - and arrived to a spare bike that hadn't been swapped to wets.

"I had a chat with Giacomo [Guidotti, crew chief] before the race, I said 'have the bike ready'," Miller explained afterwards.

"In my mind that was, like, have the bike ready immediately. In his mind that was, like, four-five laps. So, miscommunication and unfortunately today we look like w***ers."

Luckily for Pramac, Miller's gamble would have never worked with the way the rain played out. But imagine if a potential win had been thrown away in this way.

So close to a maiden sprint victory but coming up short due to his lack of wet-weather confidence, it was still an impressive display of (mostly) contained aggression from Ogura.

Getting a good launch from the second row of the grid, Ogura went all-out against Marquez in the opening corners of the sprint, and eventually got the better of the Ducati rider throughout the first phase of the race.

It didn’t last, thanks to the mixed conditions the Trackhouse Aprilia rider hates, and he crossed the line in fourth, which was still a mega effort and also much better than Ogura himself had anticipated.

“Last in the group, so there’s no reason to be happy,” was his ever self-critical description.

Winner: Brad Binder (7th)

Yes, Binder's seventh place pales in comparison with what Acosta managed eight seconds up the road - but you take the wins where you can get them, and Binder badly needed one this weekend.

He has looked totally out of sorts over one lap here, worse than usual, but basically undid all the damage from a poor qualifying into Turn 1.

There was a bit of back-and-forth combat from there, and some wet-weather improvisation, so it's not a huge surprise Binder came off well - beating Enea Bastianini and only just coming up short of picking off Pecco Bagnaia.

Winner: Diogo Moreira (8th)

Moreira made his life a bit harder than it needed to be with a mistake early on in the race - but was afforded the opportunity to make up for it by the weather.

He seemed to thrive in the cagey late-race conditions relative to those around him, working his way past the battling duo of Johann Zarco and Enea Bastianini for a rock-solid eighth place.

In the context of just this race, the performance of the two remaining Aprilias was actually pretty good considering Sepang has long been one of its nemesis circuits for the RS-GP.

However, in the broader scheme of 2026, where it just lost its most valuable asset in Jorge Martin and is praying for a miracle with Bezzecchi, it’s a circuit where it cannot afford to be outscored by Marquez.

But that’s exactly what happened on Saturday, despite the best efforts of Ogura to disrupt the Ducati rider’s momentum. In a race that threatened chaos, it could have been one to upset Marquez, and it just didn't.

Similarly, Bezzecchi could have thrown caution to the wind and just gone for it, knowing he has no pressure and no real championship chance. He didn’t, only passing Ogura - who steadfastly denied Aprilia orders hinted at by Marquez.

Ogura's denial rings true, but nobody would really begrudge Aprilia if it did want to try to keep its riders' title aspirations alive through team orders. As it stands, even team orders would be nowhere near enough.

title: Railway engineering work over Christmas will cause 10 days of disruption
author: Gwyn Topham Transport correspondent
text:
London Paddington and Birmingham New Street stations will shut for five days but most routes will stay open

Passengers travelling on some of Great Britain’s busiest railway lines at Christmas have been warned of significant disruption from 10 days of engineering works.

Work will close London’s Paddington station – affecting intercity trains to the west of England and Wales until January – as well as Birmingham New Street, the UK’s busiest station outside the capital, for five days over the holiday period.

Passengers travelling between London , north-east England and Scotland will have to negotiate the part closure of the east coast mainline on Christmas Eve. Direct trains from the capital to parts of Essex and Norfolk will also be cut for much of the festive period.

Network Rail said most routes would still stay open and that the Christmas period, when train services generally stop for 25 and 26 December, remained the best time to conduct essential works.

Engineers hope to use the quieter festive days to carry out about £152m of works to improve reliability and capacity.

The biggest engineering work is expected on the lines leading into London Paddington, including replacing a junction near Slough. Most Great Western services to Wales and the west of England will start and finish at Reading, with some services diverting around Oxford to London Euston, from 27 December until 4 January.

The work also means Elizabeth line services west of Paddington and Heathrow Express services will not resume after Christmas until 31 January.

Birmingham’s main station, New Street, will be closed from the start of Christmas Eve until 29 December to replace overhead power supplies. No trains will stop or pass through, with rail replacement buses serving the city centre.

Passengers using east coast mainline services run by LNER and other operators may wish to avoid travel on Christmas Eve. Work at Doncaster means trains between London, north-east England and Scotland will be partly replaced by rail replacement buses from Newark to York, adding two hours to journeys.

The Great Eastern mainline out of London Liverpool Street will be closed for 10 days from Christmas Day for track replacement in east London, meaning no Greater Anglia or Elizabeth line rains will run through the area, with no direct trains from Norwich to London.

TransPennine services between Leeds and Manchester will be slowed for six weeks from Christmas Day with the closure of Huddersfield station.

Network Rail’s group director, system operator, Anit Chandarana, said: “Christmas is a time when many people want to be with family and friends, and most of the railway will be open to help them get there. We have worked with train operators to keep services running wherever we can on the busiest travel days and to provide alternative journey options where work affects the usual route.

“We are sorry that some passengers will face disruption. The days between Christmas and new year are by far the quietest of the year and give us the best opportunity to complete major projects such as the power supply upgrades at Birmingham and Paddington. Our teams will do everything they can to keep people moving, and we urge passengers to check their journeys before setting off.”

title: ‘We were mortgage-free at 45, here’s how you can do it too’
author: Holly Mead
text:
Even modest overpayments can save you a fortune. We look at the best ways to pay off your biggest debt early

W hen Adrian Massey was made redundant from his job as a food developer in 2010, the bill that worried him the most was the mortgage. Just over a decade later he and his wife, Tulay, had cleared their debt early, saving themselves £30,000 and freeing up some money to start their own business.

The couple had bought their six-bedroom home in Banbury, Oxfordshire, for £280,000 two years before he lost his job.

With an interest rate on their mortgage of 6.1%, the couple’s monthly payment was about £1,400. “It felt like a burden; a chain around my neck,” says Adrian, 50. “I started thinking about the best way to pay it down.

“It dawned on me what could happen if you overpay even a relatively modest amount. You can really start to make a difference.”

When he started his next job he set up a standing order to overpay the mortgage. “We looked at our current income and outgoings, and then, based on our spare cash, we decided how much did we want to put into clearing the mortgage without overstretching ourselves,” he says.

They decided they could afford £500 a month. After that, any pay rises they received were funnelled into the mortgage, and the couple would sometimes add a lump sum of up to £2,000 from savings.

When their five-year, fixed rate deal ended in 2013, they remortgaged to a rate of 2.5%, choosing a tracker deal that had no limits on overpayments.

The extra they paid each month started to make an even bigger difference. By 2021, Adrian and Tulay were mortgage-free – seven years ahead of schedule.

“I know that, purely from a financial point of view, there are advantages to investing more in the stock market because of the returns you get, but the freedom was more important to me,” he says. “It has meant I have been able to invest in myself and the life I want to lead, rather than being shackled to this payment.”

The money that used to go into repayments has been used to set up a business, ATM Food Innovations, and Adrian has also upped his pension contributions.

“Making the final payment felt really good; it’s a real sense of relief and liberation,” he says. “You know that whatever happens, no one can take your house away.”

With interest rates rising, it is no wonder that achieving mortgage-free status is a goal for so many.

Andrew Hagger, finance expert at Moneycomms, says: “For most people, repaying the mortgage means getting rid of the biggest financial commitment hanging around your neck.

“They dream of what they could do with all the extra disposable income: holidays, update the car, home improvements, or retire early. The list is endless.”

Clearing your mortgage not only means removing what is likely to be your largest monthly expense, it can also save you thousands of pounds in interest that would have been paid over the full term.

And even small overpayments can make a big difference. On a 25-year mortgage of £200,000, with an interest rate of 5%, overpaying by just £20 a month could save you £5,700 in interest and clear your debt nine months early, according to Moneycomms.

Overpaying by £50 a month on the same loan would save you £13,400 in interest, and clear the mortgage almost two years early. A £100-a-month overpayment would save £24,530 and clear the debt three years and six months ahead of schedule.

Overpayments don’t have to be on a regular basis. You could pay off a lump sums when you come to the end of your deal, or switch to a new lender, or part-way through if the terms of your loan allow it.

In the above example, a one-off overpayment of £10,000 could save £11,870 in interest and pay off the mortgage one year and two months early.

To make an overpayment, contact your lender. Often it is as simple as making a transfer to the account.

As your overpayments start to make an impact, you will typically be offered the option to reduce either your monthly payments, or the mortgage term. If repayments are comfortable, choose the latter. This means that more of your money goes towards paying off the debt and you’ll clear the balance sooner.

One downside to overpaying is that you can’t easily get the money back if you need it, so ensure you have a savings buffer in case of an emergency; typically three to six months’ of essential outgoings is recommended.

“It’s tempting to try to throw every spare penny at the mortgage, but find a balance between making progress towards being mortgage-free and retaining enough flexibility to deal with life’s unexpected costs,” says David Hollingworth, director at the mortgage broker L&C.

Understand the terms of your mortgage: most let you overpay up to 10% of the outstanding balance each year without charges. Hollingworth says: “It’s worth checking as early repayment charges can be substantial, often 3-5% of your overpayment, which can erode, or remove, the benefit of the overpayment.”

If you want to overpay without locking away your money, an offset mortgage can be a good alternative to a standard deal. These let you link a savings account to your mortgage. The savings balance is deducted from the amount you owe, reducing the amount of interest you are charged. For example, on a £200,000 mortgage with a savings balance of £10,000, you would be charged interest on £190,000 of the loan.

The trade-off is that you don’t earn interest on your savings, but they are accessible if you need them; any money withdrawn from the account is simply no longer offset from the mortgage balance. So, in the above example, if you withdrew £2,000 from the savings account, you would then be charged interest on £192,000 of the mortgage loan.

David Hollingworth, director at the mortgage broker L&C, says: “An offset can suit those with substantial cash savings or who receive lump sum bonuses. It allows your cash to work harder without limiting your ability to draw on it when required.”…

title: The Trump administration wants to give married parents money to stay at home. Will it be enough?
author: Gaya Gupta in New York
text:
Experts say the proposed program prioritizes parents in ‘traditional families’, ignoring the flexibility needed that all families need to support themselves

Erica Hall and her husband knew that raising kids wouldn’t be cheap.

They intentionally had their children five years apart because paying for two in daycare would have been too expensive. When her first child was born, Hall had to self-fund her maternity leave by drawing on savings. And recently, Hall was laid off from her tech job, leaving her at a crossroads.

“Do we move to a lower-cost daycare? What kind of job should I look for? Can I dial back now?” said Hall, who lives in Seattle. And perhaps the most essential of all questions: “Do we need to completely 100% replace my income?”

More American families than ever consist of two working parents: 52% are dual-income households, compared to 31% in 1975, according to the Pew Research Center. Eight out of 10 of these families say the arrangement has been beneficial to their finances.

Despite this shift in family dynamics, the Trump administration has remained focused on an agenda that emphasizes a “traditional” family structure, where one parent stays home to take care of children.

As part of this agenda, the White House is considering a program that would pay parents $9,000 annually to stay at home, using reallocated funds that are now used for federal programs that typically support single mothers and low-income families, according to the New York Times.

The plan was reportedly proffered by JD Vance, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, who has proclaimed himself a defender of “pro-family” policies. The vice-president penned a Wall Street Journal op-ed in 2021 criticizing federal spending on daycare, claiming that “young children from average, healthy homes can be harmed by spending long hours in childcare.”

“It turns out that normal Americans care more about their families than their jobs, and want a family policy that doesn’t shunt their kids into crap daycare so they can enjoy more ‘freedom’ in the paid labor force,” he wrote on social media at the time.

As vice-president, Vance has continued to angle himself as a defender of families. “To the radicals who wish to abolish my family and the thousands and millions of other families across our country, we have a simple message for them: stay the hell away from our kids!” Vance said at the Republican’s midterm convention in September.

But experts and parents who spoke to the Guardian said the proposed program for stay-at-home parents prioritizes a single type of family structure and ignores the flexibility that families need to support themselves and their children.

“Families of all compositions need help right now. All families do. We should not pit families against each other,” said Chandra Childers, a senior policy and economic analyst at the Economic Policy Institute.

For Natalia Goodnow of Pittsburgh, being a stay-at-home mother of two was a temporary choice that allowed her family to save on the cost of childcare while she went back to school and pursued a second master’s degree. After she graduated, she was forced to delay her next job search after graduating because the waitlist for her child’s daycare, like many in the country, had grew significantly after the pandemic.

Now, Goodnow is balancing taking care of her children while also building up her own consulting business, which she believes will afford her flexibility to work around her daughter’s schedule. She doesn’t expect she’ll ever stop working in some capacity.

“I’m not built to be just a stay-at-home parent,” she said,

There’s also a risk to relying on one parent’s income. Even though her family is able to live “somewhat stable” on just her husband’s income, Goodnow said she’s worried that his career as a physician, combined with the responsibility to support the whole family himself, will lead to burnout.

“I have to have a second income stream created to give him flexibility to scale down, because it’s just not sustainable,” she said, pointing out that the proposed $9,000 wouldn’t be enough to match what she would make if she worked.

Jillian Whitlow, a mom of three who is pregnant with her fourth child, wishes at times that she could stay at home to take care of her children, but after launching a successful marketing business, her husband left his job as a mechanic to take care of their kids.

The choice stemmed from practicality. The cost of daycare for her children was greater than their monthly mortgage payment.

Though Whitlow’s family, who live in Texas, is in a better financial place than they’ve ever been, they still feel the pain of rising costs and are still paying off student debt and loans on their mobile home. Still, Whitlow sees the White House’s proposal as an unnecessary interference in personal family decisions.

“I would love it if there was a lot less government in all of our lives,” she said, “I would love it if each individual family had more freedom to make the decisions that they want to make about the best way to raise their families.”

“It should be up to me and my family to make that decision, and not the government pushing me to stay at home,” Goodnow said.

Childcare costs can pose a major financial burden on families. Forty per cent of households, including those that have one parent who works less than full-time, spend an outsized percentage of their income on childcare, according to a recent report from the Georgetown Law Center on Poverty and Inequality.

The White House’s plan, by reallocating federal funds from the Department of Health and Human Services that have typically gone to low-income, single-parent families, could actually making childcare even more expensive or less available, Childers said.

“The minute you start draining resources that go into funding this childcare pool, then rates have to rise on other families, some of whom may already be stretching to make it as it is,” she said.…
