title: ‘Plantation tourism’: court victory signals hope in Jamaica’s fight to keep beaches public
author: Natricia Duncan in Montego Bay and Anthony Lugg; photographs by Ina Sotirova
text:
A temporary injunction in the coastline battle for beaches to be publicly accessible, not sealed off for private developments, is just a step in fighting what islanders call a tourism model that disadvantages Jamaicans

W hen the Australian human rights lawyer Eva Buzo emerged from the sea on to the shores of One Man Beach in Montego Bay on Sunday after her gruelling, nearly 11-hour-long swim, the thunderous pulse of welcome drums was drowned out by the chants of “free beach” from jubilant supporters.

Here in Jamaica’s tourism capital, against a backdrop of jagged mountains and sunset-tinted clouds, Buzo – a celebrated marathon swimmer – said she was pleased to help support the important work of the Jamaica Beach Birthright Environmental Movement (Jabbem) and others fighting for free public access to Jamaica’s beaches.

“People’s rights are more important these days than ever, and people keep on trying to encroach on our fundamental freedoms,” she said, calling the privatisation of beaches a colonial legacy. But for Jabbem, her swim was not the most significant milestone this month in its fight for public access.

That came earlier in October, when Jabbem celebrated a rare victory in one of several court cases to end the 1956 Beach Control Act that had given the state ownership of the island’s foreshore and seabed. The act has allowed successive administrations to restrict access to beaches and sell off coastlines to wealthy luxury hoteliers.

In October, however, the court issued an injunction preventing the government from continuing to restrict access to Little Dunn’s River in St Ann while the case continues.

“This victory means a lot for the Jamaican people. It means that our case is strong,” said Dr Devon Taylor, an immunologist with a PhD in biochemistry, who founded Jabbem in 2020.

Wilbourn Carr, 73, who is involved in another fight for beach access in Portland parish, in Jamaica, said the temporary injunction offered hope for other cases.

“The matter of beach access is right across Jamaica. And we just had some success at Little Dunn’s River with that injunction. It gives us hope. Because the fact is that one judge now believes that Jamaicans should have access ,” he said.

The Jamaican government has said it will appeal. In an interview, the environment minister, Matthew Samuda, said there was no basis for protest. He said the government was safeguarding critical tourism investment and protecting communities from crime, while improving beach access through updated legislation requiring future developments to create access points and investment in community leisure spaces.

In the case of Little Dunn’s River, Samuda said access had been restricted after a murder.

“Because of the cultural sensitivity and the love that certain residents of St Ann and those who travel far and wide to come to the facility have for the space, the government intervened and said it would put up appropriate security structures and would facilitate free access to this area on a weekend basis, Friday, Saturday and Sunday,” he said, describing this as “structured management” that also provided benefits such as lifeguards.

Describing tourism as the “largest foreign exchange earner” and the main source of income for nearly 200,000 Jamaicans, Samuda accused activists of portraying the industry as “the enemy”.

He said: “176,000 people aren’t protesting anything to do with beach access, but 176,000 people are feeding their families because of our tourism product … Let’s not put their needs and their concerns on one side.”

Taylor, however, rejected crime prevention as justification for beach closures, pointing out that “the Beach Control Act of 1956 predates the level of crime seen in Jamaica and was never a tool to control crime”. He referred to the Little Dunn’s River restrictions as an illegal “collective punishment of the Jamaican people” that had nothing to do with solving an alleged murder.

“So you could close it until forever, until you solve this murder, which you have not solved,” he said. “You present no evidence that this place was still under threat … So we refute Little Dunn’s River was closed to solve some murder or to stop more from happening, because four years later you only allow the people to use it on Saturdays and Sundays. We deserve leisure seven days a week.”

Paul Roberts, a British architect living in Jamaica and Jabbem’s St Ann community coordinator, argued that the government is creating a false impression that Jamaicans cannot be trusted.

“It’s a load of rubbish,” he said. “I’ve been coming here for 15 years now and I’ve never had any trouble. I’ve never been robbed, I’ve never been mugged and I’ve never faced any issues.”

Campaigners did not oppose hotels, Taylor said, but rather a “plantation tourism” model that disadvantaged Jamaicans.

“Cheap labour of the Jamaican people, degradation of the environment, exclusion of the Jamaican people from the foreshore, plantation tourism, untenable working conditions. Lock us out using colonial-era law. The industry is guilty of that,” he said.

“We the people do not want to be treated as second-class citizens in our country … we want fairness, equality and equity.”

Buzo described access to shared public spaces as a human rights issue, pointing to countries such as Australia, where she is from, and Barbados in the Caribbean that maintain public beach access alongside thriving tourism industries.

“There’s no reason why hotels can’t have beachfront properties that then front on to a public beach. It’s just this kind of exclusivity and segregation that small amounts of people think they need,” she said.

Samuda argued Jamaica was different because, although the country had “conquered our crime monster”, it had “spent 30 years being in the top three most murderous countries on the planet”.…

title: The staggering $446m Elon Musk has spent on the US midterms – visualized
author: Nick Robins-Early, Andrew Witherspoon, Will Craft, Alvaro Dominguez, and Daniel Wolfe
text:
The tech mogul’s midterm donations backing Republicans have made him the largest single-cycle political donor in modern US history

Elon Musk has poured so much money into US politics this midterms election cycle that his donations could fund half a dozen SpaceX rocket launches or buy thousands of Tesla Cybertrucks. At the Tesla Diner in Los Angeles , Musk could order more than 31.9m cheeseburgers with the money he has spent on the midterms.

Musk, the world’s richest person, has funnelled at least $445.77m into Republican-aligned political action committees (Pacs) and groups since last year, according to US Federal Election Commission data as of 29 October. The contributions have made him the Republicans’ most prominent financial backer and the largest single-cycle political donor in modern US history.

Musk’s spending is a staggering example of the SpaceX and Tesla CEO’s political influence, as he seeks to help Donald Trump’s administration retain control of Congress in the upcoming midterm elections, though current polls predict Democrats achieving a majority. The contributions are at a scale that is difficult to fathom and dwarf efforts from big name megadonors like George Soros or Michael Bloomberg, setting a new precedent for how the rich and powerful attempt to shape politics.

Only last year, Musk claimed he would step away from making large scale political donations after putting nearly $300m towards Trump’s 2024 presidential election campaign. FEC data since then shows he has not only leaned back into financing campaigns, but that his spending has dramatically ramped up as election day approaches, increasing by about $200m in the final two months of campaigning.

Musk’s money has primarily flowed into several Republican-aligned Super Pacs , with his largest contribution of $216m going into his own America Pac. The Pac has targeted 43 House and Senate races across the US, blanketting voters with television commercials, digital ads, text messages and mailers.

America Pac made 839 independent expenditures in House races and 623 in Senate races in 17 states across the country . The spending varies greatly depending on the state, however, with campaigns in battlegrounds such as Michigan and Arizona receiving more of the Pac’s support.

Musk’s Pac has spent the most in his home state of Texas, where a closely fought Senate contest between Democratic candidate James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton has turned into the most expensive race of the midterms. America Pac has overall poured more than $33m into efforts to elect Paxton, while Musk also made a $168m contribution to the Senate Leadership Fund which supports the Paxton campaign.

A large portion of America Pac’s output focuses on attack ads against Democratic candidates such as Talarico, often accusing them of being radical socialists or targeting them over supporting transgender rights. The Pac has spent $28m on anti-Talarico content, including between $300,000 and 350,000 in October on a single Google ad targeting the Texas Senate candidate.

“James Talarico supports parents being charged with child abuse if they do not support transitioning their children,” stated the ad, which was shown more than 10m times over an eight day period.

Musk has also reposted America Pac’s content to his more than 200m followers on X, the social media platform he owns. One of Musk’s posts in October amplified an America Pac attack ad and claimed: “Talarico wants to trans your kids and destroy the border.”

The nearly $446m that Musk has donated this election cycle far exceeds his contributions in the 2024 presidential race, when the tech mogul also held rallies and appeared on stage next to Trump during the campaign. While Musk has been a less visible presence in the midterms, potentially reflecting the US public’s dislike of him , behind the scenes he has greatly upped his financial support for Republicans.

Musk’s spending far outpaces all other donors in the elections, including fellow tech and finance moguls like Marc Andreessen, who also started his own Super Pac. Musk has put more money into this election cycle than what every top Silicon Valley donor, including himself, spent on the 2024 presidential election combined.

The stakes of the midterm elections are potentially high for Musk, who has closely aligned himself with the Trump administration and benefited from its lax policies toward regulating tech and artificial intelligence. SpaceX has also intertwined itself into the government more extensively, landing lucrative contracts this year for Trump’s missile defense program and the use of Musk’s Grok AI chatbot in the Pentagon.

Despite the immense and unprecedented scale of Musk’s political spending, his contributions this election are still only a tiny fraction of the centibillionaire’s overall assets.

title: How ‘sin bin’ for red light jumpers saves cyclists from being saddled with a fine
author: George Francis Lee
text:
Police scheme in City of London offers errant cyclists a choice – watch a roadside safety video or pay a £50 penalty

W hen Aman cycled through a red light in the City of London this week, he was surprised when the police pulled him over. He was positively shocked when, instead of giving him a fine, officers took him into a gazebo to watch a bike safety film.

Aman was one of 30 cyclists caught in the first 20 minutes that morning, as part of a new scheme by City of London police to dissuade cyclists from running red lights.

Many concerned pedestrians have celebrated the time-out zone and, perhaps more surprisingly, cyclists have too.

The new pop-up scheme, called “stop, look, listen, change”, gives offending riders the chance to view an educational film about the dangers of red light jumping. Those caught by police who do not want to pay a £50 fine are taken to a “sin bin” by the roadside, where they watch testimonies from visually impaired road users.

“It is about taking that time away,” said Rob McTaggart, media and engagement manager at City of London police. “Time they didn’t stay waiting for the light is now the time they’re having to spend watching the video. It’s a bit of instant justice in that regard.”

As cyclists continued to be corralled into the time-out zone, McTaggart said the police team had noticed no difference between the numbers of red light runners on hired e-bikes versus those on regular bicycles.

When the sin bin was first launched two weeks ago, roughly 70 people were brought in within90 minutes, McTaggart said. None of the halted riders opted to take the fine.

Watching the safety film, McTaggart said, was useful for spreading road education.

“Right now you can jump on a bike without any training whatsoever,” he said. “It’s about that understanding that just because you can go, it doesn’t mean you should go. We’re not going to enforce our way out of it.”

Sgt Stuart Ford, who helped create the scheme, said it was inspired by the Exchanging Places initiative , where cyclists are brought into large goods vehicles to understand risks like blind spots and difficulties in manoeuvring.

Ford said he was sympathetic to cyclists – “You can quote me: I like bikes” – but added that police “get more complaints than anything else in the city around cyclists jumping lights and their behaviour”. He added: “I’m afraid to say it but a lot of the time, the cyclist is the protagonist here.”

Ford collaborated with the National Federation of the Blind UK (NFBUK) to understand how vulnerable road users are affected by riders skipping lights or riding on the pavement.

Hyacinth Malcolm, who is fully blind, said: “I’m just lost for words as to why they [cyclists] are behaving the way they’re behaving.”

Malcolm said she had to rethink before going out for a daily coffee because of the risk of cyclists colliding with her.

Sarah Leadbetter, a disability activist with visual impairments, also said the footways were not safe for disabled people and that things were getting worse.

She said she relied on a cane, her guide dog and the rotating cone at pedestrian crossings – a small, unassuming plastic or metal cone which is attached to the underside of the push-button unit.

But, she said, she could not be certain of her safety because cyclists “suddenly come through the red light and go straight into you”.

McTaggart said the scheme had sparked discussions across the country and that there was a “huge appetite for what we’re doing here”. In the last week, pedestrians have complained of cyclists riding through the recently pedestrianised Oxford Street.

Sarah Gayton, street access campaign coordinator from NFBUK, commended the new education scheme, but hoped to see the fine increased to £300 and further action taken by the government. “Something has got to give,” she said. “We need designs that work for everybody.”

While some have pitted cyclists and pedestrians against each other, Tom Fyans, CEO of the charity London Cycling Campaign, said he also wanted to see more changes in London’s road designs to better suit all road users.

Standing at the busy junction of Old Street roundabout in the east of the capital, he said: “London isn’t designed for cycling, it’s getting better, but it’s designed for cars. What we need to see is far more cycle-friendly, pedestrian-friendly designs where the car is less important. Then you’ll see a much safer environment for everybody.”

On the new scheme, Fyans said his charity supported the measures over what he believed to be ineffective monetary penalties. He said: “Punishing cyclists with fines and criminal prosecutions, it doesn’t really work. But getting them to think about their impact on other road users – hearts and minds – is much better.”

Fyans said most cyclists do follow the Highway Code, but that a focus on bicycle users was “disproportionate” and a result of the rising number of bike users on London’s roads.

“I think there’s double standards quite often,” he said. “We’re not the biggest danger. It’s cars and speeding and drivers not paying attention that kill people on our roads. That’s the biggest challenge that needs addressing.”

Fyans, who works with Wheels for Wellbeing – a cycling disability group – said he understood the dangers for visually impaired pedestrians and wheelchair users.

But can relations between cyclists and pedestrians be improved? “Let’s address it, but let’s be proportionate about what the real problem is,” he said. “Cyclists are not really the main problem on the road when it comes to danger.”

title: Cost of living protests to spread to Germany and reignite in France on Halloween
author: Deborah Cole in Berlin and Jon Henley in Paris
text:
Activists call for people to make their anger known over poor public services including education and housing

Street protests sweeping Europe are expected to spread to Germany and reignite in France on Saturday, with police mobilised to stop potential looting and rioting on the fringes of what organisers hope will be peaceful rallies.

Weeks of, at times violent, student demonstrations have rocked Italy, Spain, Portugal, Albania and France, where activists on Halloween have again called for people to make their anger over the cost of living and deficient public services felt across the country.

In Germany, a loose alliance of groups called Gen Z regelt (Gen Z is sorting it) has called for supporters to turn out in more than 30 cities demanding more spending on schools, climate protection and housing, and against any plans to return to mandatory military service .

Alexander Throm, of the ruling conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) parliamentary group, wrote in the Handelsblatt business newspaper: “Scenes like those in France must be prevented at all costs.”

But Felix Banaszak, the co-leader of the opposition Green party, cautioned against attempts to place the youth protests under general suspicion in advance.

“The [CDU’s] rhetoric, which seeks to criminalise these protests pre-emptively and paint them as the work of marauding gangs, may even drive people towards radicalisation,” he told the RND media group.

Berlin’s police chief, Barbara Slowik Meisel, said she would deploy an additional 1,500 officers in the capital, though she had little reason to fear that people or property would come under attack.

“We have no concrete evidence of any coordinated looting operations being planned,” she said.

About 10,000 protesters, mainly pupils, students and their parents, are expected at the Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, with another smaller gathering planned in the early evening in the Mitte district.

Large rallies have also been called in Cologne, Munich, Frankfurt and Hamburg.

The team behind Gen Z regelt has used social media and its website to call on participants to exercise restraint: “Our protest is peaceful, without exception. Violence goes against everything we stand for. Only through peaceful means can we achieve something together.”

By Friday, more than 160,000 people had registered on the website saying they planned to attend the protests.

The federal pupils’ conference, a youth political lobbying group, has distanced itself from Saturday’s demonstrations, saying the initiative’s “unclear” organisational structure made the events unpredictable.

It plans to hold a separate protest in Berlin on 20 November that will include teachers and other youth movements focused on the marked decline in German school performance .

In France, the interior minister, Laurent ⁠Nuñez, said Saturday looked like “a very high risk” day, adding that 70,000 police and gendarmes, including elite units, would be deployed in an effort to quell violence on the sidelines of the new wave of protests.

Nuñez said late on Thursday that radical groups had called on social media for violent Halloween gatherings and that the biggest threat to public order would probably come after mainstream cost-of-living demonstrations had officially ended.

“We are seeing many calls from the labour movement, the radicalised far left and certain radicalised gilets jaunes [yellow vests], urging people to attend rallies on public streets starting at 8pm in many cities ‌across France,” he said.

The calls were “accompanied by various messages which are quite radical”, Nuñez added, including some demanding “revolution”. He said authorities would “tolerate zero excesses” and promised an “extremely firm” security response.

Measures introduced last weekend to protect shops would be reinforced, Nuñez said, and while peaceful demonstrations would be authorised, most would not be permitted “in city centres, where there is a risk of public disorder”.

In Paris, two separate marches planned by unions and gilets jaunes through the city centre have been banned. Instead, police have authorised a single march in the far south-east. An appeal by organisers against the decision to exclude them from the centre was rejected late on Friday night.

The interior ministry has said 410,000 people marched last Saturday, when a strong police presence mostly prevented a repeat of the widespread violence and looting that swept French cities during a first wave of mass protest on 17 October .

Unions and the gilets jaunes movement protesting over low wages, the cost of living and deteriorating public services have joined school and university students calling for better learning conditions, with a nationwide ​strike called for 5 November.

Government measures to address the students’ demands – including replacing a creaking university admissions platform and providing loans to local authorities for school renovations – did not go far enough, student leaders said.

title: Wahoo CEO talks finances, artificial intelligence and the company's 'next big opportunity'
author: josh.croxton@futurenet.com (Josh Croxton)
text:
Wahoo Fitness has returned to year on year growth following its recapitalisation in 2023, CEO Gareth Joyce has revealed.

Speaking exclusively to , Joyce opened up on a broad range of subjects, including why it took so long to update the Kickr Core despite growing the Kickr to its sixth iteration, why it launched a treadmill, the reasoning behind its partnership with Coros, and why 2038 is going to be a heck of a busy year.

He outlined a business very much with cycling still at its centre, but explained that running taking increasing amounts of importance. And he explained that there’s a busy product roadmap ahead, with "seven or eight" launches in the pipeline for 2027 following a year spent reorganising development

Joyce, an engineer and keen cyclist and runner who joined Wahoo in 2024, had never worked in the bike industry before and admits he wasn’t an obvious candidate for the CEO role, but that his then-recent experience talking a company through Chapter 11 bankruptcy made him perfectly qualified given Wahoo’s financial turbulence at the time.

He sees his role as bringing a sense of corporate structure to a startup business. He explained that Wahoo’s foundations were built on innovation, but its scale no longer supports that model of working.

"It’s no longer just a startup," he said. "We’ve got a large customer base that you have a responsibility to."

Asked whether the changes following Wahoo’s recapitalisation are working, Joyce’s answer was pretty conclusive.

"We’ve had very strong growth coming out of that," he said. "We have a great brand, great product, very committed customer base, and there were some things we needed to fix in the business which we paid attention to early on.

"We’ve seen growth year over year in all of the years since the recapitalisation, and I expect this year to be the same."

Naturally, he declined to provide any actual figures, so the extent of Wahoo’s profitability will have to remain unknown, but he affirmed that key "operational changes" are key to the business’s newfound momentum.

Among those changes was burying the hatchet with Zwift , with whom Wahoo was in a year-long lawsuit, after Wahoo claimed the Zwift Hub smart trainer infringed on its patents.

"If we work together, we can grow the industry," he said. "That was what Eric [Min, Zwift co-founder and CEO] and I set out to achieve."

The ball had already begun rolling on this before Joyce’s appointment. The lawsuit was settled in September 2023, the Kickr Core Zwift One launched in March 2024, and Joyce was appointed in April. But he says working with Zwift - and other brands - is now central to how Wahoo should expand. An example of this includes Wahoo’s partnership with competitor brand Coros.

Product plans and clearer priorities

Joyce argued that Wahoo’s innovation and its ability to come up with good ideas can make it difficult to decide which to pursue.

"You tend to become a little chaotic with your product strategy because every idea is a good idea," he said. "When you try and make every product that you think is a good idea, you end up distributing your resources and a distributed focus."

His solution to this was to revisit the company’s mission of "building the better athlete in all of us" and judge product ideas against it. Cycling remained – and still remains – the foundation, with indoor trainers, GPS computers and surrounding accessories supplying the data an athlete needs, but this is underpinned by software. The new Wahoo app was quietly rolled out this year, after a long period of beta testing.

The revised strategy also meant an overhaul of its product launch cycles, which explains some of the recent quiet on the launch front.

"This year was a pretty lean year of releases for us, which was by design," Joyce explained. "Last year, when we kind of reset the product strategy, we then had to reset the engineering program."

He expects the results to become more visible in 2027.

"Next year we have a pretty healthy set of product launches. I think we have seven or eight in the pipeline," he says. "I’m currently testing three of them as we speak. In fact, some of them are lying on my desk."

Unfortunately he turned down my invite for a game of show and tell, despite me awkwardly presenting the Wahoo Elemnt Bolt 2 that was lying on my desk.

Alongside that reset is a longer-term change to Wahoo’s product cycles and release cadence.

I asked why the Kickr Core went from 2018 to 2025 without any update, while the flagship Kickr trainer grew to its sixth iteration – seven if you count the Kickr Move.

"There was no rational reason for that replacement cadence," Joyce conceded. "The market was not demanding changes that quickly."

Wahoo is now working around different cycles for different categories: roughly three years for bike computers, four for indoor trainers, and six for heart rate monitors and treadmills.

I joked that he’s going to have a busy 2038 when those cycles overlap in their 12th year, to which he was keen to re-emphasise the use of the word "roughly" and affirmed that those are loose assumptions, rather than a fixed calendar.

The slowed approach also reflects his view on indoor cycling, and the slowing nature of the technology’s innovation.

"I think it’s now entering that phase of iterative development rather than disruptive technology," he said. "That’s not to say it’ll never happen, but just right now, there’s not something that we see on the horizon of, let’s say, five years, that would be disruptive in nature."

He immediately qualified that by adding "that doesn’t mean we’ve thought of everything."

Wahoo didn’t cut its teeth in running, but in 2024, Wahoo launched a treadmill known as the Kickr Run. As Joyce explains, the plan was to take the formula that saw Wahoo transform indoor cycling, and apply it to another sport.

It’s not quite had the same uptake in the 2.5 years since it launched as the smart trainer, but nevertheless Joyce sees it as an important growth category, and one where there’s plenty of opportunity for innovation and disruption.

"Treadmills, for a very long time, have been terrible products," he says.

And to that end, the Coros partnership adds weight to Wahoo’s move into running, but also demonstrates where Joyce believes Wahoo should avoid spreading itself thin.

The Elemnt Rival smartwatch can’t hold a candle to the quality of launches from market leader Garmin, nor can Wahoo keep up with their annual release cycle. Instead, rather than invest in a complete watch range to compete directly, it chose to work with Coros.

"To develop multiple SKUs is a very big investment, takes a lot of time, and would distract our attention from the rest of the strategy," he explained.

The goal is to provide access to products for cycling and running, indoors and outdoors, developing those products in house where possible, and partnering with others where not.

Connecting indoor and outdoor training

Joyce recognises that many of its customers aren’t exclusively doing one sport, nor are they only doing it indoors or out.

"That boundary is no longer in and out of your house. It’s just cycling," he explained.

And that’s where the Wahoo software offering comes into play. Wahoo has had multiple apps running concurrently for years, one controlling hardware and another providing training solutions, and Joyce is relieved at the recent consolidation.

"If our mission is building the better athlete in all of us, and I can’t tell you whether you’re becoming a better athlete or not, then it’s kind of hard to make that brand play."

If he can reduce the number of apps, or streamline the way in which the heart rate monitor, GPS computer and smart trainer all talk to third party suppliers, efficiencies can be found.

Two approaches to artificial intelligence

When asked about AI, Joyce separated Wahoo’s use of the fast-growing tech into two buckets: internally, how the brand uses it day to day, and externally, i.e. what AI integration might offer customers. Within the business, AI is already used extensively across software, firmware and hardware engineering.

"We’ve seen significant acceleration in our development cycles of products, particularly software," he said, pointing to faster app updates as one example.

He also said AI is being leveraged to help his Customer Service team resolve issues more quickly, while remaining entirely human.

However, for consumer-facing features, such as the AI Coach revealed by Zwift this week , or the AI-based adaptive training used by TrainerRoad, Joyce is more cautious. He believes customers may prefer to use AI services they already pay for, whether that’s the aforementioned, or a direct account with Claude or Chat GPT.

Voicing that customer’s perspective, he said: "I don’t want five licences for AI accounts. I want you to be able to pass me the data where I want it."

That helps explain why Wahoo has yet to commit to a consumer AI offering, despite the fast pace of the industry. Where Joyce does see an opportunity, however, is in Wahoo’s enormous database of accumulated workout data.

"We have records of workout data that goes back over a decade. We have the capability to translate that data into meaning, which is the next big opportunity we see, which we’re now starting to work on using machine learning and AI."

And for that database of workout data, Joyce’s data is as prevalent as any others.

"I love cycling. I love my running. To be able to go out on a Saturday and do a long ride and test stuff... yes, you could technically say that’s work, but for me it’s not."

title: How Herta compared to Perez in latest 2027 audition
author: Josh Suttill
text:
Colton Herta might still somehow be one point short of a Formula 1 superlicence after a bizarre error, but his latest Cadillac F1 outing was an important audition to replace Valtteri Bottas next year.

An incorrect calculation of his superlicence points (verified at the time by the FIA) means Herta erroneously thought completing 30 laps in his fifth FP1 outing of the season in Mexico would be enough to take him to the 40-point threshold required to finally earn him the superlicence he's been chasing for years.

"I was literally walking to go do the media stuff [after FP2], that was like the first time I had heard about it," Herta said on Friday evening.

"Obviously, we were still doing our meetings and whatnot, so I haven't talked to anybody about it. As far as I was concerned, going into the weekend, if I did 100km here, I would have 40 [points].

"So, I'm not sure what's changed, or why stuff has changed, or if it even has. I have to wait and see. I think a lot of the people that I want to talk to about this are still in the meeting. Maybe I'll have a little bit more clarity this evening."

Cadillac has gone beyond the mandated four rookie practice outings and given Herta a fifth session in Mexico to get him an extra point. It will run him again to get the final point, and had planned to anyway before the bizarre calculation error emerged.

But his Mexico outing wasn't a case of Herta simply cruising around to get the mandated 100km of running to get the point. He was given an extensive programme that wasn't too dissimilar to the one conducted by Perez - his 2027 team-mate, should Herta secure Bottas's race seat.

Herta's FP1 starts with an 11-lap stint on the hard tyres with a best lap of 1m22.452s, 1.067s slower than Perez's on the same tyres.

Herta tells his engineer he's "leaving a lot on the table" in sector one, but he's told that's where he's actually faster than Perez; instead, he's leaking time in sectors two and three.

This continues when he switches to the medium tyres, completing back-to-back stints on them with only a brief pitstop to go half a turn down on the front wing - a microadjustment to reduce the angle.

It's on that second run when Herta completes his personal best lap, a 1m21.365s, on what are seven-lap-old tyres.

Perez, by contrast, is able to complete his fastest lap on three-lap-old tyres during his first medium-tyre stint.

The actual gap between them is 0.970s. Perez puts together his best three sectors; if you combine Herta's, he closes slightly to 0.817s.

The Esses, in particular the Turn 10/11 right-left, are particularly challenging for Herta as he has to abandon one lap on the hard tyres when he cuts that corner, while another is wrecked by a wide moment there.

He complained of "big understeer everywhere in the low-speed" corners. He struggled with his approach into the Turn 12 right-hander that leads into the stadium section; Herta's minimum speed drops to 13km/h below Perez's, so here alone he ships around four tenths to Perez on their fastest short runs.

"The biggest thing was figuring out the timing for Turn 12," Herta said when The Race asked what his biggest limitation was.

"The stadium section I think was all right. More so Turn 12. And then kind of sorted it out for the long run.

"It's hard for the performance runs. You only do so many laps to sort it out in time. So unfortunately I didn't do that well. But for the long run it was better."

Herta's claim stacks up as he generally halves that time loss in Turn 12 during his longer run at the end of the session.

This is on average around eight tenths slower than Perez's, although it's hard to know the exact fuel loads of both cars.

Herta called it the "most consistent part of my running", and the data backs that up with only a half-second variation in his laptimes over a seven-lap stint. A decent effort for a driver inexperienced in F1 machinery.

Watching his FP1 onboard versus Perez, it was clear Herta needed more steering input around the lap and he was advised to better manage his throttle usage out of Turn 11 - corner exits being key to getting the most out of the 2026 power units.

He's still adapting from his usual aggressive style that worked so well for him in IndyCar, "where without power steering you can be more aggressive".

"You can have two or three or four inputs into the corner [in IndyCar], whereas in the Formula 1 car it's kind of useless effort," said Herta.

"You have to be smooth and really precise with the line. Whereas in IndyCar you can maybe get away with a little bit more of a raggedy style.

"Really, that's just down to the lack of power steering in the IndyCar."

F1 superlicence will be 'monkey off my back'

Asked if he saw himself as a realistic contender for the 2027 Cadillac seat, Herta said: "I hope so. I don't know why I'd be doing this [otherwise].

"I think Cadillac has shown a lot of faith in me in doing all these FP1s. They put a lot of resources behind me to get me ready to be in the F1 seat.

"I hope that's all reciprocated, and I can make it."

He added: "As far as 'now or never' - I don't think I can go back to IndyCar and have another chance in Formula 1. Whether that means next year or the following year. I really don't know what the plan is at the moment.

"We'll have to wait and see. I think some decisions hopefully will be made within the next month.

"It would be great the sooner the better to know going into November. You want to know what you're doing next year. For me, that's the main thing, is to know what I'm doing next year."

Herta said "social media blows things up a lot more than in reality" so he's remaining calm amid rumours of him graduating to F1.

But he did admit it will be a relief when he finally gets to the 40 superlicence points.

"Just maximising. Doing everything better. There's always time to find," Herta said when asked what he wants from his next FP1 outing.

"Just being able to maximise the short run and being able to maximise the long run. Probably a bit more in the short run than the long run.

"But I think every time I get in the car I feel more comfortable and I'm able to push a bit more.

"So I think once I kind of get that superlicence and that monkey off my back, then you can really kind of push everything as hard as you want to."

The Race understands Cadillac was impressed with the job Herta did in Mexico, even if his ultimate pace was adrift of Perez's.

It sees solid progression along Herta's F1 outings, and he remains a strong contender for a 2027 seat. At the same time, so do incumbent Bottas and the likes of Yuki Tsunoda and Mercedes reserve driver Fred Vesti.

Vesti was particularly brash after FP1, where he was only 0.111s adrift of championship leader Kimi Antonelli in the sister Mercedes.

"I've got my eyes on that [Cadillac] seat," he said. "I believe I would be very, very good in that car, and to be in F1 has been my goal ever since I started driving.

"I'm more motivated than ever; I'm extremely hungry to be on the grid."

George Russell, who Vesti replaced for FP1, even said he told Mercedes: "I want to ensure that he [Vesti] gets an opportunity to show what he can do; that's the least that we could do."

It was probably as strong an audition as Vesti could have hoped to make for the seat.

And he wasn't the only rookie to set an eye-catching pace in FP1.

Tsolov's impressive debut

Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov made the most of his F1 weekend debut to make his case for promotion to a race seat next year, lapping just 0.13s off Arvid Lindblad based on their headline laptimes on softs, and lapping two tenths quicker on mediums.

To that we must add the caveat that there was evidence of differing energy strategies, with Lindblad often faster on the back straight and Tsolov stronger on the main straight - with Lindblad suffering one of the most extreme drop-offs in speed in the field prior to braking for Turn 1.

Although Tsolov had a couple of laps deleted for track-limits violations, he was a little quicker than Lindblad in sector three, although he consistently lost time through and out of Turn 3. He was also perhaps a little conservative on the brakes into Turn 1 at the start of his best lap, perhaps not helped by the distraction of Isack Hadjar's Red Bull cruising off line approaching the corner. This was on the third push lap of his performance run on softs.

Tsolov also had a problem with the seat impeding the bloodflow to his right leg. After setting his fastest lap, he reported that "I'm running out of blood in my right leg, I cannot feel my leg", and then suggested that "the seat is compressing my leg and my blood stopped". He returned to the garage and was able to return to the cockpit for another run after briefly standing up inside the car.

"I've actually had that a few times before driving in F2," said Tsolov. "It's just the seat, I think, being a bit tighter than what we would like in my right leg. So my blood closed off.

"When you press the full throttle, you move up into the seats, so you kind of compress your legs. That was the thing, I couldn't feel it. It was a dead leg, pretty much. You get the tingly feeling. And then it just came back, obviously. I had to shake it out and after two, three minutes, it came back."

Slater's 'difficult' F1 debut

Formula 3 runner-up Freddie Slater's F1 session debut was best summed up by the radio message he received, in which it was described as "a very difficult session from a technical point of view".

That was an understatement, as he took the chequered flag after completing only 13 laps spread across six runs. Not that this was through any fault of the 18-year-old's.

He started out with three single-lap runs. The first two of those focused on gathering aerodynamic data, with aero rakes mounted behind the front wheel and a nose change in between.

He then should have been able to settle into a longer run on the hard Pirellis starting on his fifth lap, only to be told "we have to box this lap, we have an issue", entering Turn 7. This was because a fan had been left in the right-side sidepod cooling inlet, meaning Audi was fined €7500 for releasing the car in an unsafe condition.

The team then sent Slater back out, but he was immediately called back in for a lengthy stay in the garage.

He was able to return to the track with 11 minutes remaining, on a set of mediums. On his first push lap of the session, he posted a 1m22.451s, running deep in Turn 6 and compromising Turn 7. Then, on the second attempt, he locked up the front-left into Turn 1 and had to cut across the grass.

The resulting flatspot meant he had to pit to switch back to hards, on which he had one push lap that stood at his fastest of the session - elevating him to 21st ahead of Herta. That put him 1.337s behind team-mate Nico Hulkenberg, which in the circumstances of his disrupted session and posting his best time on hards on only his second full flying lap was very respectable.

"It's motorsport and that's how things go," said Slater of his stop-start running.

"Of course, it was a bit frustrating obviously not to get many, many laps, but overall that one lap that I did do was actually pretty good compared to relevant data. And a really historic day for Audi to have their first junior driver in the car.

"It's a very special day, so we look at the positives and then we focus on the results."

title: ‘The last fortress’: historic Athens cafe closes as countercultural area gentrifies
author: Helena Smith in Athens
text:
Mouria coffeehouse unable to renew lease in Exarchia, known for leftwing solidarity, resistance and radicalism

I t has been the hangout of writers, artists, poets and politicians, doctors and lawyers, radicals and revolutionaries for as long as anyone can remember. And for 44 years, Christos Vanas, the proprietor of Mouria, has let them all in.

Every day at 7am, the taciturn former waiter has been the first man to step inside the historic cafe in Exarchia, the heart of leftwing Athens . It is a ritual he has kept punctiliously, opening up the famous gathering place before he himself has had his first coffee.

“Only Saturdays are different,” says his daughter Areti, drawing on a Karelia, the aromatic Greek cigarette that, like Mouria, has been around for more than a century. “By 5am, he is here serving tsipouro and other [alcoholic] spirits to warm up the stallholders of the street market outside.”

But this weekend will be Vanas’s last. After a send-off expected to last into the small hours, the cafe’s large, iron-framed doors will shut forever on Sunday when patrons walk out of the mosaic-floored institution. It will be the closing act in a drama that began with the expiry of the premises’ lease last summer.

“It will be as if a friend died,” sighs Nontas Papayannis, a retired barrister who has frequented the cafe for the past 20 years. “Another change to Exarchia, but also another loss in a Greece that is dying before our eyes.”

Born and bred in the neighbourhood long viewed as the nerve centre of Athens’ counterculture scene, the blue-eyed septuagenarian has also kept to a regime, rocking up at his favourite watering hole “at least four times a week” within an hour of the clock striking noon.

Stelios Goutis , 83, is an actor who trod the boards for more than six decades before his fame broadened playing Papa Triantafyllos, a priest with a penchant for a tipple or two in the TV series Hara’s Cafe . He waxes lyrical about“the calming effect” of traditional eateries that have had such an outsized role in the lives of Greeks.

“A visit here is the route to relaxation,” Goutis says with thespian flair at one of Mouria’s marble-topped tables. “You stop by after work. You down a tsipouro or two, you meet friends you may or may not have arranged to meet, and all the pressures of daily life slip away. It’s a form of psychotherapy. When it goes, we’ll look back at it as a memory of good times even if it is a loss, too.”

Both men were among the 7,500 signatories of an online campaign that urged the Greek culture ministry to have the cafe declared a protected heritage site when the building’s owners announced they would not be renewing its tenancy in an area fast undergoing gentrification. The culture ministry failed to intervene.

Few districts in downtown Athens are more redolent of resistance, leftwing solidarity, radicalism and anarchist foment than Exarchia. Its spirit of anti-authoritarianism dates back to the uprising at the nearby Athens Polytechnic, an event that led to the death of dozens of students but is credited with the collapse of rightwing military rule in 1974, barely 35 years after the nation’s bitter civil war.

But with tourist numbers in the Greek capital more than doubling over the last decade, the neighbourhood of narrow, graffiti-daubed streets has also been discovered by investors, catering to the tastes and needs of foreign visitors.

“We were like the last fortress here,” says Areti, dressed in a black leather jacket and Dr Martens boots, the garb favoured by the area’s more youthful residents. “We didn’t change our menu, we didn’t raise our prices or serve Aperol spritzes and cafe lattes. It’s about nostalgia and we’ll leave with our heads held high.”

For Greeks raised in Exarchia, it was an unnerving experience to walk streets that were no longer recognisable, she lamented. “So much has changed. Everywhere you look there are new shops with signs in English and buildings turned into suites and short-term rentals. You could be anywhere.”

For many, the last straw had come when travel platforms began advertising tours of the hangouts in Exarchia patronised by hardened leftists. “There have been groups outside the cafe,” says Areti, her eyes firmly focused on her footwear. “What to say?”

Mouria is not alone. Its closure is emblematic of the decline of traditional coffee houses across Greece, even if the proliferation of third-wave and Italian-style cafes in more recent years has earned the country the reputation of having “a cafe economy”.

In villages far and wide, kafeneia once considered the life and soul of communities are vanishing, turbocharging depopulation.

But in Exarchia, among local people so fervently opposed to corporate culture, the end of the landmark coffeeshop on the corner of Charilaou Trikoupi and Kallidromiou streets is also part of a concerted effort to alter the neighbourhood’s traditional leftwing identity. Anger has similarly mounted over the construction of a metro station in Exarchia’s main square, championed by the centre-right government as a way of cleaning up a district that many conservatives regard as an affront to their own ideology. The public work, which has resulted in increased policing, has deprived residents of their one open space to gather.

“Exarchia is perhaps the only neighbourhood in Athens where the leftwing concept of the ‘revanchist city’ is applicable,” notes Nicos Souliotis, a sociologist at the National Centre for Social Research. “State policies are clearly aimed at imposing social discipline and control. The activism we have seen around Mouria is about defending the neighbourhood’s identity and established way of life.”

For Maria Tsampra, another longtime veteran of the cafe and a former employee of the defunct leftwing daily newspaper Eleftherotypia, the sociologist is spot on.…

title: Acosta wins chaotic Sepang MotoGP sprint
author: Eden Hannigan
text:
Pedro Acosta claimed victory in a bizarre Sepang MotoGP sprint that was threatened by rain late on.

Acosta came out on top of a four-way battle for the race win, prevailing by 0.578s over Marc Marquez, who increased his championship chances with second place.

Marquez is now 19 points up on the absent Jorge Martin, and 52 points clear of Marco Bezzecchi.

His brother Alex Marquez had got the start from pole position and led uncontested for four laps until he slid out of the race lead at Turn 14.

The lead was then inherited by Ai Ogura, who had moved up to second place after an aggressive opening corner tussle with Marc.

Spots of rain meant the white flag came out on lap two, allowing riders to swap bikes - with Jack Miller immediately prepared to take the gamble, but his Pramac Yamaha team not ready with his second bike, which frustrated him to no end.

Iker Lecuona, Joan Mir and Franco Morbidelli were the first group to come in and successfully switch on lap five, but were setting times almost 10 seconds off the leaders’ pace, with Maverick Vinales the only other rider electing to change towards the end of the race.

In the tricky conditions the top four bunched up, Ogura managing to hold off the challenges until Acosta attacked with three laps to spare.

Although Ogura responded to the initial overtake from Acosta, he eventually ceded the position and slumped to fourth as his wet-weather demons made him no match for Marquez and Bezzecchi. He did, however, have a huge amount of breathing room to fifth-placed Fabio Di Giannantonio.

Pecco Bagnaia overcame Brad Binder in their battle for sixth, while Diogo Moreira and Enea Bastianini picked up the final sprint points in eighth and ninth.

title: Budget 2026: how to beat the new savings tax rates
author: Hilary Osborne and Rupert Jones
text:
John Healey’s budget offered a ‘sting in the tail’ for savers by raising tax rates but there are ways to ease the pain

S avers were both winners and losers in Wednesday’s budget . In his first outing as chancellor, John Healey dropped a plan to cut the cash Isa limit for under-65s but surprised everyone with an extra tax charge on savings and property income. His predecessor, Rachel Reeves, had already announced a plan to increase the income tax rates for savers and landlords that was due to take effect in April 2027. But Healey went further, adding an additional two percentage points to each of the rates.

Jason Hollands, managing director at wealth manager Evelyn Partners, describes the higher rates as a “sting in the tail” for savers.

However, he says: “There are practical steps savers can consider to mitigate this interest tax crunch, although the right approach will depend on their circumstances.”

The levels of tax, which will apply to savers across the UK, will be 24% for basic-rate taxpayers, 44% for higher-rate taxpayers and 49% for those on the additional rate. They come into effect on 6 April.

This means it will get harder to find savings accounts that beat inflation – especially if, as expected, that stays high next year.

Anna Bowes, personal finance expert at advice firm The Private Office, says if inflation hits 3.5%, with the new tax to pay, a saver who pays basic-rate tax will need to earn 4.61% gross interest to retain the value of their money.

A higher-rate payer will need 6.25% gross, and an additional-rate taxpayer will need 6.86%. Currently, she says, these higher two rates “are impossible as far as I am aware” to find on a standard savings account.

There are, however, allowances you can use that will protect some savings, meaning you can beat inflation with a lower-paying account.

Most people can earn a chunk of interest from their savings without facing any tax bill. You don’t have to pay tax on anything earned on money held in cash Isas , and the maximum amount you can put into one in each tax year is going to stay at £20,000.

This was set to be slashed to £12,000 for anyone aged under 65 from April 2027. But Healey has ditched that plan.

Aside from Isas, other things come into play that reduce the tax you pay on savings, or mean you don’t pay any tax at all.

Your tax-free personal allowance covers all of your income, and for the 2026-27 tax year, this is £12,570.

If your personal allowance isn’t fully used up by your wages, pension or other income, HM Revenue and Customs will apply it to your savings interest.

And there are two more savings allowances that people can benefit from.

There’s the personal savings allowance (PSA), which means basic-rate taxpayers can receive £1,000 of interest each financial year without paying any tax, and higher-rate taxpayers can receive up to £500. Additional-rate taxpayers don’t get any PSA.

Until a few years ago, you would usually have needed to have a huge amount saved before exceeding the £500 or £1,000 threshold, but with accounts currently paying 5%-plus, it is much easier to get caught out.

There’s also the “starting rate for savings,” which some people on a low income can get on top of the PSA, where you can earn up to £5,000 of interest without paying tax on it. To benefit, the rest of your income (for example, wages or pension) has to be less than £17,570 a year.

The Isa allowance governs how much you put in each year while the PSA is based on how much you get back.

How quickly you use up the PSA depends on your tax position. A basic-rate taxpayer who puts £20,000 cash into a non-Isa savings account paying 5% interest will earn annual interest of exactly £1,000 – so will use up their entire PSA. If they found a higher paying account, they would face 24% tax on all the interest over £1,000, so they’d hand over 24p of every £1.

For a higher-rate taxpayer it would only take £10,000 in the same account to wipe out their £500 PSA. They would pay a rate of 44% on everything they earned over £500 – 44p in the £1.

When it comes to Isas you can put in up to £20,000 every tax year, as long as you are over 18. Once money is in a cash Isa it is protected from tax forever, so over time you can build up a huge amount of savings that don’t attract tax, as long as you don’t withdraw them.

You do not have to leave it with the same provider. You can move around to get better rates – subject to individual account rules – so it is wise to make the most of this shelter.

If you have a substantial savings nest egg you might want to review where they are held. Experts always recommend that you have emergency funds that are easy to access, so do not let a small tax bill deter you from doing that.

But Hollands says it is worth checking that you are not holding too much in savings. “Holding more cash than you need for several years can mean missing out on the potential for longer-term investment growth,” he says.

Look at your family situation. Hollands says couples who are married, or in a civil partnership, should look at their savings and allowances together.

If you have both used your Isa and personal savings allowances, but one partner pays tax at a lower rate, he says transferring cash to them could reduce an overall family tax bill.

“But this needs to be a genuine transfer: the money becomes theirs, legally and in practice, and they must be free to decide what to do with it, so trust is key,” he says.

If you’re saving for a child’s future, consider putting it in their name instead of holding it yourself. Pay into their child trust fund, or junior Isa if they already have one, or set up a junior Isa. You can pay up to £9,000 a year into a junior Isa, and all the returns are tax-free.…

title: Storm warnings for Melbourne, Canberra, Sydney and Brisbane as cold front ‘packs a punch’
author: Australian Associated Press
text:
BoM predicts hail, damaging winds and possible flash flooding across Victoria, NSW and parts of Queensland into Sunday

Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast

Storm warnings are in place for multiple capital cities across Australia’s east and south-east as a severe weather front sweeps across the country.

Heavy rain, winds and thunderstorms are forecast to hit Melbourne and eastern Victoria throughout Saturday afternoon as a cold front meets warm, humid air.

The storm front is then expected to travel further east, impacting Canberra and inland NSW before reaching the east coast on Sunday, stretching as far as southern Queensland .

The Bureau of Meteorology warned of possible flash flooding in some areas and potentially destructive winds of over 125km/h that could bring down large trees or damage property.

Melbourne and parts of Victoria recorded moderate rainfall and some lightning on Saturday morning, with a more intense band of thunderstorms forecast into the afternoon.

“It’s this follow-up band of storms which could pack a punch,” BoM meteorologist Angus Hines said on Saturday.

The storms are expected to impact Melbourne, parts of Gippsland, the north-eastern ranges, and north-central Victoria, with damaging winds the greatest risk.

The risk area will extend further north through inland NSW into the evening – up to Queensland’s southern interior and along the NSW coast south of Sydney around Wollongong and the Illawarra.

The forecast in these areas includes possible damaging winds, heavy rainfall and large hailstones.

“Expecting some very active storms here a little bit later on in the day, mid to late afternoon for many of these areas, and potentially not until the evening hours by the time we’re looking at storms getting out towards the east coast,” Hines said.

The focus of concern will shift further north on Sunday, with heavy rain and storms around Brisbane during the afternoon and early evening.

Severe thunderstorms were most likely for parts of the NSW mid-north coast, the northern rivers, parts of the tablelands and the Hunter region, with possible hail, heavy rainfall, flash flooding and destructive winds of more than 125km/h.

Areas that had recorded heightened rainfall in the past fortnight were also at risk of flash flooding, Hines said.

“If you do live through this area, tomorrow is definitely a day you’ll want to keep a watch on the radar to see if any big storms are headed your way,” he said.

A broader area of potential concern for Sunday stretches from Newcastle, north of Sydney, up to Gympie on the Sunshine Coast.

A severe wind warning is also in place across the mountains of northern Victoria and southern NSW, with wind gusts of more than 100km/h recorded on Saturday morning.

title: Eight in 10 homes in London’s poshest postcodes now sell below asking price, Coutts finds
author: Lauren Almeida
text:
Sellers in areas such as Belgravia and Mayfair face hundreds of thousands of pounds in losses as property prices fall

Eight out of 10 properties in London’s most exclusive neighbourhoods – such as Mayfair, Belgravia and Knightsbridge – now sell below asking price, according to research by Coutts, which provides private banking services to wealthy clients.

Property prices in “prime central London”, which covers the city’s most expensive postcodes, have dropped 5% in the third quarter of 2026, as the slowdown in the UK’s property market hits its wealthiest residents.

It means some affluent people are facing hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of pounds in losses to the value of their homes, with properties selling at an average 10% discount to their asking price, Coutts found.

Prices in the highest end of London’s property market are now 14% below their peak in 2014, having been hit hard by Brexit, the Covid pandemic, higher property taxes and a surge in borrowing costs. Buying and selling agents in the capital have also reported a slowdown in interest from foreign-born buyers after the abolition of the non-dom tax regime.

Exclusive areas such as Knightsbridge and Belgravia, and South Kensington have been hit the hardest, Coutts said, with prices 30.8% and 26.9% below their peaks respectively.

Alex Webster, head of lending at the bank, said buyers and sellers at the top end of the market were taking a more cautious approach, even before the chancellor, John Healey’s, first budget this week.

Sellers will now be watching to see if the budget “encourages some of that delayed activity to return”, she said. “But financing conditions and the wider economic environment will continue to influence the market.”

There has been no change in the Bank of England base rate since last December but volatility in the bond market has driven up the swap rates that influence the pricing of fixed-rate mortgages.

While the Bank of England has kept its key interest rate on hold at 3.75%, expectations are growing that next week its monetary policy committee will vote to increase the rate for the first time in three years to 4%.

In the meantime, sellers in prime central London are increasingly shying away, Coutts found, with new listings down 14% compared with the previous quarter and available stock down by 6% year-on-year.

Transactions were 9.1% lower in the third quarter of this year, it said, with the biggest slowdown in the £2m-£5m band, where transactions were down 22.3%.

However, separate research from the estate agent Savills found that buyers at the very top end of the market are driving activity, with 26 transactions above £10m in the third quarter of this year, taking the total to 127 over the past year. Together, these sales were worth £2.88bn, it found.

title: Martin concedes 2026 MotoGP title is “already lost” after Malaysian GP withdrawal
Martin admits MotoGP title 'already lost' after Sepang withdrawal
author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
text:
Aprilia MotoGP rider Jorge Martin feels the 2026 title is "already lost" following his withdrawal from the Malaysian Grand Prix weekend - but intends to ride in Qatar next week.

Martin sustained a distal radius fracture in a crash during the Phillip Island sprint, but was back to riding just six days later at Sepang, in a desperate bid to keep himself in the championship picture and minimise the damage versus points leader Marc Marquez.

But Martin was forced to give up on his weekend after three sessions, withdrawing after Saturday morning practice.

"I tried, I tried my best, I tried to ride, but for sure the process of healing is still early," he explained afterwards.

"The healing is going really fast, but not enough to be efficient on the bike. I felt that I could ride with almost no pain, but for maybe one lap. After that I started to have a lot of pain, I couldn't be constant, so watching a bit the laptimes and my performance, we decided to stop, to try to wait.

"We thought together with the team that the effort I was doing was too much to continue and yeah, nothing to gain. It was just going to be very difficult even to score one point."

Martin said he just didn't have the requisite strength under braking - and made reference to his past efforts to shortcut recovery periods, particularly in an injury-laden 2025 and specifically in his return to racing in Qatar last year, in which he ran out of energy in the race, crashed and suffered a bad injury after being hit by a rival bike.

"It wasn't the best idea to continue," he said of this weekend, "because if I continue, it [shows] that I haven't learned anything from the past.

"This happened to me in the past and I didn't want to crash or have a worse injury because of trying to race like this."

Asked by The Race how he views the championship picture in light of his withdrawal, Martin admitted: "I think now I don't have to think about the championship. Maybe I can win it, but for me it's already lost.

"So for sure I will fight till the end, not only for me, because at the end of the day I'm already a champion [in 2024], but for my team, for my people, I will fight till the end, I will try again in Qatar. Otherwise I would stay at home and rest."

Martin trails Marquez by 10 points, with Marquez in position to triple or quadruple that lead at Sepang, having placed second in qualifying.

Though Martin will return to Spain right away, as referenced above he still intends to try and race in Qatar next weekend, assuming that round goes ahead.

"During this week the improvement was incredible. I was able to ride a MotoGP with a broken wrist, so it's crazy. And I was under two minutes [in laptime]! So I'm already proud of my performance.

"My target is to go to Qatar. I will go there and I will try. Then if my feeling is the same, then I will have to stop. But this we will see in Qatar."

author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
text:
Alex Marquez took pole position for MotoGP's Malaysian Grand Prix and the sprint, as title hopeful Jorge Martin withdrew from the Sepang weekend.

Martin, who fractured his wrist a week ago at Phillip Island, did three runs totalling eight laps in the 30-minute practice session before qualifying, and had to concede defeat in terms of continuing with the weekend.

"His feeling was better, to be honest, compared with yesterday, but he was not able to force in the braking," Aprilia team manager Paolo Bonora told MotoGP.com.

"The plan is to come back to Spain as soon as possible and to push on the recovery and to do his best to recover the situation. Coming back to Spain immediately, and then we check all together, during all the days, the situation, how it is improving, and we focus to have him in Qatar."

With Martin now consigned to a non-score at Sepang, points leader Marc Marquez was close to maximising his qualifying, ultimately just 0.070s short of beating his brother.

Alex Marquez had been the leader after the initial Q2 runs already, but was shuffled down to fifth by the end of the session - only to respond with a 1m56.493s that snatched pole from Marc.

Pedro Acosta on the KTM will join the pair on the front row, having followed the elder Marquez very closely on both Q2 runs.

Aprilia pair Ai Ogura and Marco Bezzecchi completed a top five covered by just 0.175s, with Fabio Di Giannantonio in sixth another 0.174s back from Bezzecchi.

Q1 pace-setter Johann Zarco was limited to just one Q2 run but used Di Giannantonio as reference and so helped himself to eighth place, slotting in on row three between Enea Bastianini and Franco Morbidelli.

Pecco Bagnaia, another Q1 graduate, ran 'off-sequence' in Q2 - doing his sole run mid-session, with no riders around him.

After setting what proved to be his fastest lap he went off at Turn 1 and broke the windscreen in anger with his fist - though would have anyway been unlikely to improve.

He placed 10th, ahead of Joan Mir and the injury-limited Maverick Vinales, who could not match his laptime from Friday.

Honda riders Luca Marini and Diogo Moreira trailed stablemate Zarco by three and four tenths respectively in Q1, so were short of advancing into Q2 - while the rest of the field was never really in the mix.

This included Gresini's Fermin Aldeguer stand-in Iker Lecuona, who has found Sepang the most difficult so far of the tracks he's ridden this season as a MotoGP replacement rider.
