title: Ferrari is fastest in Mexico - but not for reasons rivals expected
author: Jon Noble
text:
Ferrari’s rivals were right after all, but perhaps for the wrong reasons.

The talk ahead of the Mexico Grand Prix had been that Ferrari’s smaller turbo design would give it a clear advantage at the high altitude track because it would in theory struggle less in the thinner air.

So there was little surprise in the paddock when Charles Leclerc delivered a clean sweep of fastest laps in both FP1 and FP2 on Friday - confirming the Prancing Horse as the team to beat.

What was perhaps more interesting from what we saw though - and which could play a big role in how the rest of the weekend plays out - was that Ferrari’s advantage was not coming from its turbo getting its boost pressure up quicker.

Ferrari’s straight-line speed performance was notably lacking on the second and third straights. On its soft runs Leclerc was slowest of the top four teams into Turns 4 and 12.

As Lewis Hamilton, who was sidelined by a suspected power unit problem halfway through FP2, remarked: “If you look at the speeds to the Mercedes and the Red Bull, they're still massive.

"They're still quicker at the end of the straights, like they are in every race. So the turbo is just not making a difference. They are still pulling more at the end of the straights.

“I think we're still losing a good two or three tenths. But the car is behaving really well fundamentally. Our car works really well, seemingly on a track like this.”

Ferrari’s advantage in Mexico instead was coming from an area it has excelled in all season - low speed corner performance.

It was just marginally better through the first two complexes of corners (Turns 1-3 plus Turns 4-6) as well as taking a decent chunk out of the opposition from Turn 12 into the stadium section.

That trait meant that Leclerc had the consistency needed from the tyres to deliver the strongest long run of the afternoon - leaving rivals in no doubt about who was the benchmark.

But while the opposition clearly was happy to put that favourite status on Ferrari, that does not necessarily mean that all hope is lost for everyone else.

Others certainly saw enough in the data to think that there remains a big opportunity to fight at the front.

When we look at the long run averages, Lando Norris in the McLaren, plus the Mercedes and Red Bulls were not far behind what Leclerc delivered once you factor in the influence of cool down laps and traffic.

Mexican GP FP2 long run averages Russell (soft): 1m21.442s Antonelli (medium): 1m21.487s

Leclerc (medium): 1m21.163s Piastri (soft): 1m21.642s

Norris (soft): 1m21.319s Verstappen (soft): 1m21.490s

Hadjar (soft): 1m21.369s

It was a day where certainly not everybody delivered to their maximum, as drivers battled brake locking, bumps and rapidly rising tyre temperatures.

George Russell said: “Ferrari looked very strong and that was kind of the anticipation ahead of the weekend

“I think we are still not fully on top of the new package, I think we see there's some balance limitations we have that we're struggling to overcome.

"I would say currently for Kimi and I, we're probably more outside the window, similar to what we saw in Malaysia, than inside the window like Kimi [Antonelli] achieved in Austin. Hopefully overnight we can get it back there."

Things perhaps being a bit closer than they look at first glance is even more in play when you take into account that Verstappen’s afternoon was derailed by his clash with Liam Lawson that damaged his floor.

That left the Dutchman battling a disconnected balance throughout his long run as he was lacking some key parts - so you could anticipate a potential improvement there.

As Red Bull’s technical director Pierre Wache said: “Let's see tomorrow when the floor will be repaired and how the car is better or not.”

Wache certainly felt that Ferrari was not out of reach, especially considering it has been strong in the types of turns that Mexico is full of.

“I think in low-speed corners, since the beginning of the year, they are clearly on top of the game, and they have clearly a lot of downforce for low speed. After, let's see what we can extract. I think we are not far, and hope we can challenge them.”

While the indications are of an early Ferrari advantage based on what we have seen so far, there are some important factors that mean it still cannot sleep easy tonight.

The first element is that the long runs on Friday may not be totally representative of how things will play out in the race because of track temperature variations.

The late start for FP2, allied to conditions being a bit cooler, meant that the track surface was not as hot as it will be on Sunday.

Wache said it was not nailed on which would be the optimum tyre for the race.

“The tyres are overheating in the last sector,” he said. “Clearly, the main problem is in FP2 where the track [temp] reduced by more than 10 degrees.

“For the long run it was not very representative of what we'll see in the race Sunday. Then we have to be very careful on that aspect. So the deg will be higher, and maybe the medium will be better.”

The premium on cooling around Mexico means that the pace of the cars is limited more by managing that than their theoretical best - so that could have a big impact too on how things play out on Sunday.

Overtaking is already difficult here and following close behind a rival becomes far from ideal because of the consequences of engine and brake temperatures - so it is rarely a race where cars come through the field for the win. Clean air is invaluable.

The need for Ferrari to not be in the pack is further increased by its expected turbo advantage having not manifested itself with superb top speed - something rivals were happy to see.

As McLaren’s Oscar Piastri said: “I don’t think the turbo’s going to make as much of a difference as we thought.

“They if anything looked a bit slow on the straights so, let’s wait and see tomorrow, definitely in some circumstances it will help them but I think in normal conditions it’s not as big of a factor as we first feared.”

Put the 'track position is king' element on top of a likely one-stopper where there will not be strategy variation and it puts a huge premium on single-lap pace and delivering what is needed in Q3 to take pole position.

And how many Fridays this season have ended with Ferrari topping the timesheets, looking to have the long-run potential, but then falling flat when things get serious on Saturday afternoon? We only need to go back one weekend for the last time that happened.

Ferrari knows it has a weakness on Saturday based on it not being able to get its tyres as perfectly into the operating window as its rivals - and that could well prove critical in that fight at Mexico.

As Hamilton remarked after practice: “I think the car feels like it's capable of competing in qualifying. But I don't know what it is they [the others] do in quali. Everyone seems to take a step. I don’t know if we can eke out a little bit more tomorrow.”

At a track where the lack of downforce means tyres are sliding a lot more, everything may well come down to looking after those rears.

Even Norris, who was second quickest in the afternoon, reckoned that the key would be delivering at the right moment.

“The pace is definitely there but the field is incredibly tight at the minute, so it will come down to execution in tomorrow’s qualifying,” he said.

Ferrari team boss Fred Vasseur knows that rivals have maybe not got things together as well as hoped on Friday and will come back stronger.

So with things looking as tight as they are, amid what he says are “mega extreme” conditions, the fight for pole - which could be critical to the win - may well come down to simply who can keep their tyres alive the longest in qualifying.

“It's always a challenge in Mexico,” said Vasseur. “I think it was last year that everybody was in half a tenth until Turn 10 and then you had four-tenths’ difference in two corners. I think it will be the same tomorrow.”

title: Stewards penalise Verstappen, Lawson after “unacceptable” F1 Mexico GP practice clash
Hadjar summoned for alleged paddock misconduct
author: Samarth Kanal
text:
Isack Hadjar has been summoned by the stewards after alleged misconduct in the Formula 1 paddock at the Mexican Grand Prix.

The FIA stewards called the Red Bull driver to see them for "misconduct relating to an incident in the Formula 1 paddock".

The summons does not specify why Hadjar has been summoned.

A video has circulated on social media appearing to show Hadjar pushing someone who tried to take a selfie with him. It is however unclear whether this is the reason Hadjar has been called to see the stewards at 10.15am local time on Saturday.

As per the FIA's International Sporting Code, "any words, deeds or writings that have caused moral injury or loss to the FIA, its bodies, its members or its executive officers, and more generally on the interest of motorsport and on the values defended by the FIA" can carry a fine of up to €5000.

Fines of up to €20,000 can be applied in other cases and the FIA's sporting code says: "For very serious offences, more severe penalties under the ISC [international sporting code] may be imposed."

Aggravating or mitigating circumstances can however change the penalty imposed.

title: Verstappen and Lawson get grid drops for 'clumsy' Mexico clash
author: Jack Cozens
text:
Max Verstappen and Liam Lawson have each been given one-place grid penalties for their "clumsy" clash during second Formula 1 practice at the Mexican Grand Prix.

That incident occurred early in FP2 when Verstappen, on a prep lap, tried to lunge past Lawson - on a cooldown lap before another push - into the 90-degree Turn 12 right-hander.

Lawson stayed on the outside of Verstappen through that corner, which became the inside line for the Turn 13 switchback in the stadium section, before Verstappen cut across the track at Turn 14 and got ahead of the Racing Bulls driver, though only via contact that shattered the Red Bull's left-side bargeboard, with the resulting debris prompting a red flag.

Verstappen told Sky Sports F1 it was "not very smart behaviour" from Lawson, who (alongside team-mate Arvid Lindblad) has not yet been announced at Racing Bulls for 2027 and whom Verstappen characterised as "fighting for your seat".

Verstappen said of the incident: "At the end of the day, it's not going to change my weekend."

But the clash did have consequences.

In identical statements issued to both cars, the stewards said they considered both drivers' actions "unacceptable", in particular in respect of a "warning" given at the team managers' meeting earlier on Friday.

They said both Lawson and Verstappen had called the move "clumsy" and unnecessary - a word also used by Racing Bulls team principal Alan Permane when describing the contact.

It was that message given at the team managers' meeting that ultimately condemned Verstappen and Lawson to penalties.

"Noting that there had been similar incidents this year of actions between drivers in free practice, the stewards have decided to escalate the penalty from that of a formal warning to a grid position penalty particularly in view of the warning that had been provided at the team managers' meeting and consistent with other incidents involving contact between the cars in free practice in previous years," the stewards' decision read.

Both drivers were also given one penalty point for the transgression.

title: Verstappen and Lawson given grid penalties for Mexico practice collision
text:
Ferrari's Charles Leclerc led Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli in first practice at the Mexico City Grand Prix, where the Italian is poised to clinch his first world title.

Leclerc was 0.659 seconds quicker than Antonelli, for whom a ninth-place finish will secure the championship regardless of any other results.

Only a victory by his team-mate George Russell or Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton can theoretically stop Antonelli becoming champion on Sunday. Even then, Antonelli only needs ninth place if Russell wins and 10th if Hamilton does.

Third quickest in the session was Mercedes reserve Frederik Vesti, driving Russell's car, ahead of Hamilton.

Mercedes were one of 10 teams to choose this session to do one of their mandatory rookie sessions. Only Ferrari had both race drivers in their cars.

Mexico City is chosen by many teams to run their mandatory rookie sessions because the first session is traditionally unrepresentative as a result of the dirty track surface.

Japanese Ayumu Iwasa, in for Max Verstappen at Red Bull, was fifth fastest, ahead of Alpine's Pierre Gasly and Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso.

McLaren's Oscar Piastri, Haas driver Oliver Bearman and Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad completed the top 10.

Briton Freddie Slater's first outing at a grand prix weekend for Audi did not go to plan.

Problems - including the team sending him out with a cooling fan still blocking the entry to the car's right-hand sidepod - limited his running to 14 laps - about half a standard mileage.

But he did manage to get out for the final 20 minutes or so and set the 19th fastest time.

He was just behind another Briton, Luke Browning having his latest run in the Williams.

American Colton Herta, who Cadillac are considering promoting to F1 next year in place of Valtteri Bottas, was 22nd.

Governing body the FIA says Herta, a nine-time winner in Indycar, has now done enough miles to score the 40 points he needs to secure the superlicence required to race in F1.

title: Martin withdraws from Malaysian GP, putting MotoGP title hopes at risk
The cursed cruise: how the dream of never-ending luxury at sea became a nightmare
author: Oliver Holmes in Bangkok, Daniel Boffey in London and Adeshola Ore in Melbourne
text:
The MV Odyssey was billed as the ultimate escape from Donald Trump. Instead, the oil shock caused by his war has left passengers unceremoniously dumped in Cambodia

The idea was a never-ending retirement at sea, a continuous voyage around the globe. The promise to the passengers of the MV Odyssey cruise ship – many approaching the autumn of their lives – was that on the open seas they could cut loose from the troubles of the world. But the world had other ideas.

The end came in an announcement as stark as it was brief: they had seven hours to get off. They were going no further than Cambodia .

The Odyssey, owned by Florida-based Villa Vie Residences, had first set sail from Belfast, Northern Ireland, in October 2024 with an explicit offer: Donald Trump had been re-elected to the White House, and this was a way for those ill-disposed to the president to enjoy a four-year “skip forward”.

For $319,998, a couple seeking such an escape could head off to the high seas for the length of a presidential term and come back from their journey to nowhere when the danger had passed – or not. For those who had simply had enough, there was a permanent residency option for a few hundred thousand more. Depending on the package, there were also monthly fees on top, which covered food, drinks, wifi, wellness programmes and room cleaning. They would have access to a pool, a pickleball court, a theatre, several bars and a gym. Exotic port destinations would be visited along the way.

It was by no means cheap – but the Odyssey was quite accurately billed as the “affordable” option for those interested in such a cocoon. The pioneer in the world of “residential ships”, a vessel called MS The World, offered apartments that typically ranged from $2m to $15m, with the pampered passengers getting to choose where it would go. For that experience, there was a waiting list.

The Odyssey was not in that league. Rather than built as a residential ship, it had previously been a traditional cruise liner named MS Braemar. Under that name, it had been turned away from several ports in the Caribbean during the pandemic when its passengers became ill. Cuba finally allowed it to dock, but the vessel never went into service as MS Braemar again. It was sold off by Fred Olsen cruises and adapted by its new owners. Villa Vie described the three-decade-old restructured vessel as “an intimate residential cruise ship offering a new way to live”.

At 642ft (196 metres) long, it was a relatively small ship, but at such prices, and with the world being held firmly at bay, what could go wrong? Neither the more than 200 passengers on the Odyssey nor its cruise operator foresaw the consequences of Trump’s war in Iran. The reality was, there was no escaping the US president.

On Tuesday, Villa Vie Residences issued a statement. It had run out of money owing to the soaring price of oil. Monthly fuel costs per cabin in parts of Asia had risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800, placing it “under unsustainable financial pressure”, it announced.

“Since the conflict began in late February, we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port,” the company said, explaining the slow death of its business model. “Those measures have not been enough to offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs, and we have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses.”

The Odyssey’s passengers were told to pack up their belongings before being transported on buses into the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand. “We are working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and temporary living arrangements, and are supporting residents, crew, and employees as we evaluate restructuring and recapitalisation alternatives over the next 60 days,” the company said.

“People were shell-shocked, numb, crying,” said one passenger, Kit Cassingham from the US, who spent two years on the ship with her husband, Randy. They had made their cabin into a home, putting down their own rugs and pictures on the wall. “People were angry. They were hysterical. They were sad … Disbelief,” she added. “I mean, that whole gamut of, what is it, the five stages of grief.”

Most of the passengers on the Odyssey were Americans, travelling with an international group of 156 crew members, including a ship’s doctor and two nurses. Many of the passengers were retired or digital nomads. One woman, Holly Hennessy, had been living happily with her cat, Captain, since the ship set sail two years ago.

One couple, Lanette Canen and Johan Bodin, who said they had bought a cabin with a 15-year guarantee, had been documenting their life at sea on YouTube , including the lead-up to the fateful announcement. The signs of financial distress had been apparent for weeks, they said.

“I’m Mr Super Positive, and I’ve felt really drained the last two months,” Bodin recounted in a video.

Footage from inside the ship’s lounge on the final night showed residents drinking, as rumours spread that their voyage might be over. Cruise ship staff had requested each passenger contribute $1,800 to ensure the ship had funds to travel to Bangkok.

The next day, the couple posted an update showing the inside of their cabin as a voice on the loudspeaker said the ship’s operator had “unfortunately” been “unable to secure the fuel necessary to continue operations”. An email was sent requesting that everyone disembark by 2pm.

“We knew the worst-case scenarios, but we didn’t think it would come to reality, which it did,” said Rina Cavazza, a pilates instructor from Brisbane, Australia.

Another passenger, Sherrie Cornett, wrote on Facebook that they were “dropped unceremoniously in the middle of town, left to our own devices”.…

title: 76ers 98, Knicks 93: “Unfortunately it took us too long to show up tonight.”
author: Russell Richardson
text:
Last season, en route to a World Championship, the New York Knicks (2-4) took a pleasant detour in Las Vegas to collect the Emirates NBA Cup. The road to repeating the Cup win is rocky this season, with their Group B considered to be the toughest.

Tonight, they traveled to Pennsylvania to face the 76ers at the Xfinity Mobile Arena on a garish blue and gold cartoon court. This was their first Cup game of the season and the 482nd meeting between the two franchises. The Philadelphia 76ers (5-1) came in tied with Detroit for first place in the East. All night, the star-heavy squad showed the secret to their success so far this season—a stingy, sticky defense that limited New York to 32% perimeter shooting. Our heroes fell behind by double digits toward the end of the first quarter and stayed behind until the final two minutes of the game. Quoth Laurenpal, “Unfortunately it took us too long to show up tonight.” Despite a clutch bucket from Jalen Brunson (24 PTS, 8-22 FG) for the lead late in the fourth, Tyrese Maxey (27 PTS, 10-19 FG) and the Sixers were too strong to keep down. Your final: 98-93.

Through the first half of the first quarter, the home team had the edge, with Maxey, Joel Embiid (10 PTS, 7 RBS, 7 AST), LeBron James (20 PTS, 9 RBS, 8 AST), and VJ Edgecombe (13 PTS, 8 RBS) combining for 14 points. Across the floor, Karl-Anthony Towns (22 PTS, 12 RBS), OG Anunoby (9 PTS, 4-10 FG), Mikal Bridges (12 PTS, 3 STL, 5-8 FG), and Brunson had posted 11 for the visitors.

Part of the problem for our heroes was that Philly played an almost mistake-free opening frame, committing one foul and zero turnovers. And their defensive intensity—they’re top-five in the league—complicated every Knicks shot. When Tyler Kolek (2 PTS, 4 AST, 13 MIN) subbed in with about three minutes left, he was harassed into his first TO of the season. Further proof of that good D? The good guys shot just 27% in the first period.

On one sequence, Brunson dribbled against Maxey from 18 feet, left side, one-on-one. Maxey blocked him, but Cap retained the ball and swished a jumper on his second attempt. It was a rare instance of Maxey getting outplayed. He led all first-half scorers with 15 points. Brunson managed only seven points pre-intermission.

After a Philly timeout, Mike Brown sent in Landry Shamet (0 PTS, 0-3 FG, 16 MIN), Miles McBride (10 PTS, 4-8 FG, 24 MIN), and Andre Drummond (3 PTS, 6 RBS, 12 MIN). The guests missed five shots, during which time the hosts capitalized with interior scores. After surrendering eight unanswered points, the Knicks got relief when Josh Hart (7 PTS, 6 RBS, 31 MIN) delivered from deep. By the quarter break, the home team was up 29-21.

On to the second. Philly moved the ball well and was unafraid to drive the lane, as Maxey did with an emphatic throwdown. While Brunson rested—and Jose Alvarado sat out with a sprained ankle—Kolek continued to play. He gave up a second turnover. Cap checked back in around the seven-minute mark.

At the midway point, LeBron and Hart traded bombs from the perimeter. The differential reached 14 before the Knicks began to chisel it down.

McBride made some midrange shots from the elbow. It was nice to see a little more imagination in his usage, rather than just sticking him at the arc and waiting for a pass. He also grabbed a timely offensive board in the paint among Embiid and a couple of other big bodies.

Nevertheless, the Knicks couldn’t get a run going. A corner three by Bridges cut the gap to six, but Maxey chucked from deep for three of his own. In fitting fashion, Brunson couldn’t get open for a final shot, and the halftime buzzer buzzed without an attempt. Philly up, 53-44.

The Knicks had out-rebounded Philly (23-19) and shot slightly better from deep (32% to 29%), but Philly owned everything inside the arc. The Knicks took more than half their shots from deep and scored nothing on fast breaks, which is a tough way to keep pace while conceding so much inside. No Knick had reached double digits yet; KAT led the team with nine points.

Following intermission, Hart missed from deep, Bridges threw the ball to the front row, and Maxey scored five points. Philly went up by 14, matching its biggest advantage yet.

Finding the previous events intolerable, Brunson took the reins and commanded his squad on an 11-1 run. He scored seven straight during that burst, and Bridges redeemed his TO with a steal (ripping the ball out of Edgecombe’s mitts) and a longball. After that, Nurse needed a timeout for a breather and a regroup.

Whatever advice the coach imparted, it worked. Kentavious Caldwell-Pope and Anfernee Simons (21 PTS, 5-8 3PT, 31 MIN) hit triples, Philly tightened its defense, and LeBron attacked the cup. Soon enough, the Knicks trailed by ten again and gave us great concern about their ability to rally for a lead. After a Mike Brown timeout, two consecutive Shamet turnovers and another Simons jumper further pushed the score in the wrong direction. Too many one-and-dones were a problem. The Knicks wouldn’t quit and swung back, with McBride and Brunson reducing the hole to six, but a Simons bomb with five seconds to go closed the quarter at 77-68.

Jordan Clarkson, a sparkplug in Chicago, made his first appearance to start the final frame. Alongside him: Kolek, McBride, Anunoby, and Towns. They manufactured buckets, but surrendered them, too. Simons continued to rain buckets.

One of the surprising strengths of Clarkson’s game has been his offensive rebounding. When he flew through traffic to tip in a missed McBride three, it wasn’t quite a Game Four highlight, but it sliced the differential to three. That was the closest the team had been since midway through the first. But they taketh, they giveth. Embiid drilled a jumper at the other end, and with six-ish minutes left, Mike Brown needed a timeout.

Out of the timeout, Brown’s lineup was Brunson, Clarkson, Bridges, Hart, and Towns. The choice to go with Clarkson’s offense over Anunoby’s defense was a curious gamble. Both teams were careening up and down the court at top speed, even that geezer LeBron, and when KAT rifled a bomb, a mere two points separated the two teams.

In crunch time, Brunson had a look but bricked from deep. The ball came back to him, but LeBron worked him into a jam, with Jalen having to throw the ball off him out of bounds. After the inbound, Jalen had another chance—and connected from deep for their first lead since the opening minutes!

LeBron answered with a fadeaway at 1:10 to reclaim the lead. After Cap missed a floater, Edgecombe knocked down his first triple of the night. 94-90, 34 seconds remaining.

Cap got the ball again, iso-ing on Edgecombe, but slipped and turned his right ankle in a legitimately terrifying moment. Edgecombe was called for a ticky-tack foul (foot-to-foot contact). Brunson made one freebie. 94-91, 31 seconds. At the other end, Maxey hustled through traffic and missed on a contested layup, but ’Bron swept in for the putback. That put the score at 96-91 with 12 seconds on the clock. New York needed a miracle, but the gods were fresh out. Anunoby made a dunk, and Philly added two free throws. Ball game.

Back to work on Monday, at home against the Nets. Safe travels, Knickerbockers.

title: Albanese looks for reset on world stage as ‘spot fires burn’ domestically and likely interest rate hike looms
author: Ben Doherty and AAP
text:
The prime minister will speak with King Charles and others at the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda

Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast

As “summit season” begins, reaffirming ties with fellow leaders on the world stage could be a circuit breaker for Anthony Albanese amid domestic and economic woes, analysts have said.

But a likely interest rate hike , triggered by higher-than-expected inflation , while the prime minister is overseas will make his job – and the treasurer’s – even harder.

Albanese is attending the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda from Saturday.

He will hold talks with King Charles III and allies including the UK and Canadian prime ministers, Andy Burnham and Mark Carney, at the biennial meeting.

The discussions will constitute a well-needed reset after controversies over grant funding and pressures on inflation , according to Dr Zareh Ghazarian, an associate professor of politics at Monash University.

“It is a strategically important time for him,” Ghazarian said.

“He’s got a lot of spot fires burning domestically but this is going to be an opportunity for him to present himself to be much more on the front foot.

“There’s a lot of pressure, so this trip could just be a moment to reset the political debate for people … this is a critical moment to present himself as a world leader amongst other world leaders.”

Albanese will be away when the Reserve Bank hands down its next interest rate decision on Tuesday, with markets tipping a rise to 4.85%.

It would be the fifth interest rate hike in 2026 and a challenging situation for the government to navigate, amid continuing cost-of-living pressures.

Albanese emphasised the value of attending Chogm before his departure on Saturday morning. In a crowded international calendar, the Commonwealth is occasionally dismissed as irrelevant, an anachronistic relic of a former imperial era.

“The Commonwealth heads of government meeting is an important forum,” Albanese said.

“[It provides] an opportunity to work with some of our closest partners on shared challenges, including climate change, the preservation of our oceans, trade and investment and the rise of AI.”

The issue of historical slavery, and its ongoing legacy, is likely to be a key point of contention at Chogm.

Burnham, writing in the Guardian , said having “difficult conversations to safeguard the Commonwealth for the future” was the right thing to do.

“Not just because it is in our interests, but because the Britain I believe in is confident, decent and brave. We led the world in abolishing slavery – and we can show leadership again today.”

He called the transatlantic slave trade a “brutal and barbaric violation” of people “treated as property and worked to their deaths”.

“I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions of people, and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today,” he wrote.

Caribbean nations have made renewed calls for Britain to apologise for its role in selling enslaved people for profit, and for reparations, as the King toured the Caribbean.

Burnham said: “Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process and I am open to them.” But he said he did not believe reparations for slavery was the “ right answer ”.

Australia would not be a bystander to any debate about slavery and the slave trade.

Across the 19th and early 20th centuries, Australian agriculture relied heavily on “blackbirding” : the use of coercion, trickery, bribery and kidnapping to bring more than 60,000 Pacific Islanders to work as indentured labourers in Australia, primarily on Queensland’s sugar and cotton plantations.

The Chogm meeting will kick off a busy end to the year overseas for Albanese, with international summits in Turkey, the Philippines, China and the US in coming weeks.

The foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, is currently in Atlanta, Georgia for the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting. The start of that conference has been overshadowed by the presence of Russia, with about one-third of the countries attending vowing to boycott the customary “family photo” if the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, was involved.

title: US cancels G20 ‘family photo’ after Australia, UK and others refuse to appear with Russia
author: Ben Doherty and Associated Press
text:
Marco Rubio pulls plug on traditional photo op at meeting of foreign ministers after about one-third of countries threaten boycott

The traditional “family photo” to open the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting has been abruptly cancelled in the US after a host of nations – including Australia and the UK – refused to appear beside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov.

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, pulled the plug after several European officials, the UK and Australia made it known they would boycott or walk out of the snapshot that often kicks off such international gatherings.

Rubio still opened the talks in Atlanta with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade.

“We are in a critical moment,” Rubio told his colleagues. “We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises.”

About one-third of countries at the talks made it known they would not appear beside any Russian representatives.

European Union nations had made clear they would boycott any photo with the Russians. “In no case will there be a family photo with European partners and Mr Lavrov together because … there is no normality with Russia,” Germany’s foreign affairs minister, Johann Wadephul, warned ahead of Friday’s session.

The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, promised similar. “We do not engage in that way with the Russians and have not for a number of years,” he said.

During the meeting’s opening session, Australia’s foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in front of Lavrov and said Russia’s illegal war had affected international markets and worsened global food security.

A spokesperson for Wong said Australia supported the US decision to cancel the group photo. “Australia has been clear and consistent: we will not normalise Russia’s brutal and illegal invasion of Ukraine.

“Our focus at the G20 remains on the important work before us and addressing the challenges facing the global economy.”

The schism in Atlanta is yet further evidence of the rupture caused by the Trump administration’s attempt to reintegrate Russia and its isolated president, Vladimir Putin, into the international community despite Putin’s ongoing war against Ukraine.

Diplomats who attended the opening session described it as cordial but said Russia’s position on Ukraine is unyielding – as is its opposition to Poland’s membership in the G20.

Those disagreements, which also include the Trump administration’s not inviting G20 member South Africa over the objections of others, will probably prevent the foreign ministers from producing a joint communique when the meetings wrap up on Saturday, participants said.

That did not surprise the Polish deputy prime minister and foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, representing his country at its first time as a guest at a G20 meeting.

“We have wars going on and we have participants in those wars around the table, so it’s very difficult to agree a common line,” he told reporters.

Several participants, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the closed-door talks, said all had agreed to try to overcome their differences despite the long odds and to work to make next month’s G20 leaders’ summit hosted by the president, Donald Trump, in Florida a success.

Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous meetings, was not invited this year, with US officials saying it was a deliberate choice to include only formal members of the group. Poland, not a member, is seeking formal membership with US support.

But missing from the invitation list was South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group. South Africa is embroiled in several bitter disputes with the Trump administration, and when it chaired the G20 last year, top US officials, including Trump and Rubio, shunned the meetings it hosted.

“We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary,” Phindile Kunene, a spokesperson for the South African international relations minister, Ronald Lamola, said.

title: Once again, NASA is asking for ideas to rescue Hubble from certain death
author: Stephen Clark
text:
The Hubble Space Telescope still shines in the eyes of astronomers after 36 years in orbit, but it is not as nimble as it once was. Left alone, the observatory will plunge back into the atmosphere in the early-to-mid-2030s, closing the book on one of the most famous scientific instruments of the century.

NASA last raised the orbit of Hubble in 2002, when the Space Shuttle visited the observatory for a servicing mission. The final shuttle servicing flight in 2009 did not reboost the telescope's orbit, and with the retirement of the shuttle fleet two years later, Hubble has steadily lost altitude with no way to stave off eventual destruction.

The space agency released a Request For Information (RFI) on Thursday asking commercial companies for ideas on how to reboost, service, or a controlled disposal of Hubble. Responses are due November 30. Specifically, NASA is looking for information about companies' current and near-term capabilities for capturing Hubble and boosting it to an altitude of at least 373 miles (600 km), enhancing the telescope's performance, or guiding Hubble to a controlled reentry.

title: A top-secret spy mission, a decades-old scandal – and the Austin Powers-esque saga to lift the lid
author: Sarah Basford Canales
text:
Rex Patrick’s latest transparency fight is over what he calls ‘most open secret in the history of Australian spying’ – maybe even the world

Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast

A campaign to uncover any documents relating to whether Australian spies bugged Timor-Leste to gain the upper hand in sensitive oil and gas negotiations will be a little less secret after a critical win by the former senator Rex Patrick.

The politician turned transparency advocate is trying to finally lift the lid on the top-secret mission in 2004 that became a public scandal years later after an ex-spy and a former attorney general attempted to mount a case in The Hague .

But the Australian government stands by its Glomar response – to neither confirm nor deny first that the bugging took place and second that any relevant documents exist.

On Friday, the administrative review tribunal (ART) ruled in Patrick’s favour, forcing the commonwealth to hold unclassified parts of the three-day hearing in late November in public.

Government lawyers argued the whole saga is so sensitive that even sections of the hearing open to the public should remain behind closed doors in case someone accidentally says something they shouldn’t.

Patrick told Guardian Australia the situation was a farce, arguing the bugging scandal is the “most open secret in the history of Australian spying”, maybe even the world.

Patrick’s bid to gain further insight into the affair began with a request for cabinet documents from 2004 held by the National Archives of Australia.

The Australian government’s position, along with the responsible agency, the Australian Secret Intelligence Service (Asis), remains that any such documents cannot be publicly confirmed or denied.

Asis contends that alone the records could undermine national security and Australia’s standings with other countries.

The documents would relate to Australia’s strategy for settling how much of the Timor Sea it could maintain control over after Timor-Leste officially gained independence from Indonesia in 2002.

The negotiations determined the countries’ shared control over the Greater Sunrise gasfields, which hold resources estimated to be worth more than $50bn.

Patrick’s win on Friday means at least some of the government’s defence over why it cannot publicly reveal details of the 2004 bugging – which preceded to a commercially favourable agreement for Australia against the impoverished nation – will be heard in public.

At a preliminary ART hearing last week to rule on whether part of the hearings should remain open, lawyers for the archives argued the matter is so sensitive that even sections of the hearing open to the public should remain behind closed doors in case someone accidentally says something they shouldn’t.

Parts of the hearing will already remain closed so top-secret details can be debated, but the commonwealth had argued the open hearings should also be debated in secret.

The commonwealth unsuccessfully proposed the media and the public should be barred from the open hearings but would be able to view a transcript after careful review by the nation’s foreign intelligence agency.

The deputy chief solicitor, Justin Davidson, argued last Thursday the stakes are “very high” and it would be nearly impossible to mitigate the risk of an intelligence official revealing something they shouldn’t.

“I’m not, frankly, beyond making a mistake,” Davidson said.

Ewan McMillan, an Asis deputy director general, and Michelle Chan, a deputy secretary at the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (Dfat), will offer their testimonies in late November when the case is heard in full.

Davidson had argued the unclassified details they share in an open hearing might be “interesting to the public” but not necessarily in the public interest.

On Friday, the ART deputy president Peter Britten-Jones ruled against the commonwealth, noting officials were “highly qualified and experienced” enough not to let national secrets slip in an open forum.

“The risk of an inadvertent disclosure of certificated material is negligible,” he wrote in his ruling.

Patrick said the whole administrative saga felt like a replay of an Austin Powers movie.

“Only Asis and Dfat think the operation is still a secret,” Patrick said.

“It’d be funny if it wasn’t so serious, or if the taxpayer wasn’t paying for the silk, barristers and lawyers arguing the government’s case.”

Patrick’s latest push to reveal historical documents, or at least the existence of them, comes after years of attempts.

In 2021, the former senator took the archives to the tribunal for heavily redacting a cabinet submission from 2000 outlining Australia’s negotiating strategy for bartering with its impoverished ally on the Timor Sea maritime boundary and a related minute.

The negotiations, which predated the bugging scandal by four years, were critical for Timor-Leste and Australia, because they dictated access to the Greater Sunrise gasfields.

The tribunal later released the document with fewer redactions, which showed cabinet in 2000 was concerned that Timor-Leste’s independence process may disrupt access to the oil and gas reserves in the Timor Sea, because Australia’s prior agreement with Indonesia for a 50/50 revenue split would be void.

The bugging operation occurred in 2004 when Asis operatives planted listening devices in key Timor-Leste government offices to uncover Timor-Leste’s bottom line, its negotiating tactics and the competing views of cabinet members.

In 2006, Australia ended up securing a 50/50 split of the Greater Sunrise fields, positioned 450km north-west of Darwin and 150km south of Timor-Leste. The deal was a boon for the joint venture of multinationals , led by Woodside, seeking to exploit the Timor Sea.…
